look up the digit's value, 0 to 15
repeat until the digit is used up
add the lowest bit (1 or 0) to the running count
shift the digit right by one bit

blocks.text: Run it with `0xfffffe00` (a /23) and `0xfffff800` (a /21). Reading that loop is a good exercise in what a mask is: the number of leading 1 bits.
The one-line "who am I on the network"
Combine the pieces and you have the report every troubleshooting session starts with. Break it into variables first, so each piece can be tested:

blocks.code:
iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr "$iface")
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
print "$iface  $ip  via $gw"

blocks.text: If you are offline, `iface` is empty and the next line misbehaves. A script must check for that, which is why the project below begins with a guard. The `myvalues` widget on this page can read the same facts: paste the output of the commands it suggests and it fills in `{{iface}}`, `{{myip}}`, `{{gateway}}`, `{{dns}}` and `{{subnet}}` across the whole book.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Using `en0` blindly.** On a Mac mini or a laptop on a dock, `en0` may be Ethernet and Wi-Fi may be `en1`. Derive the interface from the default route, as above.
**Reading `inet` when you meant `inet6`.** `grep inet` matches both. Use `/inet /` with the trailing space, or `ifconfig en0 inet`.
**Trusting `networksetup -getdnsservers`.** It shows manual settings only. `scutil --dns` shows what the resolver really uses.
**Treating `169.254.x.x` as an address.** It means DHCP failed and the Mac assigned itself a link-local address. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshoot).
**Comparing MAC strings from different tools.** `arp` drops leading zeros, `ifconfig` keeps them, and routers may print upper case. Normalise first.
**Forgetting that the cache is a cache.** A device missing from `arp -a` may be alive and simply not contacted lately.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Label a real ifconfig block

task.text: Read this sample and answer the questions. It is from a MacBook on Wi-Fi with a VPN client running.

task.code:
$ ifconfig
lo0: flags=8049<UP,LOOPBACK,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 16384
	inet 127.0.0.1 netmask 0xff000000
	inet6 ::1 prefixlen 128
en0: flags=8863<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 3e:5a:c0:12:9b:77
	inet6 fe80::1c3a:7d4e:9f21:5a6b%en0 prefixlen 64 secured scopeid 0xe
	inet 10.0.20.134 netmask 0xfffffc00 broadcast 10.0.23.255
	media: autoselect
	status: active
en1: flags=8822<BROADCAST,SMART,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 6a:11:22:33:44:55
	media: autoselect (none)
	status: inactive
awdl0: flags=8943<UP,BROADCAST,RUNNING,PROMISC,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
	ether 8e:77:1f:aa:c4:02
	inet6 fe80::8c77:1fff:feaa:c402%awdl0 prefixlen 64 scopeid 0x10
utun4: flags=8051<UP,POINTOPOINT,RUNNING,MULTICAST> mtu 1380
	inet 172.16.55.9 --> 172.16.55.9 netmask 0xffffffff

items.text: Which interface is the Wi-Fi connection, and how do you know it has a link?
What is the prefix length of the `en0` subnet, and what is the subnet's broadcast address?
Is `en1` in use?
What does `utun4` tell you?
Does the `ether` on `en0` look like a factory address?

hints: A mask of `0xfffffc00` has 22 one-bits (ff ff fc = 8+8+6). The broadcast address is shown for you.
A locally administered MAC has bit 1 of the first octet set: the first octet's second hex digit is 2, 6, A or E.
blocks.solution:
1. `en0`: `status: active` and the `RUNNING` flag, with an IPv4 address.
2. `0xfffffc00` is /22, so the subnet is `10.0.20.0/22` (10.0.20.0 to 10.0.23.255) and broadcast is `10.0.23.255`.
3. No: `status: inactive`, no addresses, and no `RUNNING` flag.
4. A VPN or tunnel client is connected: `POINTOPOINT`, a small MTU (1380) and an IPv4 address. The "-->" form shows a point-to-point link with no real subnet.
5. No. The first octet `3e` has the "locally administered" bit set (3e in binary ends in ...10), so this is a random, private Wi-Fi address.

why.text: Reading interface blocks quickly means checking four things in order: flags and status (is the link up), the `inet` line (what address and mask), the interface type from its name (physical, tunnel or system), and the MAC (factory or private). The same habit works on any Mac.

blocks.title: Three facts from three commands

task.text: Without typing any address by hand, print on three lines: your default interface, your IPv4 address on that interface, and your gateway. Store each in a variable first, then print them with `print -l` (one argument per line).

hints: The interface comes from `route -n get default`; feed it to `ipconfig getifaddr`.
Use `$( )` to capture each value into `iface`, `ip` and `gw`.
blocks.solution:
iface=$(route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface)
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
print -l "interface: $iface" "address: $ip" "gateway: $gw"

why.text: Each fact has a command that prints it in a fixed place; `awk` selects the line and the field, and `$( )` turns the output into a value. Nothing is hard-coded, so the same lines work on Wi-Fi, Ethernet or a dock.

blocks.title: Hex mask to prefix

task.text: Use the `awk` loop from this chapter on a mask of your own. First run it on `0xffffff00`, then replace it with the real netmask from your Mac by putting an `ifconfig` pipeline in front of it, so it prints something like `192.168.1.23/24`.

hints: Print the address with `$2` and the mask with `$4` from the line containing `inet `.
Keep the mask in an awk variable (`m=$4`) before reusing `$1`-style fields inside the loop.

why.text: The mask is only data until you count its leading ones. The loop converts each hex digit to its bit count; `a` remembers the address so the final `print` can join both pieces.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose

task.text: Run `ipconfig getifaddr en9` (an interface that does not exist) and then `echo $?`. Then write a version of your "my IP" command that never names an interface and still works, and prove it by running it. Finally explain, in one sentence, why a script that did `ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr en9)` and then `ping -c 1 $ip` would behave badly.

hints: A missing interface prints nothing, so `$ip` is empty.
`ping -c 1` with an empty argument prints a usage message instead of probing anything.
blocks.solution:
ipconfig getifaddr en9; echo $?
ipconfig getifaddr $(route -n get default | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')

why.text: The command fails silently with status 1 and no output, so an unchecked variable is empty and the next command runs with a missing argument. Deriving the interface from the default route removes the wrong guess, and checking `$?` or `[[ -n $ip ]]` catches the failure.

blocks.title: Neighbours as numbers

task.text: Using only `arp -an` and the practice terminal or your Mac, print the IP addresses of your neighbours sorted by their last octet, leaving out the broadcast address (the one ending in `.255`) and any `(incomplete)` entries.

hints: Remove parentheses from field 2 with `gsub`.
`sort -t. -k4 -n` sorts numerically on the fourth dot-separated field.
blocks.solution: arp -an | grep -v incomplete | awk '{gsub(/[()]/,"",$2); print $2}' | grep -v '\.255$' | sort -t. -k4 -n

why.text: `arp` prints each IP inside parentheses; `gsub` strips them, `grep -v` removes the lines you do not want, and `sort` with a field separator and key compares the last octet as a number rather than as text.

blocks.title: Which way does this packet go?

task.text: A Mac has this IPv4 routing table: `default via 192.168.1.1 en0`, `192.168.1.0/24 link en0`, `10.8.0.0/24 via 10.8.0.6 utun4`, `10.0.0.0/8 via 10.8.0.6 utun4`. For each destination say which route and interface is used: `192.168.1.77`, `10.8.0.50`, `10.20.30.40`, `93.184.216.34`. Then say which command would confirm your answer for one of them.

hints: The most specific (longest) matching prefix wins.
blocks.solution:
192.168.1.77: the `/24` connected route, out `en0`, delivered directly (ARP for the host).
10.8.0.50: the `10.8.0.0/24` route, via `10.8.0.6` on `utun4` (a /24 is longer than the /8).
10.20.30.40: only `10.0.0.0/8` matches, so via `10.8.0.6` on `utun4`.
93.184.216.34: nothing specific matches, so the default route: `192.168.1.1` on `en0`.
Confirm with `route -n get 10.20.30.40`.

why.text: The kernel compares the destination with every route and picks the longest prefix. `route -n get` applies the same logic and tells you the winning interface and gateway.

questions.q: In `ifconfig` output, what does `netmask 0xffffff00` mean?
questions.why: The mask is written in hex. `ff` is 255, so four octets of `ff ff ff 00` are 255.255.255.0, which is 24 one-bits.

questions.q: Which command answers "which interface would carry traffic to 93.184.216.34"?
questions.why: `route -n get` does a routing lookup for one destination and prints the interface and gateway the kernel would use.

questions.q: `networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi` prints "There aren't any DNS Servers set on Wi-Fi." What is true?

options.text: The Mac has no DNS and cannot resolve names
No DNS servers are set manually; the servers probably came from DHCP
DNS is blocked by the firewall

questions.why: That command shows only manually configured servers. The effective list, including DHCP-supplied servers, is in `scutil --dns`.

questions.q: What is `awdl0`?

options.text: An Apple wireless direct link used for AirDrop and similar features

questions.why: `awdl0` supports AirDrop, AirPlay and Sidecar. It has an IPv6 link-local address only and is not your route to the internet.

questions.q: Which flag in `netstat -rn` means "uses a gateway"?
questions.why: `G` marks routes whose next hop is another router. Connected-subnet routes lack it and show `link#N` as the gateway.

questions.q: Why do MAC addresses from `arp -a` sometimes fail to match ones from your router's page?

options.text: macOS prints octets without leading zeros, and other tools may use upper case
The router uses a different hash

questions.why: `arp` prints `0:11:32:aa:3:5d` for `00:11:32:aa:03:5d`. Pad each octet to two hex digits and lowercase everything before comparing.

blocks.text: You will build two small tools. `netinfo.zsh` prints a clean table of your own network facts. `lan-inventory.zsh` turns the ARP cache into a CSV file. Both grow in later chapters: [Reachability and path](#net-reach) adds timing, [Ports and services](#ports) adds scanning.
Step 1: Collect the facts with a guard
Create `~/lab/netinfo.zsh` (in PyCharm, or with `nano netinfo.zsh`). The first lines refuse to run when you are offline, which prevents every later line from running on empty variables.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# netinfo.zsh - one-screen summary of this Mac's network
setopt pipefail

mask2prefix() {
  print -r -- "$1" | awk '{h=substr($1,3); n=0
    for (i=1; i<=length(h); i++) {
      d = index("0123456789abcdef", substr(h,i,1)) - 1
      while (d > 0) { n += d % 2; d = int(d/2) }
    }
    print n}'
}

iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
if [[ -z $iface ]]; then
  print -u2 "netinfo: no default route; are you connected?"
  exit 1
fi

ip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface)
gw=$(route -n get default | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
mac=$(ifconfig $iface | awk '/ether/ {print $2}')
mask=$(ifconfig $iface | awk '/netmask/ {print $4}')
dns=$(scutil --dns | awk '/nameserver\[[0-9]+\]/ {print $3}' | sort -u | paste -sd, -)
port=$(networksetup -listallhardwareports | awk -v d=$iface '/^Hardware Port/ {p=substr($0,16)} $1=="Device:" && $2==d {print p}')
host=$(scutil --get LocalHostName 2>/dev/null)

blocks.text: Step 2: Print a table
Append this to the end of `netinfo.zsh`. `printf` with `%-12s` pads each label to the same width.

blocks.code:
printf '%-12s %s\n' \
  "Host"      "${host:-unknown}.local" \
  "Interface" "$iface (${port:-?})" \
  "Address"   "$ip/$(mask2prefix $mask)" \
  "Gateway"   "$gw" \
  "MAC"       "$mac" \
  "DNS"       "${dns:-none}"
chmod +x netinfo.zsh && ./netinfo.zsh

blocks.title: Make the output feed another tool

blocks.text: Add a `-j` flag in your next version that prints the same values as `key=value` lines, so another script can `source` or `grep` them. That is the shape of a useful tool: a human view and a machine view of the same data.
Step 3: Turn the ARP cache into an inventory

`lan-inventory.zsh` starts small. It reads `arp -a`, normalises each MAC (padding the octets, lower case), skips broadcast and incomplete entries, and writes a CSV with a header. Because the cache only holds recent neighbours, the file starts as a list of devices you have already talked to.

blocks.code: chmod +x lan-inventory.zsh && ./lan-inventory.zsh && column -s, -t inventory.csv

blocks.text: Step 4: Fill the cache first

The inventory is only as complete as the cache. Touch every address on your subnet once, then run it again. The sweep itself belongs to the next chapter; for now, ping the gateway and one or two devices you know, and compare the before and after row counts. Where does a device with a `?` name get its name later? That question is answered in [DNS](#dns).

Add a column for the vendor using the first three octets (the OUI, see [Addressing](#addressing)) from a small lookup table of your own. Skip addresses ending in `.255`. Make the script print the count of entries per interface.
Try it in the practice terminal

The practice terminal knows the lab network: your Mac is `192.168.1.23`, the router is `192.168.1.1`, and the Pi, NAS, printer and Home Assistant box answer in the ARP cache. It supports `ifconfig`, `ipconfig`, `route`, `netstat`, `arp`, `scutil` and `networksetup` with canned output, which is enough to rehearse every pipeline in this chapter.
Next
You know what your Mac looks like from the inside. Continue to [Reachability and path](#net-reach), where you send packets out and measure how long they take and where they travel.

terms.def: A network attachment point in the kernel, with a name like en0, that sends and receives packets
The priority list of network services in System Settings; the first connected one carries the default route
The %interface suffix on an IPv6 link-local address that says which link it belongs to
A user-space tunnel interface used by VPNs and system features
Apple Wireless Direct Link, the peer-to-peer radio mode behind AirDrop
A routing-table entry for a single address (flag H)
The route for the subnet an interface sits on; its gateway is shown as link#N
The kernel's table of recent IP-to-MAC mappings on the local link
The time-limited right to use an address handed out by a DHCP server
Received signal strength indicator, in dBm; closer to zero is stronger
Signal-to-noise ratio: signal strength minus noise level, in dB
A per-network random MAC address used instead of the hardware one

chapters.title: Reachability, Latency & Path
chapters.sub: Measure whether a host answers, how long it takes, where the packets travel and how big they can be
goals: Read ping output and statistics and explain every number in them
Use traceroute and mtr to locate where on a path latency or loss starts
Compute average, jitter, loss and 95th percentile of round-trip times with awk
Find the path MTU to a host with ping and the Don't Fragment bit
Build latency-log, a script that records round-trip times to CSV and summarises them

blocks.text: [Chapter 12](#net-local) was about what your Mac is. This chapter is about whether it can *reach* something else, how quickly, and by which route. The tools are small and old (`ping` dates from 1983) but they answer the first question in every network investigation: is the problem here, at the next hop, or far away? You will send probes, learn how the probes work so you can interpret the silence as well as the answers, and finish with `latency-log`, a recorder you can leave running while you work.

blocks.title: Probe only what you own or may test

blocks.text: `ping`, `traceroute` and `mtr` send real packets to other machines. Use your own Mac, your LAN, `localhost`, your lab host `{{labhost}}`, and well-known public services such as `example.com` or `1.1.1.1` at low rates. Do not point sweeps or high-rate pings at networks you do not own or have permission to test.
How ping works

`ping` sends an **ICMP echo request** (type 8) to a host. A host that is up, reachable and willing replies with an **ICMP echo reply** (type 0), copying the request's payload back. `ping` records the time between sending and receiving; that is the **round-trip time (RTT)**. ICMP is carried directly inside IP, with no ports: it is not TCP or UDP, which is why `ping` works as a test of the network layer alone.

blocks.code:
your Mac                                                   target
  ┌─────────┐   echo request  type 8, seq=0, 56 data bytes   ┌─────────┐
  │  ping   │ ───────────────────────────────────────────▶   │ kernel  │
  │         │                                                │ answers │
  │  timer  │ ◀───────────────────────────────────────────   │ itself  │
  └─────────┘   echo reply    type 0, seq=0, same payload    └─────────┘
      RTT = reply arrival time - request send time
      (the target's kernel replies, no application is involved)

blocks.text: Because the *kernel* of the target replies, a good ping proves the host is up and the path works in both directions, and says nothing about whether any service (web, SSH) on it is working.

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 3 192.168.1.1
PING 192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.100 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.470 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.890 ms

--- 192.168.1.1 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 1.890/2.153/2.470/0.240 ms

blocks.text: Reading one reply line

tokens.exp: size of the ICMP message: 56 data bytes plus the 8-byte ICMP header (the IP header is not counted)
who answered
the sequence number; starts at 0 on macOS, so a gap means a lost probe
the TTL the reply had on arrival, after losing one per router on the way back
round-trip time in milliseconds

blocks.title: Extracting the time from a reply line

tokens.exp: send probes
five probes, then the summary
the target
pipe the text lines into awk
the text-processing program
field separator is a regular expression: either "=" or a space
run the action only on lines containing "time="
print the second-to-last field; NF is the field count, and the last field is "ms"

blocks.text: The `ttl` value is a clue to distance. Hosts start replies from a round number: 64 (macOS, Linux, most routers), 128 (Windows) or 255 (many network devices). A reply that arrives with `ttl=56` probably started at 64, so it crossed about 8 routers on the way back. A reply from your gateway with `ttl=64` crossed none.
The summary at the end

blocks.code:
--- example.com ping statistics ---
10 packets transmitted, 9 packets received, 10.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.205/12.939/16.102/1.535 ms

items.text: **Packet loss** is the fraction of probes with no reply. Occasional single losses are normal on Wi-Fi and busy paths. Sustained loss above 1 to 2 percent is a problem; 100 percent means either no path or a host that ignores ICMP.
**min/avg/max** show the spread. A min close to the average and a high max means occasional spikes (queues, Wi-Fi retries). A high min means the whole path is slow.
**stddev** is the standard deviation of the RTTs, which you can read as a rough **jitter**. Linux calls the same field `mdev`.

blocks.text: When there is no answer, macOS prints `Request timeout for icmp_seq 5` and the probe counts as lost. Hosts can drop ICMP on purpose; firewalls and cloud hosts often do. A ping that fails does not prove the host is down. Confirm with a TCP test such as `nc -z -w 3 host 443` or `curl -sI host`, covered in [Ports and services](#ports).

blocks.name: ping
blocks.sum: Send ICMP echo requests to a host and report replies, round-trip times and loss.
blocks.syntax: ping [-c count] [-i seconds] [-s bytes] [-t timeout] [-W ms] [-D] [-n] [-q] [-o] [-S src] [-b iface] host

how.text: `ping` opens an ICMP socket (the binary is installed with the privilege it needs, so you do not run it as root), sends one echo request per interval, each with an incrementing sequence number and a timestamp in the payload, and prints a line for each reply. When you press Ctrl-C, or when `-c` probes are done, it prints the statistics.

The exit status is useful in scripts: **0** means at least one reply came back, **2** means the packets were sent but nothing answered, and any other value (for example **68**, "unknown host") means an error such as a name that does not resolve.

flags.d: Stop after N probes. Without it, `ping` runs until Ctrl-C.
Seconds between probes (default 1). Fractions work; intervals below 0.1 s need root on macOS.
Size of the data part. Default 56. Used with `-D` for MTU discovery.
Exit after s **seconds** in total, whatever has been received. A script's safety net.
How long to wait for each reply, in **milliseconds** on macOS (it is seconds on Linux).
Set the Don't Fragment bit in the IP header.
Numeric output only; do not resolve names for replies.
Quiet: print only the header and the summary.
Exit successfully after the first reply. A fast "is it up?" check.
Use this source address, which must be one of your own. Useful when you have several.
Send out of the named interface (macOS addition).

examples.desc: Four probes to a host
examples.out:
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=11.842 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=1 ttl=56 time=12.310 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=2 ttl=56 time=11.205 ms
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=3 ttl=56 time=14.987 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.205/12.586/14.987/1.441 ms

examples.desc: A quick up-or-down test for a script

anat.exp: flag: four probes, then print statistics
target: a name or an address

examples.desc: Average round-trip time only
Packet loss percentage only
Just the time values, one per line

gotchas: `-W` is milliseconds on macOS and seconds on Linux. A copied Linux command with `-W 2` waits two milliseconds here and reports everything as lost. Use `-W 2000`.
With `-c 1` and a dead host, `ping` can wait a long time before giving up. Add `-t 2` so it always returns.
Short intervals send faster than most links want. Keep `-i` at 0.2 or more unless you are testing your own gear.

blocks.text: Why ICMP deserves respect
ICMP is not only echo. It is how IP reports problems, and each message type teaches you something about the path.

head: Type
Name
When you see it
rows: code 0 network, 1 host, 3 port, 4 fragmentation needed but DF set, 13 administratively prohibited
a router tells you a better first hop exists
a router decremented TTL to 0 (code 0); the basis of `traceroute`

blocks.text: Types 3 and 11 matter most here. Type 11 is how `traceroute` finds each router. Type 3 code 4 is how path MTU discovery works, and its absence is a classic cause of connections that hang on large transfers.
Latency, jitter, loss and bandwidth
These four words are often mixed up. They are independent, and a connection can be good at one and poor at another.

head: Metric
What it measures
Typical good values
Hurts
rows: time for a packet to go there and back
under 5 ms on a LAN, 10 to 40 ms to a nearby service, 100+ ms across oceans
variation of latency between consecutive packets
probes that never get a reply
everything, because TCP retransmits and slows down
how many bits per second the link can carry

blocks.text: A fast link (high bandwidth) can still feel slow if its RTT is high, because each request waits a full round trip: loading a page that needs 30 sequential requests at 100 ms RTT takes 3 seconds before any data transfer time. Distance sets a floor: light in fibre travels about 200 km per millisecond, so 1000 km costs at least 5 ms each way.
Jitter has several definitions. A simple one for scripts is the **mean absolute difference between consecutive RTTs**, which you can compute from a ping log with `awk` in a few lines.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log
11.842
12.310
11.205
14.987
12.044
13.551
11.930
16.102
12.477
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {t=$(NF-1); if (n++) {d=t-prev; if (d<0) d=-d; s+=d}; prev=t} END {printf "jitter=%.3f ms\n", s/(n-1)}' ping.log
jitter=2.403 ms

blocks.text: The first command shows the pipeline stage you will reuse all chapter: split each line on `=` and spaces, and the second-to-last field is the number of milliseconds, because the line ends with the word `ms`. The second command is the jitter formula: remember the previous time, add the absolute difference, divide by one less than the number of samples.
Statistics from a ping log
`ping.log` in your lab is a saved `ping -c 10` run with one lost probe. It is a good dataset for the shape every latency report takes: **extract the numbers, then reduce them.**

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}' ping.log
10.0%
$ grep -c 'Request timeout' ping.log
1
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {t=$(NF-1); s+=t; n++; if (min==""||t<min) min=t; if (t>max) max=t} END {printf "n=%d min=%.3f avg=%.3f max=%.3f\n", n, min, s/n, max}' ping.log
n=9 min=11.205 avg=12.939 max=16.102

blocks.text: The `awk` reducer keeps four variables: a running sum, a count, a minimum and a maximum. Because awk variables start empty, `min==""` is the "first sample" test. This is the template for every statistic in the chapter.
Percentiles need sorting

An average hides spikes. The **95th percentile (p95)** answers "95 percent of the probes were at or below this time", and it is how latency is usually reported. To compute it with the **nearest-rank** method, sort the values and take the one at position ceil(0.95 × n).

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; print "p95 =", v[p]}'
p95 = 16.102

blocks.text: Read it as two programs: the first `awk` extracts, `sort -n` orders numerically, and the second `awk` stores every value in an array indexed by line number. `END` runs after the last line, when `NR` holds the count. The `int(...)` followed by a conditional increment is how you round up in awk, which has no `ceil`.
`sort` without `-n` compares text, so `9.5` sorts after `12.3` because `9` is greater than `1`. Any pipeline that sorts numbers needs `sort -n`, or `sort -g` for floating point with exponents.
Recipes: ping in a pipeline
These are the shapes you will reuse. Each is one sentence of purpose plus a pipeline.

**Ping every host in `hosts.txt` and rank by average RTT.** Loop with `while read`, capture the average, print it with the name, sort numerically. Hosts that do not answer get `9999` so they sort last.

blocks.code:
while read -r h; do
  avg=$(ping -c 3 -t 4 -W 1000 "$h" 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {print $5}')
  print "${avg:-9999} $h"
done < hosts.txt | sort -n

blocks.text: **Timestamp every reply.** A pipe into a `while read` loop lets you prepend anything to each line. This gives you a log you can line up with other events.

blocks.code: ping -c 10 {{host}} | while IFS= read -r line; do print "$(date '+%H:%M:%S') $line"; done

blocks.text: **Alert when a reply is slow.** `-v max=50` passes a value into awk as a variable. The pattern selects reply lines whose time exceeds it, and the action prints the sequence number (field 6 after splitting on `=` and spaces) and the time.

blocks.code: ping -c 20 {{host}} | awk -F'[= ]' -v max=50 '/time=/ && $(NF-1) > max {print "SLOW", $(NF-1), "ms at seq", $6}'

blocks.text: **Sweep a /24 for live hosts.** `seq` generates the last octet, `xargs -P` runs many pings in parallel, and a successful ping prints its address. Sixty-four at a time finishes in a few seconds. Run it only on your own LAN. Change `192.168.1` to the first three octets of your subnet.

A side effect is useful: every host that answered is now in your ARP cache, so `arp -an` immediately after the sweep lists devices that did not answer ping but did answer ARP (many phones and printers block ICMP and still answer ARP). That is the idea behind `lan-inventory`, which you started in [See your own network](#net-local).

blocks.title: Why ARP finds more than ping

blocks.text: A host on your subnet must answer ARP for traffic to reach it at all; a firewall that blocks ICMP does not stop ARP. After a sweep, run `arp -an | grep -v incomplete`. Hosts that appear with a MAC but did not print in the sweep are alive and filtering ping.
TTL and traceroute

Every IP packet has a **TTL** (time to live) field. Each router decrements it by one and drops the packet when it reaches zero, sending back an ICMP *time exceeded* message from its own address. The design protects against routing loops. `traceroute` turns the safety mechanism into a map by sending probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on, and collecting the replies.

blocks.code:
TTL=1  ──▶ [router 1] ✗ TTL hits 0 ──▶ "time exceeded" from router 1 address
  TTL=2  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ✗ ──▶ "time exceeded" from router 2 address
  TTL=3  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ──▶ [router 3] ✗ ──▶ ... from router 3
  TTL=4  ──▶ [router 1] ──▶ [router 2] ──▶ [router 3] ──▶ [destination]
                                                            │
        UDP probes: destination answers "port unreachable" (type 3 code 3) ◀┘
        ICMP probes (-I): destination answers "echo reply"

blocks.text: By default macOS `traceroute` sends **UDP** datagrams to a high port starting at 33434. Routers on the way answer with *time exceeded*; the destination, which has nothing listening there, answers *port unreachable*, which tells `traceroute` it has arrived. With `-I` it sends ICMP echo requests instead, which more networks permit.
Reading it:

items.text: Each line is one hop: the hop number, then the address (or name) of the router that answered, then the RTT of each of the three probes (`-q 3` by default).
**Hop 1** is your gateway, `192.168.1.1`. Hops 2 to 5 are your ISP's network. A private address like `10.34.0.1` at hop 2 is normal inside an ISP.

**Hop 4 shows `* * *`.** No reply within the 5 second wait. That is often not a fault: many routers forward traffic perfectly well but are configured not to send time-exceeded messages, or rate-limit them. If later hops answer, as hop 5 does, the path is fine.

**Hop 6 jumps from 11 ms to 96 ms and stays high through the destination.** A *persistent* jump marks a long link (a transatlantic hop, a congested peering point). A spike at one hop that disappears at the next means that router was slow to *answer* ICMP, not slow to *forward*.
The path shown is the path **to** the destination. The reply path can differ (asymmetric routing), so a bad hop might be on the way back.

blocks.name: traceroute
blocks.sum: Show the routers between you and a destination by sending probes with increasing TTL.
blocks.syntax: traceroute [-I] [-n] [-m max_ttl] [-q nqueries] [-w seconds] [-P proto] [-a] [-f first_ttl] [-S] host

how.text: `traceroute` sends groups of probes, three per TTL value by default. Each router that discards a probe returns an ICMP *time exceeded* message whose source address identifies that hop, and the program prints the time between sending the probe and receiving that message. It stops when the destination answers or when `-m` (maximum hops, 64 by default on macOS) is reached.

Per-hop times are not independent measurements of that link. They include the router's own delay in generating the message, which can be slow because it is done by the router's control plane. Compare the *trend* across hops rather than one number.

flags.d: Do not resolve addresses to names. Much faster, and avoids confusing reverse-DNS names.
Maximum number of hops (TTL) to try.
Probes per hop (default 3). `-q 1` is faster and easier to parse.
Seconds to wait for each reply (default 5). Lower it to finish faster when hops are silent.
Use ICMP echo instead of UDP probes.
Probe protocol: `udp`, `tcp`, `icmp` and others by name or number.
Start at TTL N, skipping the first N-1 hops (for example `-f 2` to skip your own router).
Look up the autonomous-system number for each hop.
Print a summary of unanswered probes per hop.

examples.desc: Trace the path numerically with ICMP probes
Fast, parseable trace: one probe per hop, short wait

anat.exp: wait at most 2 seconds per probe

examples.desc: The list of hop addresses, one per line (a `*` marks a silent hop)
Find the hop where RTT jumps the most
examples.code: traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 {{host}} | awk '$3+0>0 {d=$3-prev; if (d>maxd) {maxd=d; hop=$1" "$2}; prev=$3} END {print "largest jump:", maxd, "ms at hop", hop}'

gotchas: `* * *` is not proof of a fault. Trust the pattern: if nothing answers after some hop to the end, the path is blocked there; if later hops answer, the silent router merely ignores ICMP.
Some networks drop UDP probes but allow ICMP. If the default trace dies early, try `-I`; if ICMP mode reports a permission error on your system, run it with `sudo`.
notes: Annotations after a time such as `!H` (host unreachable), `!N` (network unreachable), `!X` (administratively prohibited) or `!` alone mean the reply carried an error or an unusual TTL. `man traceroute` lists them.

blocks.text: IPv6 has its own binaries on macOS: `ping6` and `traceroute6`, used like their IPv4 counterparts, for example `ping6 -c 3 2606:4700:4700::1111`. They are separate commands, not flags. If a site resolves to both address families, `ping` and `traceroute` use IPv4 and the `6` variants use IPv6, so test both when something is slow only on one.
Parsing a trace
`traceroute -n -q 1` prints one probe per hop, which makes each line a fixed shape: hop number, address, time. Pipelines get easy.

blocks.code:
$ traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 example.com | awk '{print $2}'
192.168.1.1
10.34.0.1
81.139.72.5
*
62.172.103.40
203.0.113.9
93.184.216.34
$ traceroute -n -q 1 -w 2 example.com | awk '$3+0>0 {d=$3-prev; if (d>maxd) {maxd=d; hop=$1" "$2}; prev=$3} END {print "largest jump:", maxd, "ms at hop", hop}'
largest jump: 85.375 ms at hop 6 203.0.113.9

blocks.text: The second command ignores silent hops (their third field is not a number), keeps the previous hop's time, and remembers the hop with the greatest increase. It is a one-line answer to "where did it get slow", and it matches what you read by eye above.
mtr: ping and traceroute together

`mtr` (my traceroute) runs a traceroute continuously, sending many probes to every hop, and shows loss and latency statistics per hop. One trace is a single snapshot; `mtr` shows the pattern over time, which is what you need to catch a congested or lossy link.

blocks.code: brew install mtr

blocks.title: mtr needs root and a path entry

blocks.text: `mtr` opens raw sockets, so it must run as root: `sudo mtr ...`. Homebrew installs it into `/opt/homebrew/sbin`, which `brew shellenv` adds to your `PATH` (see [Setup](#setup)). If `sudo mtr` says command not found, `sudo` is using a restricted path; run it with the full path, `sudo /opt/homebrew/sbin/mtr ...`.
How to read the report:

items.text: **Loss%** is per hop. Look at the **last** hop first. If the final hop shows 0 percent, the loss at hop 4 and hop 5 is routers refusing to answer probes, not lost traffic: your packets to hop 7 all got through.
Loss that **starts at one hop and continues to every later hop** is real. That is where traffic is being dropped.
**Snt** is probes sent; **Last, Avg, Best, Wrst** are in milliseconds; **StDev** is the spread, a jitter estimate.
A large **Wrst** next to a small **Avg** means rare spikes. A jump in **Avg** between hops that persists is the long link, as in traceroute.

blocks.name: mtr
blocks.sum: Continuously probe every hop on the path and report loss and latency statistics per hop.
blocks.syntax: sudo mtr [-r] [-w] [-n] [-c count] [-i seconds] [-T] [-P port] [-u] [-b] [-4|-6] host

how.text: `mtr` combines `traceroute` and `ping`. It first discovers the path with increasing TTL, then keeps sending probes to every hop in parallel, updating loss and latency statistics as replies arrive. In its interactive display (just `sudo mtr host`) the numbers update live; press `q` to quit. In **report mode** (`-r`) it sends `-c` rounds, prints a table and exits, which is what you capture into a file or paste into a support ticket.
By default `mtr` sends ICMP echo probes. When ICMP is filtered on the path, `-T` (TCP) with `-P 443` sends TCP SYN probes to a port that is allowed, and often gets a clearer picture.

flags.d: Report mode: run `-c` rounds, print a table, exit.
Wide report: do not truncate host names.
Numeric: skip reverse-DNS lookups.
Number of rounds (probes per hop) to send.
Seconds between rounds (default 1).
Use TCP SYN probes instead of ICMP (combine with `-P port`).
Use UDP probes.
Show both hostnames and IP addresses.
Force IPv4 or IPv6.

examples.desc: A 20-round report you can save
Probe with TCP port 443 when ICMP is filtered

anat.exp: report mode, wide, numeric, 20 rounds (flags can be bundled)

examples.desc: Which hops lose packets, with their loss percentage
Last hop's average latency

gotchas: Loss at an intermediate hop that does not continue to the last hop is ICMP rate limiting. Judge by the last hop.
`sudo mtr` can fail with "command not found" because `sudo` resets `PATH`. Use `sudo /opt/homebrew/sbin/mtr`.
notes: Column positions differ with options like `-b`. Print the report once and count columns before you trust an `awk` field number.

blocks.text: Other probes exist for special cases. `nping` (part of the `nmap` package) and `hping3` craft custom probes such as TCP SYN pings, and `arping` (`brew install arping`) pings at the ARP layer, which works even when ICMP is blocked. They are optional and used in [Ports and services](#ports); the three tools above cover nearly all daily work.
MTU: how big can a packet be

Every link has a **maximum transmission unit (MTU)**, the largest IP packet it carries. Ethernet is 1500 bytes. VPNs, PPPoE (a common DSL encapsulation) and tunnels add headers and therefore have smaller MTUs (1492, 1420, 1380 are common). If a packet is larger than a link's MTU, a router either **fragments** it into pieces or, if the packet has the **Don't Fragment (DF)** bit set, drops it and sends back ICMP type 3 code 4 (*fragmentation needed*) with the MTU it could take. TCP sets DF on its segments and relies on those ICMP messages to learn the **path MTU**. Firewalls that drop all ICMP break that mechanism, and large transfers then stall while small ones work: the "MTU black hole".
You can find the path MTU with `ping -D -s SIZE`. The `-s` value is the **data** size. The IP packet is that plus 8 bytes of ICMP header plus 20 bytes of IP header, 28 bytes in all.

blocks.code:
IP packet limit (MTU)            1500
   - IP header                       -20
   - ICMP header                      -8
   ------------------------------------
   largest ping payload              1472     ping -D -s 1472 host

blocks.title: Measuring the largest packet that fits

tokens.exp: send probes
a single probe is enough for a yes/no answer
set the Don't Fragment bit, so a too-big packet is dropped instead of split
data bytes; with 28 bytes of headers this makes a 1500-byte packet
give up after 3 seconds in total
the target

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1472 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 1472 data bytes
1480 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=12.9 ms

$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1473 example.com
PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 1473 data bytes
ping: sendto: Message too long

--- example.com ping statistics ---
1 packets transmitted, 0 packets received, 100.0% packet loss

blocks.text: The second run fails locally because 1473 + 28 = 1501 exceeds your own interface's MTU. When the limit is further along the path, you instead get a timeout or an ICMP error, depending on whether the router sends the message. The largest size that works, plus 28, is your path MTU. A loop makes the search automatic:

blocks.code:
host={{host}}
for size in 1472 1452 1432 1412 1392 1372 1272; do
  if ping -c 1 -D -s $size -t 3 -W 1500 $host > /dev/null 2>&1; then
    print "payload $size works: path MTU is $(( size + 28 ))"
    break
  else
    print "payload $size fails"
  fi
done

blocks.text: If 1472 works, you have a standard 1500-byte path. If only a smaller size works, a tunnel or PPPoE link is reducing it, and your VPN or router may need an explicit MSS clamp or MTU setting.

Fragmentation moves work to routers and to the receiver, and a single lost fragment loses the whole packet. Modern stacks avoid it with path MTU discovery: send with DF set, shrink on ICMP feedback. IPv6 routers do not fragment at all; the sender must discover the path MTU, so a filtered ICMPv6 "packet too big" message causes the same black hole more severely.
networkQuality: bandwidth and responsiveness

Apple ships a speed test, `networkQuality` (macOS 12 and later). It measures **capacity** (upload and download throughput) and a newer metric, **responsiveness**: how many round trips per minute the connection can complete *while it is saturated*. A line can have high capacity and low responsiveness if its buffers fill under load (bufferbloat), which is what makes a video call stutter when someone starts a download.

blocks.name: networkQuality
blocks.sum: Measure upload and download capacity, idle latency and responsiveness under load, using Apple's test servers.

how.text: `networkQuality` downloads and uploads data from an Apple-run server while also measuring round-trip latency, in parallel by default or one direction at a time with `-s`. It reports how fast the link is, how long a single idle round trip takes, and the **responsiveness** score in round-trips per minute (RPM): above about 1000 RPM is good, below 200 will make interactive use feel sluggish under load.

The test deliberately saturates the connection for around 20 seconds, so run it when you are not in a call. The text layout of the report has changed between macOS releases and shows capacity as `Downlink capacity` and `Uplink capacity` in newer versions.

flags.d: Run upload and download sequentially rather than at the same time.
Verbose: more detail about each measurement.
Computer-readable output (JSON) for scripts.
Bind the test to an interface, for example `en0`, to compare Wi-Fi with Ethernet.
Use a different configuration URL (for a self-hosted server).
Use iCloud Private Relay for the test.
Disable certificate validation.
Connect to this host or IP, overriding DNS for the initial configuration request.

examples.desc: A normal test
Test one interface only and save the JSON
See which fields the JSON contains before you parse it
Pretty-print a saved result

gotchas: The test uses a lot of bandwidth for its duration. On metered or tethered connections, think first.
Results from a Mac on Wi-Fi measure your Wi-Fi link plus the internet. To isolate the internet, repeat the test over Ethernet or `-I` another interface.

blocks.text: Run `ping -c 20 1.1.1.1` in one tab and `networkQuality` in another at the same time. Watch the ping times climb while the test saturates the link. The size of that climb is the bufferbloat, and it is why responsiveness is reported separately from capacity.
Common mistakes

items.text: **Treating a failed ping as a dead host.** Filtering ICMP is common. Confirm with a TCP test.
**Reading one traceroute hop as the truth.** Per-hop times include the router's own delay. Look at the trend and use `mtr` for loss.
**Alarm over `* * *`.** Judge by whether later hops answer.
**Using Linux flags on macOS.** `ping -W 2` and `ping -w 5` mean different things; `traceroute -w` is seconds, `ping -W` is milliseconds.
**Averaging without looking.** One 900 ms outlier among 100 samples moves the mean; report p95 and max too.
**Comparing tests made on different interfaces.** Wi-Fi to Ethernet differs by more than the internet does. Name the interface in every result.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Loss from a saved run

task.text: From `ping.log` in the lab, print only the packet loss percentage (for example `10.0%`), then separately count how many probes timed out using a different pattern. Both numbers must agree.

hints: The statistics line contains the word `loss`. Percent is field 7 on that line.
`grep -c` counts matching lines.
blocks.solution:
awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}' ping.log
grep -c 'Request timeout' ping.log

why.text: `awk` with a pattern selects one line and prints one field. The loss line says 10.0 percent of 10 packets, and exactly one `Request timeout` line exists, so the two views agree.

blocks.title: Five numbers from ping.log

task.text: Print `n`, `min`, `avg`, `max` and `p95` for the reply times in `ping.log` on one line each or as one summary line. Do not use the statistics line already printed by ping; compute from the individual replies.

hints: Extract the times with `awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}'`.
Sort numerically, then use `v[NR]` and `END` for the percentile; sums and counts need no sort.
blocks.solution: awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print $(NF-1)}' ping.log | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1; s+=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; printf "n=%d min=%.3f avg=%.3f max=%.3f p95=%.3f\n", NR, v[1], s/NR, v[NR], v[p]}'

why.text: After sorting, the first value is the minimum and the last is the maximum. The array lets `END` pick the element at the 95th-percentile rank, and the running sum gives the mean.

blocks.title: Path MTU on purpose

task.text: Break it, then measure it. First run `ping -c 1 -D -s 1473 example.com` and read the error. Then find the largest payload that works to `example.com` by trying sizes, and print the path MTU. Finally say what MTU you would expect from a VPN that shows `mtu 1380` on its `utun` interface.

hints: Payload plus 28 is the packet size. The error `Message too long` is local: the packet exceeds your own MTU.
Try 1472, then smaller values in steps of 20 until one works.
blocks.solution:
ping -c 1 -D -s 1473 example.com
ping -c 1 -D -s 1472 -t 3 example.com

why.text: 1473 + 28 is 1501, one byte over a 1500-byte link, so the kernel refuses to send. If 1472 works the path MTU is 1500. Through a VPN with `mtu 1380`, the largest ping payload is 1380 - 28 = 1352.

blocks.title: Rank your hosts by latency

task.text: For every name in `hosts.txt`, print the average RTT of three pings next to the name, fastest first. Hosts that do not answer must still appear, at the bottom. Remember: `ping -W` is milliseconds and a dead host can take long to give up.

hints: Use a `while read -r h` loop that reads from `hosts.txt`.
Use `${avg:-9999}` so missing values sort last, and `sort -n` at the end.
blocks.solution:
while read -r h; do
  avg=$(ping -c 3 -t 4 -W 1000 "$h" 2>/dev/null | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {print $5}')
  print "${avg:-9999} $h"
done < hosts.txt | sort -n

why.text: Each loop pass produces one line. A failed ping leaves `avg` empty, so the default `9999` pushes it to the end after the numeric sort. `-t 4` guarantees the loop cannot hang on a dead host.

blocks.title: Where does it get slow?

task.text: Here is a trace from a laptop in a cafe to a web server.

items.text: Is the silent hop 2 a fault?
Where does the latency first become large, and is it persistent?
What does hop 6 tell you?
Which tool would you run next to decide whether any packets are being lost?

hints: Compare hop 6 with hops 5 and 7.
blocks.solution:
1. No. Traffic gets through to hop 3 and beyond, so hop 2 only declines to answer.
2. At hop 3 (3.2 ms to 48.6 ms) and it stays at about 50 ms to the end, so there is a persistent extra delay of about 45 ms after the first hop. That is typical of a mobile or shared uplink such as a phone hotspot (172.20.10.x) and CGNAT (100.64.x.x).
3. Hop 6 spikes to 189 ms but hops 7 and 8 are back to 54 ms. The router at hop 6 is slow to *answer* ICMP; it forwards normally, so it is not the problem.
4. `sudo mtr -rwnc 30 198.51.100.20`, looking at loss at the final hop.

why.text: Persistent increases that carry through to the destination reflect real delay on the path. A spike at a single hop that disappears afterwards is router control-plane delay. Silence is not loss unless it continues to the end.

blocks.title: Break the timeout

task.text: `192.0.2.1` is in the TEST-NET-1 documentation range and is never routed on the internet. Ping it with `ping -c 2 -t 4 192.0.2.1`, then print the exit status. Then ping a name that does not exist, such as `nohost.invalid`, and print that exit status. Explain the two numbers.

hints: `echo $?` immediately after the command shows its exit status.
blocks.solution:
ping -c 2 -t 4 192.0.2.1; echo $?
ping -c 1 nohost.invalid; echo $?

why.text: The first run sends packets that nobody answers and exits with status 2 ("sent, no reply"). The second fails before sending anything because the name does not resolve, so ping reports an error, status 68 on macOS. A script can tell "unreachable" from "mistyped name" by the status.

questions.q: What does `ping -W 1000` set on macOS?

options.text: A wait of 1000 milliseconds for each reply

questions.why: On macOS `-W` is the per-reply wait in milliseconds. Linux uses seconds for the same flag, a common source of copy-paste errors.

questions.q: A traceroute shows `* * *` at hop 5 but hops 6 and 7 answer normally. What is the most likely meaning?

options.text: The path is broken at hop 5
Hop 5 forwards traffic but does not send time-exceeded replies

questions.why: Later hops answer, so traffic passes through hop 5. The router just does not send, or rate-limits, ICMP time-exceeded messages.

questions.q: What payload size gives a full 1500-byte packet in `ping -D -s SIZE`?
questions.why: 1500 minus 20 bytes of IP header and 8 bytes of ICMP header is 1472.

questions.q: In an mtr report, hop 4 shows 60 percent loss but the last hop shows 0 percent. What do you conclude?

options.text: Real packet loss on the path
Hop 4 rate-limits ICMP replies; the traffic itself is not being lost

questions.why: Loss that does not continue to the final hop means the router declines to answer probes, not that your packets disappear.

questions.q: Which command computes the average RTT from ping's summary line?
questions.why: The summary line reads `round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = a/b/c/d ms`. Splitting on `/` makes the average the fifth field.

questions.q: Why does `sort` need `-n` when ranking RTTs?

options.text: Without it numbers sort as text, so 9.5 comes after 12.3

questions.why: Text sort compares character by character, so a leading 9 beats a leading 1. `-n` compares numeric values.

blocks.text: Build a recorder and a summariser. The recorder appends one line per probe to a CSV; the summariser turns a CSV into the numbers you would give an ISP. Leave the recorder running during a work session and you will have evidence of when the connection degrades.
Step 1: The recorder

Create `~/lab/latency-log.zsh`. It writes a header once, then loops: take a timestamp, send one ping, extract the time (or the word `timeout`), append a CSV line, wait. The `-t 2` guarantees one dead probe cannot stall the loop.

blocks.code: chmod +x latency-log.zsh && ./latency-log.zsh {{host}} 12 2 latency.csv && tail -5 latency.csv

blocks.text: `${rtt:-timeout}` writes the word `timeout` when the pipeline produced nothing. The same marker appears for an unresolvable name, so check that `{{host}}` works with a plain `ping` first.
Step 2: The summariser
The summariser has two jobs. Loss is the share of `timeout` rows. The statistics come from the numeric rows, which need sorting for the percentile.
Step 3: Test it on data you already have
Before trusting the summariser on live data, feed it the saved lab ping run. This converts `ping.log` into the same CSV shape, so you know the expected answer (9 replies, 1 timeout, average 12.939).

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "timestamp,host,rtt_ms" > test.csv
$ awk -F'[= ]' '/time=/ {print "2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com," $(NF-1)} /timeout/ {print "2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,timeout"}' ping.log >> test.csv
$ head -4 test.csv
timestamp,host,rtt_ms
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,11.842
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,12.310
2026-10-08T09:00:00,example.com,11.205
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 {t++} NR>1 && $3=="timeout" {l++} END {printf "probes=%d lost=%d loss=%.1f%%\n", t, l, (t ? 100*l/t : 0)}' test.csv
probes=10 lost=1 loss=10.0%
$ awk -F, 'NR>1 && $3!="timeout" {print $3}' test.csv | sort -n | awk '{v[NR]=$1; s+=$1} END {p=int(0.95*NR); if (p<0.95*NR) p++; printf "n=%d min=%.2f avg=%.2f p95=%.2f max=%.2f ms\n", NR, v[1], s/NR, v[p], v[NR]}'
n=9 min=11.21 avg=12.94 p95=16.10 max=16.10 ms

blocks.text: Step 4: Run it for real

Record 20 minutes of a host you care about (your gateway, then a public service), then compare the summaries. If the gateway looks clean and the public host does not, the problem is beyond your router.

blocks.code:
./latency-log.zsh {{gateway}} 240 5 gw.csv &
./latency-log.zsh {{host}} 240 5 web.csv &
wait
./latency-summary.zsh gw.csv && ./latency-summary.zsh web.csv

blocks.text: Add a `jitter` line using the consecutive-difference formula from this chapter. Make the recorder write a `SLOW` flag when the RTT exceeds a threshold given as a fifth argument. Run it from `launchd` so it starts on login ([Scripting](#scripting) covers the plist).
Try it in the practice terminal

The practice terminal can run `ping` and `traceroute` against the lab network and `awk` over `ping.log`, so every statistics pipeline in this chapter works there. Try ranking the lab router, the Pi and the NAS by their ping averages.
Next

You can tell whether a host is reachable and how the path behaves. Continue to [DNS](#dns), where you turn names into addresses, read every record type and learn why "the internet is down" is so often a DNS problem.

chapters.title: DNS: Names, Records & Resolvers
chapters.sub: Resolve names with dig, nslookup, host and the macOS resolver, read every record type, and spot DNS problems fast
goals: Explain the path of a lookup from the stub resolver to an authoritative server
Read all sections of a dig answer, including flags, status and TTL
Query a specific resolver or an authoritative server directly and compare answers
Predict which macOS tools honour /etc/hosts, search domains and per-domain resolvers
Build dnscheck, a script that reports A, MX, NS and TXT records and compares public resolvers

blocks.text: Almost every connection starts with a question: what address belongs to this name? The Domain Name System answers it, and when it fails, everything looks broken even though the network is fine. Many outages that get described as "the internet is down" are DNS failures: `ping 1.1.1.1` works, `ping example.com` does not. In this chapter you will learn how a lookup travels, which tool sees which part of the macOS resolver, how to read a `dig` answer line by line, and how to build `dnscheck`, a small tool that tells you what the world sees for a domain.

blocks.title: Ask about domains, do not attack them

blocks.text: Looking up public records with `dig` is normal and harmless. Do not run zone transfers (`dig AXFR`) or bulk-guess subdomains against domains you do not own. Use `example.com`, `iana.org`, your own domains, and the lab. Public resolvers such as `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8` and `9.9.9.9` are fine for a few queries; do not hammer them in a tight loop.
How a lookup travels
Four kinds of machine take part in resolving `www.example.com`.

blocks.code:
stub resolver          recursive resolver        root        com. TLD     example.com
  (in your Mac)          (router/ISP/1.1.1.1)      servers     servers      authoritative
       │ 1. www.example.com A?  │                    │            │             │
       │ ─────────────────────▶ │ 2. who runs com?   │            │             │
       │                        │ ──────────────────▶│            │             │
       │                        │ ◀ ask a.gtld-servers.net        │             │
       │                        │ 3. who runs example.com?        │             │
       │                        │ ───────────────────────────────▶│             │
       │                        │ ◀ ask a.iana-servers.net        │             │
       │                        │ 4. www.example.com A?                         │
       │                        │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────▶│
       │                        │ ◀ 93.184.216.34, TTL 300                      │
       │ 5. answer + TTL        │ (now cached for 300 s)                        │
       │ ◀───────────────────── │                                               │

items.text: The **stub resolver** is the small client library inside your Mac. It does no research. It asks a configured recursive resolver and waits. On macOS the stub is part of `mDNSResponder`, which also handles `.local` names and keeps a cache.

The **recursive resolver** does the research for you. If it has the answer cached, it replies at once. If not, it asks the **root servers** who runs `com.`, asks a `com.` server who runs `example.com`, then asks the **authoritative** server, the one that holds the actual records. It caches everything it learns.
**Authoritative servers** own a zone. They give a final answer (flag `aa`) or a **referral** pointing deeper.

Every record carries a **TTL** (time to live, in seconds): how long a cache may keep it. A TTL of 300 means a change you publish reaches everyone within about five minutes at worst; 86400 means up to a day.

blocks.text: A name is read right to left. `www.example.com.` has a hidden trailing dot for the root, then the **TLD** `com`, then the **domain** `example`, then the **host label** `www`. Each dot is a potential **delegation**: the parent zone holds NS records saying "for names below here, ask these servers".

blocks.title: Why caching decides what you see

blocks.text: Because answers are cached at the stub, at the recursive resolver and often inside the application, two machines on the same network can see different answers for minutes after a change. This is why DNS changes "take time to propagate": nothing travels. Old copies simply expire at different moments.
Which tool sees which part

macOS does not use `/etc/resolv.conf` for normal lookups. Resolver settings live in the System Configuration database, which can hold **several resolvers at once**, each limited to certain domains or interfaces. You saw `scutil --dns` in [See your own network](#net-local). The consequence is that macOS command-line tools split into two families.

head: Path
Tools
What they use
rows: `/etc/hosts`, search domains, `.local` multicast DNS, per-domain resolvers in `/etc/resolver/`, VPN resolvers, the cache

Only the nameserver(s) in `/etc/resolv.conf` (generated from the primary resolver), or the one you name with `@server`. No hosts file, no search domains by default, no `.local` multicast, no per-domain routing

blocks.text: This is the single most useful fact in the chapter. **If `dig` and `ping` disagree, they took different paths.** `dig intranet.corp.example` may fail because it asked your home router, while `ping intranet.corp.example` succeeds because the system resolver sent that domain to the VPN's DNS server.
Resolver configuration in `scutil --dns`

blocks.code:
$ scutil --dns | head -40
DNS configuration

resolver #1
  search domain[0] : lan
  nameserver[0] : 192.168.1.1
  if_index : 14 (en0)
  flags    : Request A records
  reach    : 0x00020002 (Reachable,Directly Reachable Address)

resolver #2
  domain   : local
  options  : mdns
  timeout  : 5
  flags    : Request A records
  order    : 300000

resolver #3
  domain   : corp.example
  nameserver[0] : 10.8.0.1
  if_index : 16 (utun4)
  flags    : Request A records
  reach    : 0x00000002 (Reachable)
  order    : 100000

items.text: **resolver #1** is the default: names that match nothing more specific go to `192.168.1.1`. Its **search domain** `lan` means a short name is retried with `.lan` appended, so `ping pi` can find `pi.lan`.

**resolver #2** says names ending in `.local` are resolved by **multicast DNS (mDNS, Bonjour)**: the Mac asks the whole link at `224.0.0.251` port 5353 and the owning device answers. That is how `macbook.local` resolves without any server.

**resolver #3** is **split DNS**: names under `corp.example` go to `10.8.0.1` through the VPN tunnel, and nothing else does. Ordinary lookups still use your home resolver, so they stay fast and private.

blocks.text: Administrators and tools add their own per-domain resolvers by creating a file named after the domain in `/etc/resolver/`, containing `nameserver 10.1.0.53`. Local development setups use this to send `.test` names to a local DNS server such as `dnsmasq`. See `man 5 resolver`.
Encrypted DNS and DNSSEC in brief

Classic DNS travels in plain text over UDP port 53 (and TCP 53 for large answers), so your network can see and alter every lookup. **DNS over HTTPS (DoH)** and **DNS over TLS (DoT)** wrap the same questions in encryption. macOS supports them through DNS settings profiles, and browsers such as Firefox and Chrome can do their own DoH, bypassing the system resolver and local rules like a hosts file or a Pi-hole style sinkhole. When one browser resolves something differently from `ping`, check whether it has its own secure DNS setting.

**DNSSEC** is a different protection: authoritative zones sign their records, and a validating resolver checks the signatures. It proves an answer is genuine, not that the query was private. A validating resolver sets the `ad` (authenticated data) flag in its reply; `dig +dnssec` shows the signatures.
Record types
A DNS zone is a set of **resource records**. Each has an owner name, a TTL, a class (`IN`, for Internet), a type and data. The type says what the data means.

head: Type
Meaning
Example data
rows: Alias: this name is another name; resolve that one instead
Mail exchanger with a preference number (lower is tried first)
Authoritative name server for the zone
Free text: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification
Start of authority: primary server, admin mailbox, serial, refresh/retry/expire, negative TTL
Reverse mapping from an address back to a name, under `in-addr.arpa`
Service location: priority, weight, port, target
Which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain

blocks.text: Samples in this book, and the practice terminal, use `93.184.216.34`, the long-standing address of `example.com`. That domain has since moved to a different provider and returns several addresses that can change, so `dig example.com` on your Mac shows other numbers. The records, TTLs and lookup steps work the same way.
Rules that cause real trouble:

items.text: A name that has a **CNAME** cannot have other records at the same name (so you cannot put a CNAME at the bare domain `example.com`, which must have SOA and NS).
**MX** and **NS** records point at *names*, never at addresses or CNAMEs. A mail server needs its own A or AAAA record.
A **null MX** (`0 .`) states that a domain accepts no mail at all.

**PTR** records live in the reverse zone, controlled by whoever owns the *address block* (usually your ISP or cloud provider), not by the owner of the domain. IPv4 reverse names list the octets backwards: `93.184.216.34` becomes `34.216.184.93.in-addr.arpa`. IPv6 uses `ip6.arpa` with one label per hex digit.
**TXT** records for mail authentication are strings that begin `v=spf1`, `v=DKIM1` or `v=DMARC1`, and are published at the names `domain`, `selector._domainkey.domain` and `_dmarc.domain`.

blocks.text: dig: the tool for reading DNS

`dig` (domain information groper) is a DNS client that prints the raw reply. Its output looks cluttered at first, but every line has a fixed meaning. Here is a full answer from the practice terminal, which you can reproduce for any name.

blocks.code:
$ dig example.com

; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> example.com
;; global options: +cmd
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41872
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; OPT PSEUDOSECTION:
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.			IN	A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34

;; Query time: 14 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)
;; WHEN: Thu Oct 08 09:41:00 BST 2026
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 76

head: Part of the reply
What it tells you
rows: Banner: the dig version and your command line
The result code. `NOERROR` means the query worked, `NXDOMAIN` the name does not exist, `SERVFAIL` the resolver could not get an answer, `REFUSED` it will not answer you
`qr` is a response, `rd` recursion was desired, `ra` the server offers it. `aa` would mean authoritative, `ad` DNSSEC-validated, `tc` truncated (retry over TCP)
How many records each section holds
What was asked: name, class `IN`, type `A`
The records that answer it: name, TTL in seconds, class, type, data
How long this server took to answer
Which resolver actually answered, and the port

blocks.title: Asking one specific resolver for one record type

tokens.exp: the DNS client
ask this resolver instead of the system default
the name to look up
the record type (default is A)
print only the record data

blocks.text: Two more sections appear when relevant. **AUTHORITY** lists the name servers responsible for the zone (in referrals and for negative answers, where it carries the SOA that sets how long the "no such name" is cached). **ADDITIONAL** carries helpful extras, such as the addresses of those servers (glue).

Everyday work uses `dig` in short forms. `+short` prints only the data. `+noall +answer` hides everything except the answer section, keeping the TTL and record type, which makes the output easy to parse.

blocks.name: dig
blocks.sum: Send a DNS query to a chosen resolver and print the full, structured reply.

how.text: `dig` builds a DNS query for a name and record type (A by default), sends it over UDP to a server, and prints the response sections. Unlike `ping` or `curl`, it does not use the macOS system resolver: it reads the first nameserver from `/etc/resolv.conf`, or the server you name with `@server`. That makes it the right tool to ask "what does *this* resolver say?" and the wrong one to ask "what would my apps see?".

Options starting with `+` change query behaviour and output, `-x` builds a reverse lookup, and `@server` chooses the target. Order among name, type, `@server` and `+options` is free. Recursion is on by default (`+recurse`); `+norecurse` asks a server only for what it knows, which is how you query an authoritative server without it going off to research.

flags.d: Query this resolver or name server instead of the default.
Print only the record data, one answer per line.
Turn off all sections, then turn on just the answer section: name, TTL, class, type, data.
Start at the root and follow the delegations yourself, printing each referral.
Show or hide the final statistics block (query time, server, size).
Reverse lookup: build the `in-addr.arpa` (or `ip6.arpa`) name for you.
Use TCP instead of UDP; useful when a reply is truncated or UDP is blocked.
Ask for DNSSEC records (RRSIG) and show the `ad` flag if the resolver validated.
Do not ask the server to research; it answers from its own data only.
Per-try timeout in seconds, and number of tries. Use `+time=2 +tries=1` in scripts so dead servers do not stall them.
Omit the leading banner lines.
Batch mode: run one query per line of a file, each line holding dig arguments such as a name or `example.com MX`.
Force IPv4 or IPv6 transport.

Ask a specific public resolver

Mail servers by priority, best first, hostnames only

Show the result code of a query

gotchas: `dig +short` on an alias prints the **CNAME target first**, then the addresses. To get only IPs, filter with `grep -E '^[0-9.]+$'` or ask for the final answer with `awk`.
`dig` does not read `/etc/hosts` and does not append search domains (`+nosearch` is the default). A short name like `pi` returns nothing even though `ping pi` works.

A reply that never comes ends with `;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached`. That is a network or firewall problem, not a missing name. A missing name is a quick reply with status NXDOMAIN.
notes: At the time of writing macOS ships ISC `dig` 9.10.6 (check with `dig -v`). `brew install bind` provides a current build, which prints a few extra lines such as COOKIE but is used the same way.

blocks.text: Status values and flags you will actually meet

head: Status or flag
Meaning
What to do
rows: The name exists but has no record of the type you asked
Try another type, such as AAAA or CNAME
Check spelling, check the zone, check which resolver you asked
The resolver tried and failed: broken delegation, unreachable authoritative servers, DNSSEC validation failure
Ask another resolver; query the authoritative server directly
The server declines to answer you
You asked a server that does not offer recursion or has an access list
The answer came from an authoritative server
You are looking at the source of truth
Missing `ra` means you queried an authoritative-only server
Truncated; the full answer did not fit in UDP
Only trust it from a resolver you trust

blocks.text: Watching the cache count down
Ask a caching resolver for the same record twice and look at the TTL. It counts down, because you are seeing the resolver's cached copy and its remaining life.

blocks.code:
$ dig +noall +answer @1.1.1.1 example.com
example.com.		219	IN	A	93.184.216.34
$ sleep 30; dig +noall +answer @1.1.1.1 example.com
example.com.		189	IN	A	93.184.216.34
$ dig +noall +answer @a.iana-servers.net. example.com
example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34

blocks.text: The cached copy shows the remaining life (219, then 189). The authoritative server always reports the full configured TTL, because it owns the record rather than a copy. Seeing a TTL lower than the zone's value is how you recognise a cached answer. Large providers run many caches behind one address, so successive queries sometimes show jumping TTLs.
+trace: do the resolver's job by hand

`dig +trace` starts at the root and follows each referral itself, without using any cache. It shows exactly who delegates to whom, which makes it the right tool for "the domain works on some resolvers but not others".

blocks.code:
$ dig +trace example.com
; <<>> DiG 9.10.6 <<>> +trace example.com
;; global options: +cmd
.			518400	IN	NS	a.root-servers.net.
.			518400	IN	NS	b.root-servers.net.
...
;; Received 811 bytes from 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1) in 21 ms

com.			172800	IN	NS	a.gtld-servers.net.
com.			172800	IN	NS	b.gtld-servers.net.
...
;; Received 1173 bytes from 198.41.0.4#53(a.root-servers.net) in 24 ms

example.com.		172800	IN	NS	a.iana-servers.net.
example.com.		172800	IN	NS	b.iana-servers.net.
;; Received 187 bytes from 192.5.6.30#53(a.gtld-servers.net) in 31 ms

example.com.		300	IN	A	93.184.216.34
;; Received 56 bytes from 199.43.135.53#53(a.iana-servers.net) in 88 ms

blocks.text: Each block is one hop of the chain you drew earlier: your resolver's list of root servers, the root's referral to `com.`, the `com.` servers' referral to `example.com`, and finally the authoritative answer. If a trace stops with `SERVFAIL` or no answer at one step, the break is in that delegation.
The other DNS tools

`nslookup`, `host` and `whois` ship with macOS and are simpler than `dig`. Like `dig`, `nslookup` and `host` talk to DNS servers directly. The two native macOS tools, `dscacheutil` and `dns-sd`, go through the system's own machinery.

blocks.name: nslookup
blocks.sum: A simple DNS lookup client with a plain, human-oriented output and an interactive mode.

how.text: `nslookup` asks a DNS server for a name and prints the server it used and the answer. By default it labels the reply "Non-authoritative answer" when it came from a cache. Run with no arguments it starts an interactive prompt where `set type=MX` changes the record type and `server 1.1.1.1` changes the resolver; press Ctrl-D to leave. Like `dig`, it uses DNS only, not the hosts file.

Optional last argument: ask this DNS server.

examples.out:
Server:		1.1.1.1
Address:	1.1.1.1#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name:	example.com
Address: 93.184.216.34

examples.desc: Extract the addresses from the answer

gotchas: The first `Address:` line is the **server's** (with `#53`), the later ones are the answer. A pattern like `^Address: ` (with the space) skips the server line, which prints `Address:<tab>`.

blocks.name: host
blocks.sum: Print DNS answers as short English sentences; the quickest way to see A, AAAA and MX together.

how.text: `host` queries A, AAAA and MX records by default and prints one sentence per record, so a single command shows how a name is reachable and where its mail goes. With an IP address instead of a name it performs the reverse lookup automatically. It uses DNS only.

blocks.name: whois
blocks.sum: Look up registration data for a domain or an IP block: registrar, dates, name servers, owner contact when public.

how.text: `whois` is a separate, much older protocol (TCP port 43) than DNS. It queries a registry or regional internet registry for who registered a domain or who owns an address block. Many registries now redact personal contact details. The record often contains the **registrar**, the **creation and expiry dates** and the **name servers**, which are useful evidence when a domain stops resolving because it expired.

flags.d: Ask a specific whois server instead of letting `whois` choose.

examples.desc: When does a domain expire?
Pull out the dates
Which network owns an address?

gotchas: Field names differ between registries (`Registry Expiry Date`, `Expiration Date`, `paid-till`), so grep case-insensitively with alternations.

blocks.name: dscacheutil
blocks.sum: Look up a name through the macOS system resolver, and manage its cache.
blocks.syntax: dscacheutil -q host -a name hostname | -q host -a ip_address addr | -flushcache | -cachedump | -statistics

how.text: `dscacheutil` talks to the Directory Services cache that fronts the system resolver. `-q host -a name HOST` is the one lookup tool that behaves exactly like an application: it honours `/etc/hosts`, search domains, mDNS and per-domain resolvers. If `dig` says the name resolves and `dscacheutil -q host` does not (or the other way round), you have found the difference between "DNS" and "what my apps see".
`-flushcache` discards the cached entries. On current macOS that is only part of a full flush; see the next card.

blocks.name: dns-sd
blocks.sum: Browse and resolve Bonjour (multicast DNS) services and names on the local link.
blocks.syntax: dns-sd -B type domain | -L name type domain | -G v4|v6|v4v6 hostname | -q name [type]

how.text: `dns-sd` is the command-line client for DNS Service Discovery and multicast DNS. `-B` browses for instances of a service type on the local network (`_ssh._tcp`, `_airplay._tcp`, `_ipp._tcp` for printers), `-L` resolves one instance to a host and port, and `-G` resolves a `.local` name to addresses. The command keeps running and prints changes as devices appear and leave; press Ctrl-C to stop.

gotchas: `dns-sd` never exits by itself. For scripts, wrap it in a timeout. macOS has no `timeout` command; `brew install coreutils` provides `gtimeout`. Instance names with spaces break the `$NF` trick, which keeps only the last word.

blocks.text: /etc/hosts: the oldest DNS
Before DNS, every machine had one file mapping names to addresses. It still exists, and the system resolver reads it **before asking any DNS server**.

blocks.name: /etc/hosts
blocks.sum: A local text file that maps names to addresses and overrides DNS for every program that uses the system resolver.
blocks.syntax: ADDRESS NAME [ALIAS ...]      # one mapping per line, # starts a comment

how.text: Each line is an address followed by one or more names, separated by spaces or tabs. The default file defines `localhost` for IPv4 and IPv6 and `broadcasthost`. Apps that call the system resolver (browsers, `curl`, `ping`, `ssh`) check this file first, so a line here wins over any DNS record. `dig`, `host` and `nslookup` do not read it.

The file is root-owned, so editing needs `sudo`. Changes normally apply immediately; if an app still shows the old address, flush the cache (next section). Common uses: pointing a development name at `127.0.0.1`, testing a site on a new server before changing DNS, and blocking a domain by mapping it to `0.0.0.0`.

examples.desc: Add a development name (appends one line)
Back it up before editing

the first name (use the reserved .test suffix for development)
