blocks.text: Dates and Intl, briefly
A `Date` holds a single number: milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, the Unix epoch (Python's `time.time()` counts seconds). Everything else is interpretation. The traps:

items.text: **Months count from 0**: `new Date(2026, 9, 5)` is 5 October. Days of the month count from 1.

**Parsing depends on the string.** An ISO string ending in `Z` or an offset is unambiguous. A date-only ISO string (`'2026-10-05'`) is read as UTC midnight, but a date-time without an offset (`'2026-10-05T10:00'`) is read as **local** time. Other formats are implementation-defined; do not rely on them.
`getHours()` and friends use the machine's time zone; `getUTCHours()` and `toISOString()` use UTC. Logs and APIs should use UTC.
Subtracting two dates gives milliseconds.

blocks.text: `getUTCMonth()` is 9 for October and `getUTCDay()` is 1 for Monday (Sunday is 0). The `Intl` formatters handle time zones and languages correctly, which is far safer than building date strings by hand.

`Date` has well-known design flaws, and its replacement, the `Temporal` API (separate types for instants, wall-clock times and time zones, months counted from 1), is shipping: Firefox 139 (2025), Chrome and Edge 144 (2026) and Node.js 26 have it, while Safari has it only in Safari Technology Preview as of Safari 27.2 (November 2026). Until it reaches a stable Safari, `Date` plus `Intl` is what runs everywhere; MDN's compatibility table shows the current state.

blocks.name: new Date()
blocks.sum: Create a date-time object from now, a timestamp, an ISO string or date parts.
blocks.syntax: new Date()    new Date(ms)    new Date(isoString)    new Date(year, monthIndex, day, h, m, s)    Date.now()

how.text: Internally a `Date` is milliseconds since the Unix epoch in UTC. `new Date()` is now, `Date.now()` returns now as a number. With parts, months are 0-based and the parts are local time; `Date.UTC(...)` takes the same parts as UTC and returns milliseconds. `toISOString()` always prints UTC with a `Z`, and `JSON.stringify` uses it. Dates are mutable (`setUTCHours` changes the object), so copy before changing: `new Date(d)`.

examples.desc: Parse, compute, print in UTC
Turn epoch seconds from a log into ISO strings

gotchas: `new Date('2026-10-05T10:00')` (no Z, no offset) is local time, so the same code gives different instants on machines in different zones.

blocks.text: Python and JavaScript side by side
Keep this table open for the first weeks; most early bugs are a Python habit applied to JavaScript.

head: Idea
Python
JavaScript
rows: `[d.name for d in ds if d.up]`
UTF-16 code units (`[...s].length` for code points)
`xs.toSorted((a, b) => a - b)` (the default is text order)

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Using `==`.** It converts types with rules that are not even transitive. Use `===` and `!==`, and convert input explicitly with `Number()`.
**Sorting numbers with plain `sort()`.** It sorts as text: `[10, 9, 1]` becomes `[1, 10, 9]`. Pass `(a, b) => a - b`.
**`arr.map(parseInt)`.** The index becomes the radix. Use `map(Number)` or a wrapper.
**Defaults with `||`.** `port || 22` replaces a real 0; `name || 'guest'` replaces a real empty string. Use `??`.
**Testing an array for emptiness with `if (arr)`.** Empty arrays and objects are truthy. Test `arr.length`.
**`return` on its own line.** ASI returns `undefined`. Keep the value on the same line.
**Forgetting that `replace` with a string changes only the first match.** Use `replaceAll`.
**Mutating when you meant to copy.** `sort`, `reverse` and `splice` change the array; spread copies are shallow. Use `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced`, `structuredClone`.
**Comparing objects with `===`.** It compares identity. Compare an `id`, or the JSON of small plain objects.
**Trusting `toFixed` and floats for money.** `toFixed` returns a string and rounds the binary value. Count cents in integers or use BigInt.
**Month 10 is November.** `new Date(2026, 10, 5)` is 5 November; months are 0-based.
**Expecting JSON to keep types.** Dates become strings, Maps and Sets become `{}`, `undefined` disappears.

blocks.text: Practice

The JavaScript exercises run in the page and are checked automatically. They run as classic scripts, so there is no top-level `await`; code that fetches is wrapped in an `async function main()` that is then called.

blocks.title: Node in your Terminal

task.text: Prove the language is the same outside the browser. In Terminal:

items.text: Start the Node REPL and evaluate `0.1 + 0.2`, `typeof null` and `[10, 9, 1].sort()`. Quit with `.exit`.

Create `~/lab/web/js/ports.js` that prints the command-line arguments as numbers sorted numerically, so that `node ports.js 8080 22 443` prints `[ 22, 443, 8080 ]`. Command-line arguments are in `process.argv`; the first two items are the path of `node` and of the script.

hints: `process.argv.slice(2)` gives just your arguments, as strings.
Convert with `.map(Number)` and sort with a comparator, `(a, b) => a - b`.
blocks.solution:
mkdir -p ~/lab/web/js && cd ~/lab/web/js
echo 'console.log(process.argv.slice(2).map(Number).toSorted((a, b) => a - b))' > ports.js
node ports.js 8080 22 443

why.text: `process.argv` is Node's `sys.argv`. Everything on the command line arrives as text, so the conversion with `Number` is required, and without the comparator `sort` would order the numbers as strings. `console.log` printed the array in the same format the jsrun boxes use.

blocks.title: Parse a CSV string into objects

task.text: Write `parseCsv(text)` that turns CSV text with a header row into an array of objects, one per data row, using the header names as keys. Trim spaces around every field and skip blank lines. Values stay strings. Then print the names of the hosts in `csv`, separated by single spaces: `router macbook pi`.

hints: Split the text into lines with `split('\n')`, trim each line and drop empty ones with `filter`.

The first line gives the keys: `const keys = lines[0].split(',').map((k) => k.trim())`. For each other line, build pairs with `keys.map((k, i) => [k, fields[i]])` and turn them into an object with `Object.fromEntries`.

why.text: This is the same split, trim, filter, map pipeline you would write in Python, with `Object.fromEntries` playing the role of `dict(zip(keys, fields))`. Real CSV can contain quoted fields with commas inside; for that, use a library (or Python's `csv` module), because a plain `split(',')` cannot handle it.

blocks.title: Group devices by type with reduce

task.text: Write `groupByType(devices)` that returns an object mapping each device type to an array of device **names**, in the order the devices appear. Then fetch `/api/devices` from the practice server and print `JSON.stringify(groupByType(devices))`. The expected output starts with `{"router":["router"],"laptop":["macbook"],"server":["pi","homeassistant"]`.

hints: Start the accumulator as `{}`. For each device, make sure `acc[d.type]` is an array (`acc[d.type] ??= []`), then push the name.
The callback must `return acc` at the end, or the next iteration receives `undefined`.

why.text: `??=` creates the array the first time a type appears, and returning the accumulator threads it through every call. Newer runtimes (Node 21+, Chrome 117+, Safari 17.4+) have this built in: `Object.groupBy(devices, (d) => d.type)` returns arrays of whole devices in an object with no prototype, and `Map.groupBy` returns a Map.

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: two silent bugs

task.text: This settings validator and port sorter run without errors and give wrong answers. Run it, read the output, then fix both functions:

items.text: `missing(obj)` must return the keys whose value is an empty string, `null` or `undefined`. A value of `0` is a real value. For the settings below it should print `[]`.
`sortedPorts(list)` must return a new array sorted numerically ascending, **without changing** the array it was given. It should print `[ 22, 80, 443, 8080 ]`.

hints: Run the starter first. What does `0 == ''` evaluate to? And what does `null == ''`?
For the sort, two things are wrong: the default order is text order, and `sort` changes the original. `toSorted` with a comparator fixes both.

why.text: `0 == ''` is true because the empty string converts to 0, while `null == ''` and `undefined == ''` are false, so the loose test was wrong in both directions. Spelling out the three cases with `===` (or `obj[k] === '' || obj[k] == null`, the one accepted use of `==`) states the rule exactly. The default `sort` compared `'22'`, `'443'`, `'80'`, `'8080'` as text and reordered the caller's array; `toSorted` with `(a, b) => a - b` returns a numeric copy.

blocks.title: Format a port table with padStart

task.text: Write `formatTable(rows)` where each row is `{ port, proto, service }`. Return one string with one line per row, sorted by port ascending (do not reorder the input array). Each line is: the port right-aligned in 5 characters, one space, the protocol left-aligned in 4 characters, one space, the service name. Lines are joined with `\n`, with no trailing newline. Print the table for `rows`. The first line is `   22 tcp  ssh`.

hints: `String(r.port).padStart(5)` and `r.proto.padEnd(4)` produce the two fixed-width columns.
Sort a copy with `rows.toSorted((a, b) => a.port - b.port)`, `map` each row to its line, then `join('\n')`.

why.text: `padStart` and `padEnd` do the job of Python's `:>5` and `:<4` format specs. Building the lines with `map` and joining at the end avoids a trailing newline, and an empty array naturally produces an empty string. `toSorted` keeps the caller's array in its original order.

blocks.title: Predict the coercions

task.text: Without running anything, write down the value of each expression. Then check your answers in a jsrun box or the Node REPL.

task.code:
'5' + 3 - 2
'5' - 3 + 2
true + true
[] + {}
typeof NaN
null + 1
undefined + 1
[10, 1, 2].sort()

blocks.solution: 51, 4, 2, '[object Object]', 'number', 1, NaN, [1, 10, 2]

why.text: Work left to right and remember that only `+` prefers strings. `'5' + 3` is `'53'`, then `'53' - 2` converts back to a number: 51. `'5' - 3` is 2, plus 2 is 4. Booleans convert to 1 and 0. `[] + {}` converts both objects to strings (`''` and `'[object Object]'`) and concatenates. NaN is a number value. `null` converts to 0 and `undefined` to NaN. The default sort compares `'10'`, `'1'`, `'2'` as text. If you got all eight, the coercion rules have stuck; if not, the table in the operators section is the one to reread.

questions.q: What does `typeof null` return?
questions.why: A bug from the first implementation, kept for compatibility. Test for null with `value === null`.

questions.q: What does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` return?

options.text: A TypeError, because sort needs a comparator

questions.why: Without a comparator, elements are compared as strings, and `'10'` sorts before `'9'`. Use `(a, b) => a - b` for numbers.

questions.q: `const port = config.port ?? 8080` with `config.port` set to 0. What is `port`?
questions.why: `??` falls back only for `null` and `undefined`, so the configured 0 is kept. `||` would have given 8080.

questions.q: Which value is truthy in JavaScript but falsy in Python?
questions.why: Every object, including `[]` and `{}`, is truthy in JavaScript. Test `arr.length` instead.

questions.q: What does `JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: [undefined, NaN] })` produce?
questions.why: Properties with `undefined` values are omitted; inside arrays, `undefined` and `NaN` become `null` so positions are kept.

questions.q: A `let` variable is read on a line above its declaration in the same block. What happens?

options.text: A ReferenceError is thrown (temporal dead zone)
It reads the global variable of the same name
A SyntaxError stops the whole script before it runs

questions.why: `let` and `const` are hoisted but stay uninitialized until their line runs. Only `var` reads as `undefined` early.

chapters.title: JavaScript in Depth: Functions, Objects, Modules and Async
chapters.sub: Closures, this, prototypes and classes, iterators, errors, modules, the event loop, promises, fetch and regular expressions
goals: Explain closures and predict what this refers to in any call
Model data with prototypes and classes, including private fields, accessors and static factories

blocks.text: The previous chapter covered values and the built-in methods that shape them. This one covers the parts of JavaScript that make it a different language from Python rather than Python with braces: functions that remember where they were created, a `this` decided at call time, objects that inherit from other objects, modules loaded over the network, and a single thread that never waits, which is why almost every web API returns a promise. You will build a `Device` class with private fields, an iterable `Subnet`, a fetch wrapper with a timeout and retries against the practice server, and a log parser with named regex groups. Every output below is exact; run the boxes, then change them.
Scope and closures

JavaScript uses **lexical scope**: a function can read the variables of every scope in which it was *written*, from the inside out, regardless of where it is later called. Blocks, functions and modules each create a scope. When a name is used, the engine looks in the current scope, then the enclosing one, and so on out to the global scope; the first match wins, and no match is a `ReferenceError`.

blocks.code:
module scope      const lab = 'lab.local'
  └─ function scope    function makeCounter(label) { let count = 0; ...
     └─ function scope    hit() { count += 1; return `${label}: ${count}` }
                          ⟪y:count⟫ and ⟪y:label⟫ are not local to hit(): found one level out
                          ⟪y:lab⟫ would be found two levels out

blocks.text: A **closure** is a function together with the scope it was created in. When `makeCounter` returns, its local variables do not disappear: the returned methods still reference them, so they live as long as those methods do. Each call to `makeCounter` creates a fresh scope, so every counter has its own private `count`.

Nothing outside can read or change `count`; the only access is through `hit` and `reset`. Unlike Python, an inner function may assign to an outer variable without a `nonlocal` declaration. Closures are how JavaScript builds private state, callbacks that carry context, and wrappers that add behaviour to a function:

blocks.out:
opening connection to pi
{ host: 'pi', id: 1 } { host: 'pi', id: 1 }

blocks.text: The loop and closure trap
`var` creates one variable for the whole function, while `let` in a `for` header creates a new binding for every iteration. Callbacks that run later see the variable as it is *then*:

blocks.out:
var 3
var 3
var 3
let 0
let 1
let 2

blocks.text: All three `var` callbacks close over the same `i`, which is 3 by the time the timers fire. Each `let` callback closed over its own `j`. This bug filled forums for twenty years; `let` ended it.
How this is decided

In Python, `self` is an explicit parameter bound when you access a method. In JavaScript, `this` is an implicit parameter whose value depends on **how the function is called**, not where it is defined. The rules, in order of priority:

head: Call form
`this` inside the function
Example
rows: `undefined` in strict code (modules, classes); `globalThis` in sloppy scripts
whatever `this` was where the arrow was written

blocks.out:
router at 192.168.1.1
TypeError
nas at 192.168.1.60
nas at 192.168.1.60 router at 192.168.1.1
undefined

blocks.text: Copying the method into `detached` dropped the object: the plain call made `this` undefined, and reading `this.name` threw a `TypeError`. The same thing happens when you pass a method as a callback, such as `setTimeout(router.describe, 100)` or `button.addEventListener('click', obj.handle)`, because the receiving code calls it as a plain function. The fixes are `bind`, or an arrow function that calls the method: `setTimeout(() => router.describe(), 100)`.
Arrow functions have no `this` of their own; they use the `this` of the code around them. That makes them right for callbacks inside methods and wrong as methods:

blocks.out:
plain function callback: TypeError
[ 'pi 12 ms', 'pi 9 ms' ] undefined

blocks.text: The arrow callback saw `start`'s `this` (the poller); the `function` callback was called plainly by `forEach` and got `undefined`. `arrowMethod` was written at the top level of the module, where `this` is undefined, so calling it on `poller` changes nothing.

blocks.name: Function.prototype.bind()
blocks.sum: Create a new function whose this (and optionally leading arguments) are fixed.

how.text: The bound function ignores how it is later called: `this` is always `thisArg`, and `presetArgs` are placed before any new arguments (partial application). Binding again has no effect. Use it when handing a method to code that will call it as a plain function: timers, event listeners, array callbacks.

examples.desc: Fix this and preset an argument
examples.out: pi x1 pi x3 [ 'pi x1', 'pi x2' ]

examples.desc: Pass a bound method as a callback in a chain

gotchas: Arrow functions ignore `bind`; their `this` is fixed where they were written.

blocks.name: Function.prototype.call()
blocks.sum: Call a function once with an explicit this; apply does the same with an array of arguments.

how.text: `call` invokes the function immediately with `this` set to `thisArg`. `apply` is identical except that the arguments come as one array, which mattered before spread syntax existed (`Math.max.apply(null, nums)` is now `Math.max(...nums)`). Borrowing a method for another object is the classic use.

examples.desc: Borrow a method
Borrow Array methods for an array-like object

blocks.text: Objects and prototypes

Every object has a hidden link, its **prototype** (the spec writes it `[[Prototype]]`), pointing at another object or `null`. When you read a property the object does not have, the engine follows that link and looks there, then follows the next link, until it finds the property or reaches `null`. This **prototype chain** is how JavaScript shares methods: arrays find `map` on `Array.prototype`, and every plain object finds `toString` on `Object.prototype`. Writing a property always creates it on the object itself, which **shadows** any inherited one.

blocks.code:
pi ──[[Prototype]]──▶ deviceProto ──[[Prototype]]──▶ Object.prototype ──▶ null
   { name: 'pi',          { describe(),                  { toString(), hasOwnProperty(),
     ip: '192.168.1.50' }    online: true }                 valueOf(), ... }

   pi.ip        found on pi itself
   pi.describe  not on pi → found on deviceProto
   pi.toString  not on pi, not on deviceProto → found on Object.prototype
   pi.mac       searched all the way to null → ⟪y:undefined⟫

blocks.out:
pi (192.168.1.50) true false true
true [ 'name', 'ip' ] true false
true null

blocks.text: `Object.create(proto)` makes a new empty object whose prototype is `proto`. `nas.online = false` created an own property on `nas`; the shared `deviceProto.online` stayed `true`.
prototype versus __proto__

Two similar names cause most of the confusion. Every ordinary function has a property called **`prototype`**: an object that becomes the prototype of objects created by calling that function with `new`. `obj.__proto__` is an old accessor that reads an object's own prototype link; prefer `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`. Before classes existed, this is how types were written:

blocks.out:
Device { name: 'router', ip: '192.168.1.1' } router (192.168.1.1)
true true
true true

blocks.text: `new Device(...)` does four things: creates an empty object, sets its prototype to `Device.prototype`, runs `Device` with `this` pointing at the new object, and returns it. `describe` exists once, on the prototype, and every device shares it.

Adding methods to `Array.prototype` or `Object.prototype` changes every array or object in the program, including those inside libraries, and can clash with methods the language adds later. (`Array.prototype.flatten` was renamed `flat` in 2018 because an old library had already defined `flatten` differently.)

blocks.name: Object.create()
blocks.sum: Create a new object with a chosen prototype (or none).

how.text: The new object is empty and its prototype link points at `proto`, so it inherits everything `proto` has. `Object.create(null)` makes an object with no prototype at all: no `toString`, no inherited keys, which makes it a safe dictionary for arbitrary keys such as `'__proto__'`. `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` and `Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, proto)` read and (slowly) change the link afterwards.

examples.desc: Inherit, shadow, and a prototype-free dictionary
Give several plain objects shared defaults

blocks.text: Classes

`class` syntax is a cleaner way to write the constructor-and-prototype pattern above, with extras the old pattern lacked: **fields** declared in the class body, truly **private** members whose names start with `#`, **accessors** (`get`/`set`), **static** members on the class itself, and `extends`/`super` for inheritance. Underneath it is still prototypes: `typeof Device` is `'function'` and methods live on `Device.prototype`.

blocks.out:
Device { id: 1, name: 'pi' } pi@192.168.1.50 router@192.168.1.1 (WAN 203.0.113.7)
true true false 2
[{"id":1,"name":"pi","ip":"192.168.1.50"},{"id":2,"name":"router","ip":"192.168.1.1"}]
TypeError bad IPv4 address: 999.1
[ 'id', 'name' ] true false function
[ 'constructor', 'ip', 'label', 'markSeen', 'toJSON' ] [class Router extends Device]

blocks.text: Read the output against the code:

items.text: Printing `pi` shows only the **public own properties** `id` and `name`. `#ip` and `#lastSeen` are private, and `ip` and `label` are accessors that live on the prototype.

`#nextId` is a private static field shared by every instance, so the router got id 2. Code outside the class cannot even mention `pi.#ip`: it is a `SyntaxError` before the program runs. `#ip in obj` (used by `isDevice`) is the only safe way to test whether an object has the private field.
The setter validated the address on construction and on later assignment, and threw a `TypeError` whose message is our own.
`Router` inherited `toJSON`, so `JSON.stringify` used it and dropped `wanIp`. `super.label` called the parent's getter.
In a subclass constructor, `super(...)` must run before `this` is used; forgetting it throws a `ReferenceError`.

head: Python
JavaScript
rows: `this.name = name;` (`this` is implicit, never a parameter)
`static fromLine() {}` (no `cls`; use `this` or the class name)

blocks.name: class
blocks.sum: Declare a constructor function and its prototype methods with class syntax.
blocks.syntax: class Name { field = value; #private; constructor(args) { ... } method() { ... } get x() { ... } static make() { ... } }

how.text: The `constructor` runs on `new Name(...)`; fields are initialized on each instance just before the constructor body runs (in a subclass, right after `super()` returns). Methods, getters and setters go on `Name.prototype`. Class bodies are always strict mode, and classes are not hoisted the way function declarations are: using one above its declaration throws a `ReferenceError`. Calling a class without `new` throws a `TypeError`.

examples.desc: A minimal class
Build instances from data and use their methods in a chain

blocks.name: extends
blocks.sum: Make a class inherit from another class (or constructor); super calls the parent.
blocks.syntax: class Child extends Parent { constructor(...args) { super(...args); ... } method() { return super.method(); } }

how.text: `extends` sets two prototype links: `Child.prototype` inherits from `Parent.prototype` (instance methods) and `Child` inherits from `Parent` (static methods). In a constructor, `super(...)` runs the parent constructor and must be called before `this` is touched; a subclass without a constructor gets one that passes all arguments through. Elsewhere, `super.name` reaches the parent's version of a method or accessor.

examples.desc: Override and extend a method
Treat a mixed list of subclasses uniformly
examples.code: const report = [new Host('printer'), new Server('pi')].map((h) => h.describe()).join('\n');

gotchas: Prefer composition (an object that holds another) when the relationship is "has a" rather than "is a"; deep class hierarchies are hard to change.

blocks.name: #private class fields
blocks.sum: Fields and methods whose names start with # are accessible only inside the class body.
blocks.syntax: class C { #secret = 1; #helper() {} static #count = 0; read() { return this.#secret; } static has(o) { return #secret in o; } }

how.text: Privacy is enforced by the language: outside the class, `obj.#secret` is a syntax error, the field does not appear in `Object.keys`, `JSON.stringify` or `console.log`, and proxies and reflection cannot reach it. Every private name must be declared in the class body. `#name in obj` checks whether an object was constructed by this class (a brand check) without throwing.

examples.desc: Private state behind a public method
Expose a computed, read-only view of private data

gotchas: Private fields hide data from other code, not from the user. Anything in browser JavaScript, private or not, can be read in DevTools; never ship secrets to the client.

blocks.name: get / set accessors
blocks.sum: Define a property whose reads and writes run functions.

how.text: An accessor looks like a data property to the caller (`dev.ip`, `dev.ip = x`) but runs code: a getter computes a value on every read, a setter can validate or convert on every write. A getter without a setter makes the property read-only (assignment silently fails in sloppy code and throws a `TypeError` in strict code). They work in classes and object literals alike, and `console.log` shows them as `[Getter]`, `[Setter]` or `[Getter/Setter]` when they are own properties.

examples.desc: A computed property and a validated one
Accessors read like fields in a pipeline

blocks.name: static
blocks.sum: Declare methods and fields on the class itself rather than on instances.
blocks.syntax: class C { static count = 0; static #registry = new Map(); static from(data) { return new this(data); } }

how.text: Static members are reached through the class (`Device.fromLine(...)`), not through instances. Typical uses are **factory methods** that build instances from other formats, counters and registries shared by all instances, and constants. Inside a static method, `this` is the class it was called on, so `new this(...)` in a parent's factory builds the right subclass. Static members are inherited by subclasses through `extends`.

examples.desc: A static factory and a static counter
Parse many lines with a static factory

blocks.name: instanceof
blocks.sum: Test whether a constructor's prototype appears in an object's prototype chain.

how.text: `x instanceof C` walks `x`'s prototype chain looking for `C.prototype`. It works for classes, built-ins (`Array`, `Date`, `Map`, `Error` and its subclasses) and old constructor functions. Primitives are never instances (`'pi' instanceof String` is false). It is the normal way to choose a branch in a `catch` block by error type.

examples.desc: Classes, built-ins and primitives
Keep only the instances of one class from a mixed list
examples.code: const routers = inventory.filter((x) => x instanceof Router).map((r) => r.name);

gotchas: Objects from another realm (an iframe, a Node `vm` context) have different built-in prototypes, so `instanceof Array` can be false for a real array. `Array.isArray` works across realms.

blocks.text: Map and Set

A plain object is a fine record (fixed, known keys), but a poor dictionary: keys become strings, integer-like keys are reordered, inherited names such as `toString` already appear to exist, and there is no size property. **Map** is the dedicated dictionary and **Set** the dedicated collection of unique values.

The counting loop is Python's `Counter` written by hand. Spreading a Map gives `[key, value]` pairs, ready for array methods. `JSON.stringify(hits)` is `'{}'`, because a Map keeps its entries internally rather than as properties.

The Set methods `union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference` and `isSubsetOf` are recent (Node 22, Chrome 122, Safari 17, Firefox 127); the last line before the fetch shows the portable form with `filter` and `has`. `Map.groupBy` and `Object.groupBy` group an iterable by the key a callback returns. **WeakMap** and **WeakSet** hold their keys weakly, so an entry disappears when nothing else references the key object; libraries use them to attach data to DOM nodes without leaking memory.

blocks.name: Map
blocks.sum: A key-value collection with keys of any type, kept in insertion order.
blocks.syntax: new Map(iterableOfPairs?)    m.set(k, v)  m.get(k)  m.has(k)  m.delete(k)  m.clear()  m.size

how.text: Keys are compared with SameValueZero (like `===`, except that `NaN` equals `NaN`), so two different objects are two different keys even if they look alike. `set` returns the map, so calls chain. Iterating yields `[key, value]` pairs in insertion order; `keys()`, `values()` and `entries()` return iterators. Convert with `new Map(Object.entries(obj))` and `Object.fromEntries(map)`.

examples.desc: Count, look up and convert
examples.code:
const m = new Map([['ssh', 22]]).set('https', 443).set('ssh', 2222);
console.log(m, m.get('ssh'), m.size, [...m.values()], Object.fromEntries(m));

examples.desc: Top talkers from log lines, sorted by count
examples.code: const top = [...lines.reduce((m, l) => m.set(l.split(' ')[0], (m.get(l.split(' ')[0]) ?? 0) + 1), new Map())].toSorted((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 3);

gotchas: `m[key] = value` does not use the Map; it creates an ordinary property on the Map object. Always use `set` and `get`.

blocks.name: Set
blocks.sum: A collection of unique values, kept in insertion order.
blocks.syntax: new Set(iterable?)    s.add(v)  s.has(v)  s.delete(v)  s.size    a.union(b)  a.intersection(b)  a.difference(b)

how.text: Adding a value that is already present does nothing, so `new Set(array)` removes duplicates and `[...new Set(array)]` turns the result back into an array. `has` is a constant-time lookup, much faster than `array.includes` on large lists. The set-algebra methods return new Sets and accept any set-like argument.

examples.desc: De-duplicate and compare port sets
Unique client IPs from a log, sorted

blocks.name: Object.groupBy()
blocks.sum: Group the items of an iterable by the key a callback returns (Map.groupBy returns a Map).
blocks.syntax: Object.groupBy(items, (item, index) => key)    Map.groupBy(items, (item, index) => key)

how.text: Each item lands in the array for its key, in the original order. `Object.groupBy` returns an object with **no prototype** (so `console.log` labels it `[Object: null prototype]`) and string keys; `Map.groupBy` returns a Map, which keeps non-string keys such as numbers or objects intact. Available in Node 21+, Chrome 117+, Safari 17.4+ and Firefox 119+; elsewhere use `reduce`.

examples.desc: Group devices by online state
examples.code:
const devs = [{ n: 'pi', up: true }, { n: 'nas', up: false }, { n: 'router', up: true }];
console.log(Object.groupBy(devs, (d) => (d.up ? 'up' : 'down')));

examples.desc: Group, then count per group

blocks.text: Iterators and generators

`for...of`, spread, array destructuring, `Array.from`, `new Map(...)`, `new Set(...)` and `Promise.all` all accept any **iterable**: an object with a method under the key `Symbol.iterator` that returns an **iterator**. An iterator is an object with a `next()` method that returns `{ value, done }` each time it is called. Arrays, strings, Maps, Sets and NodeLists are iterable; plain objects are not.

blocks.out: { value: 22, done: false } { value: 443, done: false } { value: undefined, done: true }

blocks.text: Writing `next()` by hand is tedious, so JavaScript has **generators**, which work like Python's: a `function*` returns a generator object without running its body; each `next()` runs the body until the next `yield`, hands that value out, and pauses there. A generator is both an iterator and an iterable, so a generator method under `Symbol.iterator` makes any class iterable. Because values are produced on demand, a generator can describe a sequence that is huge or endless:

The `/8` network has over 16 million host addresses, yet destructuring two of them generated exactly two: the generator paused after the second `yield` and was then discarded. `break` in `for...of` likewise stops the generator.

`take(mapIt(numbers(...)))` is a lazy pipeline, the same shape as a Python generator pipeline or a shell pipe: nothing runs until the spread asks for values, and only three are ever computed. The last line uses **iterator helpers** (`map`, `filter`, `take`, `drop`, `toArray` directly on iterators), which are available in Node 22+, Chrome 122+, Firefox 131+ and Safari 18.4+, so every current browser has them.

blocks.name: function*
blocks.sum: Declare a generator: a function that produces a sequence of values lazily with yield.
blocks.syntax: function* name(args) { yield value; yield* otherIterable; return; }    *[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }

how.text: Calling a generator function runs none of its body; it returns a generator object. Each `next()` resumes the body until the next `yield` (giving `{ value, done: false }`) or the end (giving `{ value: undefined, done: true }`). `yield*` delegates to another iterable, and `return` finishes early. Consumers that stop early (`break`, destructuring) close the generator, which runs any `finally` block inside it.

examples.desc: A finite generator and delegation
Generate lazily, then process with array methods

blocks.name: Symbol.iterator
blocks.sum: The well-known symbol under which an object provides its iterator, making it usable with for...of and spread.
blocks.syntax: obj[Symbol.iterator]() -> iterator with next() -> { value, done }

how.text: The **iterable protocol**: anything with a `[Symbol.iterator]()` method that returns an iterator works with every iteration construct. The simplest implementation is a generator method, `*[Symbol.iterator]() { ... }`. Calling the method yourself gives a fresh iterator whose `next()` you can drive manually.

examples.desc: Make a plain object iterable
Any iterable feeds new Set, Map and Array.from directly

blocks.text: Errors

`throw` stops the current function and unwinds the call stack until a `catch` handles the value. You can throw anything, but throw `Error` objects (or subclasses): only they carry a `message`, a `name` and a `stack` trace. The built-in types you will meet are `TypeError` (wrong kind of value, such as calling `undefined`), `ReferenceError` (unknown name or TDZ), `SyntaxError` (bad code, or bad JSON from `JSON.parse`), `RangeError` (number out of range) and `AggregateError` (several errors at once, from `Promise.any`).

There is one `catch` per `try`, with no typed clauses as in Python's `except ValueError:`, so you test the type yourself with `instanceof` and **rethrow** anything you did not expect. `finally` runs whether the `try` block finished, returned or threw.

blocks.out:
found pi
  lookup done for 3
DeviceNotFoundError: device 9 not found (id 9)
  lookup done for 9
bad input: id must be an integer, got string
  lookup done for "3"

blocks.text: Setting `this.name` in the subclass makes logs and stack traces show the custom type. When you catch a low-level error and throw a higher-level one, pass the original as **`cause`** (ES2022) so nothing is lost; it is the equivalent of Python's `raise ... from err`.

blocks.out:
config file is not valid JSON <- SyntaxError
finally runs before the return completes
from try
optional catch binding: no (err) needed when you ignore it

blocks.text: An error nobody catches is **uncaught**. In a browser the console shows it in red as `Uncaught TypeError: ...`, the rest of that script or callback stops, and the page keeps running other code. In Node the process prints the stack trace and exits with status 1. This box ends with one on purpose:

Error messages for built-in errors are worded by the engine: V8 says "Cannot read properties of null (reading 'name')" where Safari says "null is not an object (evaluating 'device.name')". Match on `err.name` or `instanceof`, never on message text.

blocks.name: try...catch...finally
blocks.sum: Run code, handle any exception it throws, and always run cleanup code.

how.text: If anything in the `try` block throws, the rest of the block is skipped and `catch` receives the thrown value; the binding `(err)` may be omitted when it is unused. `finally` runs after either, even when the `try` or `catch` block executes `return`, `break` or `throw`. A `return` inside `finally` overrides everything, so avoid it. Errors thrown inside callbacks that run later (timers, event handlers, promise callbacks without `await`) escape the surrounding `try`.

examples.desc: Catch by type, rethrow the rest
examples.out:
22
not a port: ssh
not a port: 70000

examples.desc: Keep the valid values from a list instead of failing on the first bad one
examples.code: const ports = ['22', 'x', '443'].flatMap((t) => { try { return [parsePort(t)]; } catch { return []; } });

gotchas: `try { setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('x'); }) } catch {}` catches nothing: the callback runs later, after the `try` has finished. Put the `try` inside the callback, or use `await` inside an async function.

blocks.name: throw
blocks.sum: Raise an exception; throw new Error objects or subclasses with a message and optional cause.
blocks.syntax: throw new Error(message, { cause })    throw new TypeError(message)    class MyError extends Error {}

how.text: `throw` accepts any value, but only `Error` objects record a stack trace and play well with tools; throwing strings loses that information. Pick the closest built-in type (`TypeError` for wrong types, `RangeError` for out-of-range values) or subclass `Error`, setting `this.name` in the constructor. The `cause` option chains the underlying error.

examples.desc: A custom error with a cause
examples.out: HttpError HTTP 503 for /api/flaky 503 upstream down true

examples.desc: Throw from a validation step inside a chain, catch once outside
examples.code: try { const ips = input.split(',').map((s) => { if (!/^\d+(\.\d+){3}$/.test(s)) throw new TypeError(`bad ip ${s}`); return s; }); } catch (e) { console.log(e.message); }

blocks.text: Modules

A **module** is a file with its own scope. Nothing it declares is visible elsewhere unless it `export`s it, and nothing from elsewhere is visible inside it unless it `import`s it. ES modules (ESM), standard since ES2015, are what browsers and modern Node use. Compared with classic scripts, modules are always strict, have their own top-level scope (no accidental globals), may use top-level `await`, are evaluated **once** however many files import them, and in a browser are deferred until the HTML has been parsed.
Build a two-module program in `~/lab/web/modules` (create the files in your editor or with `nano`):

blocks.code: Open the console
{ "type": "module" }

blocks.text: `package.json` with `"type": "module"` tells Node to treat `.js` files in this folder as ES modules (browsers ignore the file; the [Node.js chapter](#node) explains the details). Run it in Node first:

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab/web/modules
$ node app.js
192.168.1.50   private
8.8.8.8        public
172.20.1.1     private
1.1.1.1        public
false 3 [ 'PRIVATE', 'default', 'inSubnet', 'ipToInt' ]

blocks.title: One import line, three kinds of import

tokens.exp: static import: resolved before any code in the file runs
the default export, under any local name you choose
a named export, under its exported name
a named export renamed locally
the module specifier: a relative URL, with ./ and the extension

blocks.text: `import * as net` gives a **module namespace object** holding every export; its keys come out sorted, and the default export appears as `default`. Imports are **live, read-only bindings**: if `net.js` changed the value of an exported `let`, importers would see the new value, but an importer cannot assign to an imported name.
Modules need HTTP in the browser
Now double-click `index.html` (or `open index.html`) and look at the console. Chrome refuses to load the module:

blocks.code:
Access to script at 'file:///Users/you/lab/web/modules/app.js' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy: Cross origin requests are only supported for protocol schemes: chrome, chrome-untrusted, data, http, https.
Failed to load resource: net::ERR_FAILED

blocks.text: Module scripts are always fetched in CORS mode, and a page opened from `file://` has the opaque origin `null`, so the browser will not read the file. Serve the folder over HTTP instead, in one Terminal tab:

Open `http://localhost:8000/` (`open http://localhost:8000/` from a second tab). The server log shows the **module graph** being fetched: the page, then `app.js`, then `net.js`, which the browser discovered by reading `app.js`'s import line. The console prints the same five lines as Node. Module files must be served with a JavaScript MIME type; check it with curl:

blocks.code:
$ curl -sI http://localhost:8000/app.js
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.15.2
Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:26:16 GMT
Content-type: text/javascript
Content-Length: 356
Last-Modified: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:25:52 GMT

index.html
    └─ <script type="module" src="app.js">          fetched after the HTML is parsed
         app.js ──import──▶ net.js                    fetched when app.js is parsed
           │                  exports: default isPrivate, ipToInt, inSubnet, PRIVATE
           └─ import('./report.js')  ⟪d:dynamic: fetched only when this line runs⟫

blocks.text: Three browser rules differ from Node and Python. Specifiers must be URLs: `'./net.js'` with the `./` and the extension, never `'net'`. A **bare specifier** such as `'lodash'` works only with an import map or a bundler (Vite, esbuild), which resolve npm packages. And every module is a separate HTTP request, which bundlers combine for production.
**Dynamic `import()`** loads a module at run time and returns a promise for its namespace. Use it to load heavy code only when needed:
CommonJS, briefly

Before ESM, Node used **CommonJS**: `require()` loads a module synchronously and `module.exports` defines what it provides. Most npm packages and older tutorials still use it, and Node supports both (the [Node.js chapter](#node) covers interop). It does not work in browsers without a bundler.

blocks.name: export
blocks.sum: Make a module's declarations available to importers, by name or as the default.
blocks.syntax: export const x = 1;    export function f() {}    export { a, b as c };    export default value;    export * from './other.js';

how.text: Named exports are imported by their exact names; a module can have any number. One **default** export per module is imported under any name the importer picks. `export { name } from './x.js'` and `export * from './x.js'` re-export another module's bindings, which is how a folder offers a single entry file. Exports are static: they must appear at the top level, never inside `if` or functions.

examples.desc: Named and default exports seen through a namespace (a data: URL stands in for a file)
Gather a module's exports and pass them on as one object
examples.code: import * as net from './net.js'; export const helpers = { ...net, version: 1 };

gotchas: Prefer named exports for libraries: they are checked by name, autocomplete well and rename consistently, while every importer can call a default export something different.

blocks.name: import
blocks.sum: Bring another module's exports into this module's scope.
blocks.syntax: import def from './m.js';    import { a, b as c } from './m.js';    import * as ns from './m.js';    import './side-effect.js';

how.text: Static imports are hoisted: the whole module graph is fetched, parsed and linked before any of its code runs, which is why a missing export is reported before the first line executes. Specifiers are URLs in browsers (relative paths need `./` or `../` and the file extension) and paths or package names in Node (`'node:fs'` for built-ins). Imported bindings are live and read-only.

examples.desc: A static import with a default and a named export (a data: URL stands in for a file)
examples.code:
import hello, { port } from 'data:text/javascript,export const port = 22; export default () => "hi";';
console.log(port, hello());

examples.desc: Import helpers and chain them in the importing module
examples.code:
import { ipToInt } from './net.js';
const sorted = ips.toSorted((a, b) => ipToInt(a) - ipToInt(b));

gotchas: Opening a page with `<script type="module">` from `file://` fails with a CORS error in Chrome. Serve the folder with `python3 -m http.server`.

blocks.name: import()
blocks.sum: Load a module at run time; returns a promise for its namespace object.

how.text: Unlike the `import` statement, `import()` is an expression usable anywhere, including inside functions and conditionals, and the specifier may be computed. The module is fetched and evaluated the first time; later calls get the same cached namespace. It works in classic scripts and CommonJS too, which makes it the bridge from old code to ES modules.

examples.desc: Load the same module twice: evaluated once, cached
Choose a module by feature, then use it

blocks.text: The event loop

JavaScript runs your code on **one thread**. There is never a second line of your code running at the same moment, so there are no data races, and also nothing that waits: a network request or a timer is handed to the host (the browser, or libuv in Node), and your code keeps going. When the host finishes, it queues a callback, and the **event loop** runs it when the call stack is empty.

blocks.code:
┌─────────────┐    hand off     ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │ ⟪y:call stack⟫  │ ──────────────▶ │ host: timers, network,   │
   │ (your code) │                 │ disk, DOM events         │
   └──────▲──────┘                 └────────────┬─────────────┘
          │                                     │ done: queue the callback
          │        ┌───────────────────────┐    ▼
          │ ⟪g:first⟫  │ microtask queue       │  ┌───────────────────────┐
          ├─────── │ promise callbacks,    │  │ task queue            │
          │        │ await continuations,  │  │ timers, I/O, events   │
          │        │ queueMicrotask        │  └───────────┬───────────┘
          │        └───────────────────────┘              │ ⟪c:then one task⟫
          └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   loop: script → drain ALL microtasks → (browser may render) → ONE task → repeat

blocks.text: Two queues matter. **Tasks** (also called macrotasks) come from timers, network and I/O completions and user events. **Microtasks** come from promise reactions (`then`, `catch`, `finally`), `await` continuations and `queueMicrotask`. After the script, and after every task, the engine runs **all** queued microtasks, including any that those microtasks queue, before it takes the next task. Step through the four programs in the widget (the chips switch between them), then predict the box below before running it.

blocks.out:
sync: script starts
sync: async function body
sync: script ends
microtask: then
microtask: queueMicrotask
microtask: after await
task: timeout 0
task: timeout 10

blocks.text: The body of an async function runs synchronously until its first `await`, so it printed second. The three microtasks ran in the order they were queued, all before the zero-delay timer: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` means "as a task, as soon as possible", never "now". Browsers also clamp the delay to at least 4 ms once timers are nested five levels deep, and inactive tabs throttle timers to once per second or less.
Because everything shares one thread, a long computation blocks timers, network callbacks, clicks and rendering until it finishes:

blocks.out:
loop done
the 0 ms timer ran after the loop: true

blocks.text: In a page, those 200 ms are a frozen tab. Split long work into chunks (`await` a zero-delay timer between chunks) or move it to a Web Worker, which runs on a separate thread and talks to the page by messages. Node's loop has extra phases and two Node-only queues (`process.nextTick` and `setImmediate`); the [Node.js chapter](#node) covers them.

blocks.name: setTimeout()
blocks.sum: Run a function once, as a task, after at least the given delay; clearTimeout cancels it.

how.text: The host starts a timer and, when it expires, queues `fn` as a task; it runs when the call stack is empty and earlier tasks are done, so the delay is a minimum. Extra arguments are passed to `fn`. In browsers the id is a number; in Node it is a `Timeout` object (still accepted by `clearTimeout`). Wrapping it in a promise gives the `sleep` helper JavaScript lacks.

examples.desc: Order of timers and a sleep helper
Wait between retries in a loop
examples.code: for (const ms of [100, 200, 400]) { if (await tryOnce()) break; await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)); }

gotchas: `setTimeout(obj.method, 100)` loses `this`. Write `setTimeout(() => obj.method(), 100)`.

blocks.name: setInterval()
blocks.sum: Run a function repeatedly every delay milliseconds until clearInterval is called.

how.text: Each expiry queues `fn` as a task. If a run takes longer than the interval, calls do not stack up in parallel; they run late. For polling a server, a chain of `setTimeout` calls, each scheduled after the previous request finished, is safer than `setInterval`, which keeps firing even while a slow request is still pending. Always keep the id so you can stop it.

examples.desc: Poll three times, then stop
examples.code:
let n = 0;
const id = setInterval(() => { n++; console.log('status check', n); if (n === 3) clearInterval(id); }, 50);
examples.out:
status check 1
status check 2
status check 3

examples.desc: Poll the practice server's status every 2 seconds (stop with clearInterval(timer))
examples.code: const timer = setInterval(() => fetch('/api/status').then((r) => r.json()).then((s) => console.log(`${s.online}/${s.devices} online`)), 2000);

blocks.name: queueMicrotask()
blocks.sum: Queue a function as a microtask: it runs after the current code, before any timer or other task.

how.text: The function joins the same queue that promise callbacks use, so it runs as soon as the current call stack empties and before rendering or the next task. Libraries use it to batch work ("do this once, after the current burst of changes"). A microtask that keeps queueing microtasks starves the task queue just as surely as an endless loop.

examples.desc: Microtask before task
Batch several updates into one render
examples.code: let pending = false; function scheduleRender() { if (!pending) { pending = true; queueMicrotask(() => { pending = false; render(); }); } }

blocks.text: Promises

Before promises, asynchronous APIs took a **callback**. Node's convention is error-first: `callback(err, result)`. One step is fine; several dependent steps nest into a pyramid, and every level must handle its own errors. A **Promise** is an object representing a result that will exist later. It starts **pending** and settles exactly once, either **fulfilled** with a value or **rejected** with a reason (normally an `Error`). You attach reactions with `then`, `catch` and `finally`, and they run as microtasks, even if the promise had already settled.

blocks.code:
resolve(value)
                   ┌──────────────────▶  ⟪g:fulfilled⟫  ──▶ .then(onFulfilled) callbacks
   new Promise ──▶ pending                       (each .then returns a new promise)
                   └──────────────────▶  ⟪r:rejected⟫   ──▶ .catch(onRejected) callbacks
                      reject(error) or a throw     .finally runs either way

blocks.out:
callback: 192.168.1.50
promise: 192.168.1.1
promise rejected: NXDOMAIN tv

blocks.text: `resolveHostP` is the standard way to wrap a callback API ("promisify" it; Node ships `util.promisify` for error-first callbacks).
Chaining

`then` returns a **new** promise that settles with whatever its callback returns. Return a plain value and the next `then` receives it; return a promise and the chain waits for it; throw and the chain skips to the next `catch`. A `catch` that returns normally puts the chain back on the success path.

blocks.out:
caught RangeError too big: 7
finally: clean up
after catch: recovered

blocks.text: A rejection that no `catch` handles is reported as an **unhandled rejection**: the browser console shows `Uncaught (in promise)`, and Node prints the error and exits with status 1. Always end a chain with `catch`, or `await` it inside `try`.
Running promises together

head: Combinator
Settles when
Result
Use it for
rows: all fulfil, or the first rejects
array of values in input order
independent requests that must all succeed
array of `{ status, value }` or `{ status, reason }`
batch jobs where some may fail
the first fulfils, or all reject

blocks.out:
5 of 6 online; [ 'pi', 'homeassistant' ]
[ 'pi', '404 for /api/devices/9', '500 for /api/error' ]
all() rejected: 404 for /api/devices/9
race: timeout after 300 ms
any: router
AggregateError [ '500 for /api/error', '404 for /api/devices/9' ]

blocks.text: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one input rejects, but it cannot cancel the others: they keep running and their results are thrown away. The race shows the same thing: the slow request still completed 1.2 seconds after the timeout won, which is why real timeouts use `AbortController` (in the fetch section) to actually stop the request.

blocks.name: Promise
blocks.sum: Create a promise from a function that receives resolve and reject; Promise.resolve and Promise.reject make settled ones.
blocks.syntax: new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })    Promise.resolve(value)    Promise.reject(error)    Promise.withResolvers()

how.text: The executor function runs immediately and synchronously. Call `resolve(value)` once the result exists or `reject(error)` on failure; later calls are ignored, and an exception thrown inside the executor rejects the promise. Resolving with another promise makes this one follow it. Wrap callback-style APIs this way; for code that already returns promises, `async` functions are clearer than `new Promise`.

examples.desc: Promisify a timer and settle once
Turn a callback API into a promise, then chain on it
examples.code: const ip = await new Promise((res, rej) => resolveHost('pi', (err, v) => (err ? rej(err) : res(v))));

gotchas: Creating a promise does not make code run in the background: the executor runs synchronously, on the one thread. Only the host's work (timers, network) happens elsewhere.

blocks.name: Promise.prototype.then()
blocks.sum: Register callbacks for fulfilment (and optionally rejection); returns a new promise for chaining. catch and finally are shorthands.

how.text: Callbacks always run as microtasks, after the current code. The returned promise resolves with the callback's return value, follows a returned promise, or rejects with a thrown error, which is what makes linear chains possible. `catch(f)` is `then(undefined, f)`. `finally(f)` runs `f` with no argument on either outcome and passes the original result or error through unchanged.

examples.desc: Values, promises and errors flowing through a chain
examples.code:
Promise.resolve(2)
  .then((n) => n * 10)
  .then((n) => { throw new Error(`stop at ${n}`); })
  .catch((e) => e.message)
  .then((msg) => console.log('chain result:', msg));

examples.desc: fetch, check, parse, transform in one chain

blocks.name: Promise.all()
blocks.sum: Wait for several promises in parallel; fulfils with all values in order, or rejects with the first error.

how.text: All inputs are already running when you pass them in (calling `fetch` starts the request), so `Promise.all` only waits. The result array matches input order, not completion order. Non-promise values are passed through. One rejection rejects the whole thing immediately; use `allSettled` when partial results are acceptable.

examples.desc: Two requests in parallel, destructured
examples.code:
const [s, d] = await Promise.all([fetch('/api/status').then((r) => r.json()), fetch('/api/devices/3').then((r) => r.json())]);
console.log(s.host, d.name, await Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2)]));

examples.desc: Fetch details for many ids at once
examples.code: const names = (await Promise.all([1, 3, 6].map((id) => fetch(`/api/devices/${id}`).then((r) => r.json())))).map((d) => d.name);

gotchas: `await` inside a `for` loop runs requests one after another. To run them in parallel, create all the promises first (`ids.map(...)`) and await `Promise.all` once.

blocks.name: Promise.allSettled()
blocks.sum: Wait for every promise to settle and report each outcome; never rejects.

how.text: Each result is `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`, in input order. Use it for batch operations such as checking many hosts, where one failure should not hide the other answers.

examples.desc: Mixed outcomes
examples.code:
const rs = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve('up'), Promise.reject(new Error('down'))]);
console.log(rs.map((r) => r.status), rs[1].reason.message);

examples.desc: Split results into successes and failures

blocks.name: Promise.race()
blocks.sum: Settle like the first input promise to settle, fulfilled or rejected.

how.text: The classic use is a timeout: race the real work against a promise that rejects after N milliseconds. The losers are not cancelled; they run to completion and their results are ignored. `Promise.any` is the variant that ignores rejections and waits for the first success.

examples.desc: A timer race
examples.code:
const after = (ms, v) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms, v));
console.log(await Promise.race([after(50, 'slow'), after(10, 'fast')]));

examples.desc: Give any promise a deadline
examples.code: const withDeadline = (p, ms) => Promise.race([p, new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(new Error('deadline')), ms))]);

blocks.name: Promise.any()
blocks.sum: Fulfil with the first input that fulfils; reject with an AggregateError only if all reject.

how.text: Rejections are ignored while at least one input can still succeed. If every input rejects, the result rejects with an `AggregateError` whose `errors` array holds every reason in input order. Use it to take the fastest of several equivalent sources, such as mirrors or redundant DNS resolvers.

examples.desc: First success wins
The fastest of several resolvers
examples.code: const answer = await Promise.any(['https://cors.example/a', 'https://api.example.com/a'].map((u) => fetch(u).then((r) => r.json())));

blocks.text: async and await

`async` and `await` let you write promise code that reads top to bottom. An **async function** always returns a promise: returning a value fulfils it, throwing rejects it. Inside it, **`await p`** pauses that function (not the program) until `p` settles, then evaluates to the value or throws the rejection, so ordinary `try`/`catch` handles asynchronous errors. While the function is paused, the event loop runs other code; its continuation is queued as a microtask when the promise settles. In ES modules, including every jsrun box, `await` also works at the top level.
Logging `p` without `await` shows `Promise { <pending> }`: forgetting `await` is the most common async bug, and the symptom is a promise where you expected data.
Sequential or parallel
`await` in a loop waits for each request before starting the next. When the requests are independent, start them all and await them together:

blocks.out: [ 'router', 'pi', 'homeassistant' ] [ 'router', 'pi', 'homeassistant' ] sequential took over twice as long: true

blocks.text: Each practice-server response takes about 40 ms, so the loop took about 120 ms and the parallel version about 40. Against a real API over Wi-Fi the difference is the same in shape and larger in size. Use the loop only when each request needs the previous result, or when you must limit the load on the server.
The callback-taking array methods do not understand promises. `forEach` with an `async` callback starts every call and returns immediately, without waiting:

Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential work and `Promise.all(arr.map(async ...))` for parallel work. `for await (const x of source)` loops over **async iterables**, such as a response body stream in Node, awaiting each item.

blocks.name: async function
blocks.sum: Declare a function that always returns a promise and may use await inside.
blocks.syntax: async function f() { ... }    const f = async (x) => { ... }    class C { async load() { ... } }

how.text: The body runs synchronously until the first `await`; from then on the function is suspended and resumed by microtasks. `return v` fulfils the returned promise with `v` (or follows it, if `v` is a promise); `throw` rejects it. Callers either `await` the result or attach `then`/`catch`. Arrow functions and methods can be async too.

examples.desc: Return and throw become fulfil and reject
An async step in a pipeline

blocks.name: await
blocks.sum: Pause an async function (or module) until a promise settles, then continue with its value or throw its error.

how.text: Allowed inside async functions and at the top level of ES modules. A non-promise value is wrapped and returned on the next microtask. A rejection becomes a thrown exception at the `await`, so `try`/`catch`/`finally` work as they do for synchronous code. Each `await` gives other queued work a chance to run, so state may have changed when the function resumes.

examples.desc: Await values, promises and failures
examples.code:
console.log(await 5, await Promise.resolve('resolved'));
try { await Promise.reject(new Error('refused')); } catch (e) { console.log('caught', e.message); }

examples.desc: Two awaits in one expression: response, then body

gotchas: `await` inside `forEach`, `map` or `filter` callbacks does not make the outer code wait. Use `for...of`, or `await Promise.all(arr.map(async ...))`.

blocks.text: fetch in depth

`fetch(url, options)` sends an HTTP request and returns a promise for a **Response**. The promise fulfils as soon as the status line and headers arrive; the body is read separately with `json()`, `text()`, `blob()` or `arrayBuffer()`, each returning another promise. The key rule: **fetch rejects only when no HTTP response arrived** (DNS failure, refused connection, CORS block, abort). A 404 or 500 is a successful fetch of an error page, so you must check `res.ok` (true for 200 to 299) or `res.status` yourself.

blocks.out:
true 200 OK http://lab.local/api/devices?type=server
application/json; charset=utf-8 2
[ '192.168.1.50', '192.168.1.90' ]
second read of the body: TypeError
false 404 { error: 'device 9 not found' }
no response at all: TypeError

blocks.text: A body is a stream and can be read once (`res.clone()` before reading if you need it twice). Header names are case-insensitive. Network failures reject with a `TypeError` whose message depends on the browser ("Failed to fetch" in Chrome, "Load failed" in Safari), so test the type, not the text.
Sending data and headers

To send JSON, set `method`, a `Content-Type` header and a string body made by `JSON.stringify`. The practice server answers a valid new device with `201 Created` and a `Location` header, and invalid input with `400` or `422` and a JSON error body, which your code should read and show:

blocks.title: A POST request with a JSON body

tokens.exp: send a request to this URL; the second argument holds the options
the HTTP method (GET is the default)
tell the server how the body is encoded
the body must be a string (or FormData, Blob, URLSearchParams)
the promise fulfils with a Response once the headers arrive, whatever the status

blocks.text: `URLSearchParams` encoded `pi & nas` safely; building query strings by concatenation breaks on `&`, `=` and spaces. The echo endpoint shows exactly what your code sent.

`lab-token` is a practice value. A real API key or password in browser JavaScript is readable by anyone who opens DevTools (Sources and Network show everything the page loads and sends). Keep secrets on a server you control and let it call the API; in Node, read them from environment variables, never from committed files.
Timeouts and cancellation
`fetch` has no timeout option. An **AbortController** provides a signal you pass to `fetch`; calling `abort()` cancels the request, closes the connection and rejects the promise with an `AbortError`:

The `finally` clears the timer on both paths. Modern runtimes also offer `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)`, a ready-made signal that aborts after `ms` and rejects the fetch with a `TimeoutError` instead of an `AbortError`, and `AbortSignal.any([a, b])` to combine a user's cancel button with a timeout.
Retrying

Transient failures (503, 429, a dropped Wi-Fi connection) deserve a retry with a pause; permanent ones (400, 404) do not. `/api/flaky` fails every other call with `503` and a `Retry-After` header in seconds:

blocks.out:
attempt 1: 503, retrying in 1000 ms
{ ok: true, attempt: 2 }

blocks.text: Real clients add **exponential backoff** (double the wait each time) with some random jitter, so that thousands of clients do not retry at the same instant. Now watch requests happen. Click both buttons a few times, then select a row in the Network pane to see its headers and body:

blocks.code: --- js const out = document.querySelector('#out'); function show(text) { const li = document.createElement('li'); li.textContent = text; out.append(li); } document.querySelector('#load').addEventListener('click', async () => { const res = await fetch('/api/devices?online=true'); const list = await res.json(); show(`${res.status}: ${list.map((d) => d.name).join(', ')}`); }); document.querySelector('#flaky').addEventListener('click', async () => { const res = await fetch('/api/flaky'); show(`flaky answered ${res.status} (Retry-After: ${res.headers.get('retry-after') ?? 'none'})`); });

blocks.text: In the Network pane, compare a `503` and a `200` from `/api/flaky` and find the `Retry-After` response header. Then switch to the Console and type `await (await fetch('/api/me', { headers: { Authorization: 'Bearer lab-token' } })).json()`; the request appears in Network with your `Authorization` header.

blocks.name: fetch()
blocks.sum: Send an HTTP request and get a promise for the Response; rejects only on network failure.
blocks.syntax: fetch(url, { method, headers, body, signal, credentials, cache, redirect }) -> Promise<Response>

how.text: The promise fulfils when the response headers arrive, with `res.status`, `res.ok`, `res.statusText`, `res.headers` and `res.url`; read the body with `await res.json()` (or `text()`, `blob()`, `arrayBuffer()`), once. HTTP error statuses do not reject: check `res.ok`. Requests to another origin are subject to CORS, which the browser enforces when reading the response. Global in browsers and in Node 18+.

examples.desc: Status, a header and the JSON body
The classic three-stage chain
The same data from Terminal with curl, for comparison
examples.code: curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/nodejs/node | node -e 'const r = JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8")); console.log(r.full_name, r.stargazers_count)'

gotchas: `if (res.status === 200)` misses 201 and 204. Use `res.ok` for "any success".

blocks.name: Response.prototype.json()
blocks.sum: Read a response body to the end and parse it as JSON.

how.text: Returns a promise for the parsed value; invalid JSON rejects with a `SyntaxError`. The body can be consumed only once: a second `json()` or `text()` rejects with a `TypeError`. `res.json()` ignores the `Content-Type` header, so check it (or read `text()` first) when an error page might come back as HTML. A `204 No Content` response has no body to parse.

examples.desc: Parse, then try to read again
Check the type before parsing
examples.code: const res = await fetch(url); const data = res.headers.get('content-type')?.includes('json') ? await res.json() : await res.text();

blocks.name: AbortController
blocks.sum: Create a signal that can cancel fetch requests (and other abortable operations) on demand.
blocks.syntax: const c = new AbortController();  fetch(url, { signal: c.signal });  c.abort();    AbortSignal.timeout(ms)

how.text: `controller.signal` is passed to one or more operations; `controller.abort()` cancels them all, and the pending fetch rejects with a `DOMException` named `AbortError`. A controller is single-use. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` returns a signal that aborts by itself (rejecting with `TimeoutError`), and `AbortSignal.any(signals)` aborts when any of several signals does. Event listeners accept a `signal` option too, which removes them on abort.

examples.desc: Abort a slow request
Cancel the previous search when the user types again
examples.code: let current; async function search(q) { current?.abort(); current = new AbortController(); return (await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, { signal: current.signal })).json(); }

blocks.text: Regular expressions

JavaScript has regular expressions built into the syntax: `/pattern/flags` is a **RegExp literal**, compiled once when the code loads. `new RegExp(string, flags)` builds one from a string at run time, where every backslash must be doubled (`new RegExp('\\d+')`). The pattern language is the one you met with `grep -E` and Python's `re` ([Text tools](#text), [Files and regex in Python](#py-files)), and the widget below runs JavaScript's own engine.

head: Flag
Meaning
rows: global: find every match (`match`, `matchAll`, `replace` and `replaceAll` use it)
multiline: `^` and `$` match at every line break, not just the ends of the string
Unicode: code points, `\u{...}` escapes and `\p{...}` property classes; `v` is its stricter successor
sticky: match only exactly at `lastIndex` (for tokenizers)
indices: record start and end positions of each group

head: Method
Returns
Typical use
rows: without `g`: first match with groups; with `g`: array of all matched strings
extract several groups from every match
new string; `rep` may use `$1`, `$<name>` or be a function
splitting on variable whitespace or several separators
next match object or `null`; advances `lastIndex` with `g` or `y`

blocks.text: Parse the combined log format of `~/lab/access.log` with **named groups**, `(?<name>...)`, which put every field in `match.groups`:

blocks.out:
45.33.32.156    GET   404 /api/v1/orders
198.51.100.8    GET   304 /images/logo.png
172.16.5.9      GET   401 /.env
198.51.100.23   POST  403 /wp-login.php
[ 404, 304, 401, 403 ] 3 client errors

blocks.text: The `m` flag makes `^` match at the start of every line, and `g` lets `matchAll` find them all. `(?:...)` groups without capturing.

blocks.title: The start of the log-line pattern

tokens.exp: start of a line (with the m flag)
open a group named ip
one to three digits, then three times: a dot and one to three digits; (?:...) groups without capturing
close the ip group
two runs of non-space characters: the identity and user fields, usually -
a literal [, then everything up to ] captured as time, then the ]

blocks.text: Line three is the classic trap: a regex with the `g` (or `y`) flag remembers where its last match ended in `lastIndex`, so calling `test` repeatedly on the same string walks through the matches and eventually returns `false`. Use a regex without `g` for `test`, or reset `lastIndex = 0`. The replacement function received each match and returned its replacement, here masking the last octet for a log you want to share.

Named groups are `(?<name>...)` in JavaScript and `(?P<name>...)` in Python. JavaScript has no verbose (`re.X`) mode, so long patterns are built from smaller ones or commented in code. `\d` matches only ASCII 0-9 in JavaScript but any Unicode digit in Python 3. In JavaScript `$` without the `m` flag matches only at the very end; Python's `$` also matches before a final newline. There is no `re.match` that anchors implicitly: write `^`.

blocks.name: RegExp
blocks.sum: A regular expression object, written as a /pattern/flags literal or built with new RegExp(string, flags).
blocks.syntax: /pattern/flags    new RegExp(patternString, flags)    re.source  re.flags  re.lastIndex

how.text: Literals are compiled when the script loads and are best for fixed patterns. The constructor builds patterns at run time, for example from user input, but the string needs doubled backslashes and any user text must be escaped first (`RegExp.escape(text)` in the newest runtimes, or `text.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')`). A regex with `g` or `y` is stateful through `lastIndex`.

examples.desc: Literal versus constructor
Build a pattern from a list of hostnames
examples.code: const re = new RegExp(`^(?:${['pi', 'nas', 'router'].join('|')})\\.lan$`); const ok = ['pi.lan', 'tv.lan'].filter((h) => re.test(h));

blocks.name: RegExp.prototype.test()
blocks.sum: Return true if the pattern matches somewhere in the string.

how.text: The fastest way to ask "does it match?". Anchor with `^` and `$` to validate a whole string. With the `g` or `y` flag, `test` starts at `lastIndex` and updates it, so repeated calls on the same regex alternate between true and false; validation patterns should not have `g`.

examples.desc: Validate whole strings
Filter lines that look like errors

blocks.name: String.prototype.match()
blocks.sum: Match a string against a regex: the first match with its groups, or every matched string with the g flag.

how.text: Without `g`, the result is like `exec`: index 0 is the whole match, 1 onward are the groups, plus `index`, `input` and `groups` properties. With `g`, it is a plain array of every matched substring and the groups are lost. No match gives `null`, not an empty array, so guard with `?? []` before using array methods.

examples.desc: Groups without g, all matches with g
Extract all IPs from text and de-duplicate

blocks.name: String.prototype.matchAll()
blocks.sum: Return an iterator of every match object, with groups, for a global regex.

how.text: Each item is a full match object (index 0, numbered groups, `.index`, `.groups`), which `match` with `g` throws away. The regex must have the `g` flag, or a `TypeError` is thrown. The result is an iterator: loop over it with `for...of` or spread it into an array; it does not touch the original regex's `lastIndex`.

examples.desc: Key-value pairs from a config line
examples.code:
const line = 'host=pi port=22 user=admin';
for (const m of line.matchAll(/(?<key>\w+)=(?<value>\S+)/g)) console.log(m.groups.key, '->', m.groups.value);

examples.desc: Turn all key=value pairs into an object

blocks.name: String.prototype.replace() with a RegExp
blocks.sum: Replace regex matches using a template with $1 and $<name>, or a function that computes each replacement.
blocks.syntax: str.replace(regex, replacementString | (match, ...groups, index, input, groups) => string)

how.text: Without `g` only the first match is replaced; with `g` every match is. In a replacement string, `$&` is the whole match, `$1` to `$99` are numbered groups and `$<name>` is a named group. A replacement function receives the match, then each group, then the index, the input and the groups object, and returns the replacement text. `replaceAll` with a regex requires `g`.

examples.desc: Template and function replacements
Anonymise the last octet of every IP in a log before sharing it

blocks.text: Modern patterns: options objects and deep copies

JavaScript has no keyword arguments. The idiom is a single **options object** destructured in the parameter list, with defaults for each field and `= {}` so that calling with no argument works. Callers name only what they change, in any order, and adding an option later breaks nobody:

blocks.out:
pi ports=22,80,443 timeout=500ms
nas ports=445 timeout=500ms (verbose)
undefined ports=22,80,443 timeout=500ms

blocks.text: For copies, you now have three tools with different depths. Spread copies one level. A JSON round trip copies plain data deeply but turns dates into strings, drops Sets and fails on cycles. **`structuredClone`** (browsers and Node 17+) copies deeply and keeps dates, Maps, Sets, typed arrays and even circular references; it refuses functions and does not keep class prototypes.

blocks.out:
30 20 TypeError
true true true false
DataCloneError

blocks.text: Changing the VLAN through `shallow` changed the original (they share `net`); changing it through `deep` did not. JSON could not handle the cycle, and cloning a function threw a `DataCloneError`.

blocks.name: structuredClone()
blocks.sum: Make a deep copy of a value, preserving dates, Maps, Sets and circular references.

how.text: Uses the structured clone algorithm that browsers use to send data between windows and workers. Supported: primitives, plain objects and arrays, `Date`, `RegExp`, `Map`, `Set`, `ArrayBuffer` and typed arrays, `Blob`, `Error` objects, and graphs with cycles. Not supported: functions and DOM nodes, which throw a `DataCloneError`. Class instances are copied as plain objects, losing their methods and private fields.

examples.desc: Deep copy of nested data
Snapshot state before changing it, to compare later
examples.code: const before = structuredClone(state); applyUpdate(state); const changed = JSON.stringify(before) !== JSON.stringify(state);

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **Passing a method as a callback.** `setTimeout(obj.tick, 100)` and `addEventListener('click', obj.handle)` lose `this`. Use an arrow wrapper or `bind`.
**Using an arrow function as a method.** It takes `this` from the surrounding code, not from the object. Use method syntax in objects and classes.
**Forgetting `await`.** You get `Promise { <pending> }` instead of data, and errors become unhandled rejections.
**Treating a 404 as a fetch failure.** `fetch` resolves for every HTTP status. Check `res.ok`.
**`await` inside `forEach`.** Nothing waits. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all(arr.map(async ...))`.
**Awaiting independent requests one by one.** Start them together with `Promise.all`.
**A `g` regex reused with `test`.** `lastIndex` makes results alternate. Drop `g` for validation.
**Opening module pages from `file://`.** Serve the folder over HTTP.
**`super()` missing or late in a subclass constructor.** `this` cannot be used before it.
**Catching everything and continuing.** Catch the types you can handle and rethrow the rest, or a bug turns into silent wrong output.
**Relying on engine error messages.** They differ between V8 and JavaScriptCore; test `err.name` or `instanceof`.
**Secrets in client JavaScript.** Private fields and minified code are still readable in DevTools.

blocks.text: Practice
The JavaScript exercises are checked in the page. They run as classic scripts: async code goes in an `async function main()` that the program calls.

blocks.title: Fetch in parallel with Promise.all

task.text: The starter works but awaits its two requests one after the other. Rewrite `summary()` so that it starts both requests at once and awaits them together with `Promise.all`. It must still return exactly `5/6 online; offline: nas; servers: pi, homeassistant` (built from `/api/status` and `/api/devices`), which the program prints.

hints: Create both promises before any `await`: `const [statusRes, devicesRes] = await Promise.all([fetch('/api/status'), fetch('/api/devices')]);`
