blocks.name: element.style
blocks.sum: Read and write an element's inline style declarations; getComputedStyle() reads the final values after the cascade.

how.text: `el.style` is the element's **inline** `style` attribute as an object with camelCase properties (`backgroundColor` for `background-color`). It only shows what was set inline, so `el.style.color` is usually `''` even when a stylesheet makes the text red. Values are strings with units: `el.style.width = 40 + '%'`. Custom properties need `setProperty('--bar', '40%')`.

`getComputedStyle(el)` returns the resolved values after every stylesheet, inheritance and inline rule, in absolute units (`rgb(...)`, `px`). It is read-only and forces style calculation, so do not call it in tight loops.

blocks.text: Creating, inserting and removing

New content is built from nodes. `document.createElement('li')` makes a detached element; you fill it with `textContent` and attributes, then attach it somewhere. Since 2016 or so every engine supports the convenient insertion methods below, which accept any number of nodes **and strings** (strings become text nodes, never HTML).

blocks.text: Inserting a node that is already in the tree **moves** it; a node has exactly one parent. Clone it if you want two.
Batches: DocumentFragment and template

Each insertion into a live document may invalidate style and layout. Appending 500 rows one by one is usually fine in modern engines because layout runs lazily, but reading a layout value in between (see [Performance](#perf)) makes it slow. A `DocumentFragment` is a lightweight, parentless container: build the rows inside it, then insert the fragment once. Appending a fragment moves its children and leaves it empty.

A `<template>` element holds inert markup: it is parsed but not rendered, its images do not load, and its scripts do not run. Its `.content` is a `DocumentFragment` you clone for each record. This keeps the markup in HTML, where it belongs, and the data in JavaScript.

blocks.name: document.createElement()
blocks.sum: Create a new, detached element with the given tag name.

how.text: Returns an element that belongs to the document but is not in the tree yet, so nothing renders until you insert it. Set its text with `textContent`, attributes with `setAttribute` or properties, then attach it with `append`, `before` and friends. In an HTML document the tag name is lower-cased and the element is in the HTML namespace.
`Object.assign(document.createElement('a'), { href: '/api/status', textContent: 'status' })` is a compact way to create and configure in one expression.

gotchas: SVG elements need `document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'rect')`; `createElement('rect')` makes an unknown HTML element that never draws (see [SVG](#xml/svg)).

blocks.name: element.append()
blocks.sum: Insert nodes or strings after the last child of an element (prepend inserts before the first).

how.text: Accepts any number of `Node`s and strings; strings become `Text` nodes, never HTML, so `append(userInput)` is XSS-safe. A node that is already in the document is **moved**, not copied. A `DocumentFragment` argument inserts its children and leaves the fragment empty.
The older `appendChild(node)` takes exactly one node, rejects strings and returns the inserted node.

examples.desc: A label and a value inside one element
Fetch, map to elements, insert all at once

gotchas: `list.append('x')` shows the literal text `x`. That is the point; build an element if you want bold.

blocks.name: element.before()
blocks.sum: Insert nodes or strings just before (or with after(), just after) an element, as its siblings.

how.text: Places the new nodes immediately before or after `el` in its parent. It works like `append` (strings become text, existing nodes move) and replaces the old `parent.insertBefore(node, el.nextSibling)` dance.

examples.desc: Insert a heading above the table
Add an error message right after the field that failed

blocks.name: element.remove()
blocks.sum: Detach an element from the tree; replaceWith() swaps it for other nodes and replaceChildren() empties or refills a parent.

how.text: `remove()` takes the element out of its parent. The object still exists while you hold a reference, so you can insert it elsewhere later. Its event listeners are garbage-collected with it once nothing points at it. `replaceWith` removes the element and inserts the given nodes in its place in one step.

`replaceChildren()` with no arguments removes every child, the clean way to clear a list before re-rendering; with arguments it clears and appends in one operation, so the user never sees an empty intermediate state.

examples.desc: Remove a deleted device's row
Re-render a list from new data in one swap

gotchas: Removing items while looping over a **live** collection (`children`, `getElementsBy...`) skips elements. Loop over a static copy: `[...list.children].forEach((li) => li.remove())`.

blocks.name: element.insertAdjacentHTML()
blocks.sum: Parse an HTML string and insert the nodes at one of four positions relative to an element.

how.text: Parses the string as HTML in the context of the element and inserts the result without touching existing children, so it is faster than `innerHTML +=` and keeps listeners on the old nodes. The positions are named after the element's tags: `beforebegin` (before the opening tag, a sibling), `afterbegin` (first child), `beforeend` (last child), `afterend` (after the closing tag, a sibling).
The companions `insertAdjacentElement(pos, el)` and `insertAdjacentText(pos, text)` insert a node or plain text at the same positions without parsing.

examples.desc: Add a static notice at the top of a panel
Append escaped rows from data

gotchas: It is an HTML sink: the same XSS rules as `innerHTML` apply. Escape every value or use `insertAdjacentText`.

blocks.name: document.createDocumentFragment()
blocks.sum: Create an empty, parentless container to build many nodes before inserting them in one operation.

how.text: A fragment is a minimal document-like node with no parent and no rendering. Nodes appended to it do not touch the live page, so building a big list inside it costs no style or layout work. When you append the fragment to the document, its children move into the tree in one operation and the fragment becomes empty, ready for reuse.

examples.desc: Build 254 host rows off-screen
examples.code: const frag = document.createDocumentFragment(); for (let i = 1; i < 255; i++) frag.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: `192.168.1.${i}` })); list.append(frag);

examples.desc: Fill a fragment from data, then swap it in

blocks.name: template.content.cloneNode()
blocks.sum: Deep-copy the inert markup inside a template element so you can fill it with data and insert it.

how.text: The `<template>` element's children are parsed into a separate `DocumentFragment` (`.content`) owned by an inert document: nothing renders, images do not load, scripts do not run, and `template.children` is empty. Each `cloneNode(true)` gives you a fresh deep copy of that fragment. Query inside the copy, set `textContent` and attributes, then append it. `document.importNode(tpl.content, true)` does the same and adopts the nodes into the document.

examples.desc: One row per device from a template
examples.code: const row = tpl.content.cloneNode(true); row.querySelector('.name').textContent = d.name; tbody.append(row);

examples.desc: Template to fragment to page, for a whole list
examples.code: tbody.replaceChildren(...devices.map((d) => { const r = tpl.content.cloneNode(true); r.querySelector('.name').textContent = d.name; return r; }));

gotchas: Call `cloneNode(true)`. With `false` (or no argument in old code) you get an empty fragment.

blocks.text: Events in depth

The browser fires an **event** object whenever something happens: a click, a key press, a form submission, a network-driven image load, the document finishing parsing. Your code subscribes with `addEventListener`, and the browser calls your function from the event loop when the event occurs (see [the event loop](#js-deeper) for the queueing rules).

tokens.exp: the target: any Node, window or document
the event type, a string without the "on" prefix
{...}, => the listener; it receives the Event object

tokens.tok: { once: true, passive: true, capture: false, signal }
tokens.exp: options: run once, promise not to call preventDefault, which phase, abort to remove
returns undefined

head: Option
Effect
Typical use
rows: the listener removes itself after the first call
run during the capture phase (on the way down) instead of the bubble phase
intercept before children see the event
promise not to call `preventDefault()`, so the browser can scroll without waiting
the listener is removed when the `AbortController` aborts
remove many listeners at once on teardown

blocks.text: Inside the listener, the **event object** tells you what happened:

head: Property / method
Meaning
rows: the deepest element where the event started (what was actually clicked)
the element whose listener is running now (the one you attached to)
cancel the browser's default action (follow a link, submit a form, type a character)
stop the event travelling to further elements
keyboard: the character produced (`'/'`, `'Enter'`) and the physical key (`'Slash'`, `'Enter'`)
pointer position relative to the viewport / to the whole document
`true` for real user actions, `false` for events your code dispatched

blocks.text: This program attaches four listeners to a form and its button, then clicks the button twice from code. Predict the output, then run it.

blocks.page: <form id="add"><input name="name" value="pi"> <button>Add</button></form>
blocks.out:
form, capture phase 1
button, at target 2 trusted: false
form, bubble phase 3 BUTTON FORM
--- second click
form, capture phase 1
form, bubble phase 3 BUTTON FORM
submit event

blocks.text: The first click travelled down to the button (capture), hit it (target), and bubbled back up. The button's listener called `preventDefault()`, which cancelled the button's default action, submitting the form. The listener had `once: true`, so on the second click it was gone, nothing cancelled the default, and the form's `submit` event fired. Without the `preventDefault()` in that submit listener, the browser would have navigated away (in your own pages, a full reload).
Propagation: capture, target, bubble

blocks.code:
⟪c:1. CAPTURE⟫ (down)                         ⟪m:3. BUBBLE⟫ (up)
   window ─────────────┐                          ┌──────────── window
   document ───────────┤                          ├──────────── document
   <body> ─────────────┤                          ├──────────── <body>
   <section#panel> ────┤                          ├──── <section#panel>   ◀ stopPropagation() here
   <div.card> ─────────┤                          ├──────── <div.card>       stops the rest
                       ▼                          │
                 ⟪y:2. TARGET⟫  <button#save>  ───────┘ 
                  listeners on the target run in registration order

blocks.text: Every event dispatched into the tree takes this path. Capture listeners run on the way down from `window`; then the target's own listeners; then, **if the event bubbles**, bubble listeners from the parent up to `window`. Most events bubble: `click`, `input`, `change`, `submit`, `keydown`. Some do not: `focus` and `blur` (use `focusin` and `focusout`, which do), `mouseenter` and `mouseleave`, and `load` or `error` on an ``. `stopPropagation()` stops the journey at the current element; `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on that same element. Neither cancels the default action; that is `preventDefault()`'s job.

Click the button in the widget and read the log. Then tick `stopPropagation()` and see `body` and `document` never hear about the click. Tick **delegate** and click the list items: one listener on the `ul` handles all three.
Event delegation

Because clicks bubble, you do not need a listener on every row. Put **one** listener on a stable container and ask, inside it, which item the click came from with `e.target.closest(...)`. This uses less memory, needs no clean-up when rows are removed, and, most importantly, works for rows that **do not exist yet** when the listener is attached.

blocks.page:
• router 192.168.1.1
  • nas 192.168.1.60
blocks.out:
direct: router 192.168.1.1
delegated: router
delegated: pi

blocks.text: The `pi` row was created after the loop ran, so it has no direct listener. The delegated one caught the click anyway, even though the click landed on the `<b>` inside the row: `closest('li')` climbed from `b` to `li`.
Which events, and when the page is ready

head: Event
Fires when
Bubbles
Notes
rows: primary button pressed and released on the same element, or Enter/Space on a focused button
keyboard activation is free if you use `<button>`, not a `<div>`
the value of an input, textarea or select changes, on every keystroke
the change is committed: blur for text fields, immediately for checkboxes, radios, selects
a form is submitted by button, Enter in a field, or `requestSubmit()`
one model for every pointer type
the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run (images may still load)
the page and every sub-resource (images, styles) finished
rarely what you want; later than DOMContentLoaded
the tab is hidden or shown

blocks.text: The most common DOM bug of all is a script that runs before the elements it needs exist. A classic `<script src="app.js">` in `<head>` runs as soon as the parser reaches it, **before** `<body>` is parsed, so `document.querySelector('#status')` returns `null` and the next line throws `TypeError: Cannot set properties of null`. The fixes, best first:

head: Script tag
Runs when
Order
rows: after parsing (modules are deferred by default)
when the parser reaches it (elements above exist)
as soon as it downloads, maybe before parsing ends
**any** order: only for independent scripts such as analytics

blocks.text: With `defer` or `type="module"` you do not need `document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', ...)` at all.

Last key: (none)

--- js const q = document.querySelector('#q'); const keyOut = document.querySelector('#key'); document.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => { keyOut.textContent = `key=${JSON.stringify(e.key)} code=${e.code} shift=${e.shiftKey} in=${e.target.tagName}`; if (e.key === '/' && e.target !== q) { // a site-wide shortcut, like GitHub's e.preventDefault(); // do not type the "/" anywhere q.focus(); } else if (e.key === 'Escape' && e.target === q) { q.value = ''; q.blur(); } }); q.addEventListener('focus', () => console.log('focus (does not bubble)')); document.addEventListener('focusin', (e) => console.log('focusin bubbled up from #' + e.target.id)); q.addEventListener('input', () => console.log('input:', q.value)); q.addEventListener('change', () => console.log('change (committed):', q.value));

(Chrome also has `getEventListeners($0)` to list the listeners on the selected element; this drawer does not.)

blocks.name: element.addEventListener()
blocks.sum: Register a function to be called whenever an event of the given type reaches the element.
blocks.syntax: target.addEventListener(type, listener, { once, capture, passive, signal } | useCapture)

how.text: Adds `listener` to the target's list for `type`. When an event of that type is dispatched and its path passes through the target in the matching phase (bubble by default, capture with `capture: true`), the browser calls the listener with the event object; `this` inside a `function` listener is `e.currentTarget` (arrow functions keep the outer `this`). Several listeners can share a type and run in registration order. Adding the very same function twice for the same type and phase is ignored.
The older `el.onclick = fn` property holds exactly one handler and a second assignment silently replaces the first. Prefer `addEventListener`.

examples.desc: React to a button click
One-time handler
Select many, attach to each (fine for a fixed set; use delegation for dynamic lists)
Remove a whole group of listeners with one abort
examples.code: const ac = new AbortController(); window.addEventListener('resize', onResize, { signal: ac.signal }); document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey, { signal: ac.signal }); ac.abort();

anat.exp: static list of the ping buttons
attach a click listener to that button
ping(b.closest('tr').dataset.ip)) => on click, climb to the row and ping its IP

gotchas: `addEventListener('click', load())` **calls** `load` immediately and registers its return value. Pass the function itself: `load` or `() => load()`.

blocks.name: element.removeEventListener()
blocks.sum: Unregister a listener previously added with the same type, function and capture flag.

how.text: The browser finds the listener by the triple (type, function object, capture flag). It must be the **same function object**, so an inline arrow function can never be removed: the arrow you pass to `removeEventListener` is a new function. Keep a named reference, or use the `signal` option and an `AbortController`, which removes any number of listeners with one `abort()` call.

examples.desc: Stop listening to scroll after the first time the footer is reached
examples.code: function onScroll() { if (nearBottom()) { loadMore(); window.removeEventListener('scroll', onScroll); } } window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });

examples.desc: Teardown with an AbortController
examples.code: const ac = new AbortController(); el.addEventListener('click', handler, { signal: ac.signal }); ac.signal.addEventListener('abort', () => console.log('listeners removed')); ac.abort();

gotchas: A listener added with `{ capture: true }` is only removed by a call that also passes `{ capture: true }`.

blocks.name: event.target
blocks.sum: The element where the event started; currentTarget is the element whose listener is running.

how.text: When you click the `<b>` inside an `<li>` inside a `<ul>` that has the listener, `e.target` is the `<b>` and `e.currentTarget` is the `<ul>`. `target` stays the same for the whole journey; `currentTarget` changes at each stop and is `null` once dispatch is over (so read it synchronously, not after an `await`).
For delegation, start at `target` and climb with `closest()` to the item you care about.

examples.desc: Which row and which container?
Target to item to data to request
examples.code: ul.addEventListener('click', (e) => { const id = e.target.closest('li')?.dataset.id; if (id) fetch(`/api/devices/${id}`).then((r) => r.json()).then((d) => console.log(d.name, d.ip)); });

gotchas: `e.target` can be a text-level element such as ``, `` inside your item. Never compare it directly with the item; use `closest()`.

blocks.name: event.preventDefault()
blocks.sum: Cancel the browser's default action for this event, such as following a link or submitting a form.

how.text: Many events have a built-in consequence that runs after all listeners: a `submit` navigates to the form's `action`, a click on a link follows `href`, a `keydown` types a character, a checkbox click toggles it. Calling `preventDefault()` in any listener during dispatch cancels that consequence (if the event is cancelable). `defaultPrevented` tells later listeners that someone already did.
It does **not** stop propagation; other listeners still run.

examples.desc: Handle a form with JavaScript instead of a page load
Intercept links into an in-page router
examples.code: document.addEventListener('click', (e) => { const a = e.target.closest('a[data-route]'); if (a) { e.preventDefault(); show(a.getAttribute('href')); } });

gotchas: Has no effect in a listener registered with `passive: true` (Chrome logs a warning) or on events that are not cancelable.

blocks.name: event.stopPropagation()
blocks.sum: Stop the event from reaching any further elements on its capture or bubble path.

how.text: Dispatch continues to the remaining listeners on the current element, then stops: ancestors (bubbling) or descendants (capturing) never see the event. `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on the current element. Use it sparingly: a click that never reaches `document` breaks every "close the menu when you click elsewhere" handler.

examples.desc: A delete button inside a clickable row
Prefer checking the target over stopping propagation

blocks.name: element.dispatchEvent()
blocks.sum: Fire an event at an element yourself, including CustomEvent objects that carry your own data.
blocks.syntax: target.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(type, { detail, bubbles, cancelable })) -> boolean

how.text: Runs the full capture, target and bubble path **synchronously**: every listener has finished before `dispatchEvent` returns. It returns `false` if a listener called `preventDefault()` on a cancelable event. Events you create default to `bubbles: false`, so pass `bubbles: true` when ancestors should hear them. `isTrusted` is `false` for these. A `CustomEvent` with a namespaced type (`device:selected`) and a `detail` payload lets one part of a page announce something without knowing who listens.

examples.desc: Announce a selection
examples.code: li.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('device:selected', { detail: { id: 3 }, bubbles: true }));

examples.desc: Listen high, dispatch low

gotchas: Dispatching `new Event('click')` does not trigger default actions such as following a link; `el.click()` does run the activation behaviour.

blocks.text: Forms, FormData and validation

A form submission is an event like any other. Listen for `submit` on the **form** (it fires for button clicks and for Enter in a text field), call `preventDefault()`, read the fields with `FormData`, and send them with `fetch`. You keep the browser's free features: Enter to submit, autofill, password managers, and built-in validation.

`new FormData(form)` collects exactly what a real submission would send: each successful control with a `name`. Unchecked checkboxes, disabled fields and fields without a `name` are left out, and every value is a string (`'on'` for a checked box without a `value`).

<form id="add">
  <input name="name" value="pi" required>
  <input name="ip" value="192.168.1.50" required pattern="\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}">
  <select name="type"><option>server</option><option selected>storage</option></select>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="online" checked> online</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="monitor"> monitor</label>
  <input name="note" value="rack 2" disabled>
  <input value="no name attribute">
  <button>Add</button>
</form>

blocks.text: The constraint validation API is what the browser uses for `required`, `type="email"`, `pattern`, `min`/`max` and `maxlength`:

items.text: `el.validity` is a `ValidityState` with one flag per rule (`valueMissing`, `typeMismatch`, `patternMismatch`, `rangeOverflow`, `tooLong`, `customError`) and a summary `valid`.
`form.checkValidity()` and `el.checkValidity()` return a boolean and fire `invalid` events; `reportValidity()` also shows the browser's message bubbles.

`el.setCustomValidity(msg)` marks a field invalid with your own message, for rules HTML cannot express (octets above 255, a name that is already taken). **Reset it with `''`** or the field stays invalid forever.

`form.requestSubmit()` behaves like clicking a submit button: validation runs first, and `submit` fires only if everything passes. The older `form.submit()` skips both validation and the `submit` event, so your listener never runs.

A `novalidate` attribute on the form switches the browser's checks off at submit time so your code (or the server) reports errors; the CSS pseudo-classes `:invalid` and `:user-invalid` (only after the user has interacted) still work for styling.

blocks.text: The server must validate anyway: anyone can send a request with `curl` and skip your page entirely. The practice API does, and it answers with `400` or `422` and a JSON error. Use this playground and its **Network** pane:

attrs.title: Add a device: POST JSON and show the API's answer

blocks.code:
--- css
form { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 8px 12px; align-items: center; }
input:user-invalid { outline: 2px solid #b00020; }
.error { color: #b00020; }
.ok { color: #11632b; }
pre { background: #f4f6f8; padding: 8px; font-size: 12px; }
--- js
const form = document.querySelector('#add');
const msg = document.querySelector('#msg');
const bodyOut = document.querySelector('#body');

form.addEventListener('submit', async (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();                                  // no page reload
  // if (!form.reportValidity()) return;               // let the browser check first
  const data = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(form));
  data.online = form.elements.online.checked;          // FormData would send "on" or nothing
  const res = await fetch('/api/devices', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(data),
  });
  const json = await res.json();
  msg.className = res.ok ? 'ok' : 'error';
  msg.textContent = res.ok ? `${res.status} Created ${json.name} (id ${json.id})` : `${res.status}: ${json.error}`;
  bodyOut.textContent = JSON.stringify(json, null, 2);
  console.log(res.status, res.headers.get('Location'));
  if (res.ok) form.reset();
});

items.text: Submit the empty form. The API answers `400` with `name and ip are required`. Click the request in **Network** and read the request body your code sent.
Enter a name and `192.168.1.300x`: `422 ip is not an IPv4 address`.
Enter a valid device: `201`, a `Location: /api/devices/7` header, and the new object. Submit again: id 8.

Uncomment the `reportValidity()` line and press Run. Now the browser blocks bad input before any request is sent, and nothing appears in Network. Both layers are useful: the browser for instant feedback, the server for the truth.

blocks.name: new FormData()
blocks.sum: Collect a form's named, enabled, successful controls as key/value pairs ready to send or inspect.
blocks.syntax: new FormData(form?, submitter?)    fd.get(name)  fd.getAll(name)  fd.set(name, value)  fd.append(name, value)  fd.has(name)  fd.entries()

how.text: Reads the form the way a real submission would: only controls with a `name`, not disabled, checkboxes and radios only when checked, `<select multiple>` once per selected option. Values are strings, or `File` objects for file inputs. It is iterable, so `Object.fromEntries(fd)` gives a plain object (keeping the last value for repeated names; use `getAll` for those).

Passed directly as a `fetch` body, it is sent as `multipart/form-data` with a generated boundary, which is what file uploads need. Wrap it as `new URLSearchParams(fd)` for `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, or convert to an object and `JSON.stringify` it for a JSON API.

Form to JSON to API

how.text: The constraint validation API exposes the browser's built-in rules (`required`, `type`, `pattern`, `min`, `max`, `minlength`) as `el.validity` flags. `setCustomValidity('msg')` sets the `customError` flag, so the field fails `checkValidity()`, matches `:invalid`, blocks `requestSubmit()` and shows your message in the bubble. Passing `''` clears it, and you must do that yourself, usually in an `input` listener, or the field never becomes valid again.
`checkValidity()` is silent; `reportValidity()` also focuses the first bad field and shows the message.

blocks.text: Rendering lists from data

Most interactive pages follow one loop: **fetch data, turn it into elements, put them on the page, react to events, repeat.** Write the "turn into elements" part as a function of the data (`render(devices)`), and always handle three states besides success: **loading**, **empty** and **error**. A list that silently stays blank when the API returns `500` is the most common front-end bug report.

blocks.out:
/api/error -> Could not load devices (HTTP 500). 0
/api/devices?type=camera -> No devices match. 0
/api/devices -> 6 devices 6
nas

blocks.text: `fetch` only rejects on network failure; an HTTP `500` is a successful *response*, which is why the code checks `res.ok` (status 200-299) and throws itself. Details of `fetch`, `res.ok` and `AbortController` are in [JavaScript in Depth](#js-deeper).
Re-render or update?

`replaceChildren(fragment)` throws away the old rows and builds new ones. It is simple and correct, and for a few hundred rows it is fast. It also destroys state the user cares about: focus inside a row, a half-typed edit, the scroll position of a nested box, a CSS transition in progress. When that matters, **update in place**: keep a `Map` from id to element, change only the rows whose data changed, add new ids, remove missing ones. Frameworks like React and Vue automate exactly this "keyed diff"; doing it by hand once teaches you what they do.
Timers in the UI: polling and debouncing

**Polling** means asking the server again on a schedule (`/api/status` every 5 seconds) and showing when you last succeeded. Prefer a `setTimeout` chain, which schedules the next request only after the previous one finished, to `setInterval`, which fires on schedule even if a slow response is still pending and can stack requests on a bad network. Stop polling when the tab is hidden (`document.visibilityState === 'hidden'`, `visibilitychange` event) to save battery and server load.

**Debouncing** means waiting until the user stops typing before acting. Without it, typing `printer` into a search box fires seven requests and the responses can arrive out of order, so the list may end up showing results for `pri`. A debounce restarts a timer on every call and only runs the function when the timer survives:

blocks.out:
search for nas
search for printer

blocks.text: Three calls at 0 ms and one at 50 ms all landed inside the 200 ms quiet window, so only the last (`nas`) ran, at 250 ms. The call at 600 ms came after a pause and ran too. This block is plain JavaScript with no DOM, so it runs the same in Node. The closure over `timer` is what makes it work ([closures](#js-deeper)). Pair a debounce with an `AbortController` so that a response for an old query can never overwrite a newer one.

blocks.text: Remembering state with localStorage

`localStorage` is a small, synchronous key/value store per **origin** (scheme + host + port), shared by every tab of that origin and kept across restarts. `sessionStorage` has the same API but lives only as long as the tab. Both store **strings only**: anything else is converted with `String()`, so objects must go through `JSON.stringify` and come back with `JSON.parse`.

blocks.out:
string 51
{ type: 'server', onlineOnly: true }
null
[object Object]
3

blocks.text: What it is good for: UI preferences such as a theme, a saved filter, a collapsed panel, an unsent draft. What it is not for: anything secret. Every script on the origin can read it, so one XSS bug leaks every token stored there; an `HttpOnly` cookie set by the server is out of script's reach. Quotas are roughly 5 MB per origin in current browsers (hedged: browsers differ), `setItem` throws `QuotaExceededError` when full, and private-browsing modes or blocked site data can make it throw or start empty, so wrap access in `try`/`catch` and keep the page working without it. A `storage` event fires in the *other* tabs of the origin when one tab changes a value.

attrs.title: Theme and filter that survive a reload

blocks.code: --- css body.dark { background: #15191d; color: #e6e6e6; } body.dark button, body.dark select { background: #2a3036; color: #e6e6e6; border: 1px solid #4a535b; } --- js const KEY = 'lab-prefs'; function loadPrefs() { try { return { theme: 'light', type: '', ...JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)) }; } catch { return { theme: 'light', type: '' }; } // bad JSON or storage blocked } function savePrefs(p) { try { localStorage.setItem(KEY, JSON.stringify(p)); } catch (err) { console.warn('not saved:', err.name); } } const prefs = loadPrefs(); if (localStorage.getItem(KEY) === null && matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches) prefs.theme = 'dark'; const select = document.querySelector('#type'); function apply() { document.body.classList.toggle('dark', prefs.theme === 'dark'); select.value = prefs.type; fetch('/api/devices' + (prefs.type ? '?type=' + prefs.type : '')) .then((r) => r.json()) .then((ds) => document.querySelector('#devices').replaceChildren(...ds.map((d) => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: `${d.name} (${d.type})` })))); } document.querySelector('#theme').addEventListener('click', () => { prefs.theme = prefs.theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'; savePrefs(prefs); apply(); }); select.addEventListener('change', () => { prefs.type = select.value; savePrefs(prefs); apply(); }); apply();

blocks.text: Performance: batching, layout and observers

To draw a frame the engine runs a pipeline: compute **style** for the elements that changed, compute **layout** (sizes and positions), **paint** pixels, then **composite** layers. DOM writes do not run that pipeline immediately; they mark things dirty, and the work happens once before the next frame. A *read* of a layout value (`offsetWidth`, `offsetTop`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, `scrollHeight`, `getComputedStyle().width`, `innerText`) forces the engine to bring layout up to date **now** so it can answer. Alternate writes and reads in a loop and you force a full layout per iteration: **layout thrashing**.

blocks.code:
⟪r:thrashing⟫  write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ▸ write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ▸ write ▸ ⟪r:READ⟫ ▸ layout ...   N layouts
 ⟪g:batched⟫    ⟪g:READ READ READ ...⟫ ▸ (1 layout) ▸ write write write ... ▸ next frame: 1 layout     2 layouts
               └──────── JavaScript task ────────┘        └─ style ▸ layout ▸ paint ▸ composite ─┘

blocks.text: Rules that keep pages fast:

items.text: **Read first, then write.** Gather every measurement you need, then apply every change.
**Batch insertions** with a `DocumentFragment`, `append(...nodes)` or `replaceChildren`.
**Toggle a class** instead of setting five inline properties; CSS does the rest in one style pass.
**Animate with `transform` and `opacity`**, which the compositor can move without layout; and schedule visual work with `requestAnimationFrame`.
**Delegate** events instead of attaching thousands of listeners.

blocks.code: --- css #bars div { height: 3px; margin: 1px 0; background: #4c8bf5; width: 50%; } --- js const bars = document.querySelector('#bars'); for (let i = 0; i < 800; i++) bars.append(document.createElement('div')); const all = [...bars.children]; document.querySelector('#slow').addEventListener('click', () => { console.time('interleaved'); for (const b of all) { const w = b.offsetWidth; // READ: forces layout, because... b.style.width = (w % 300) + 20 + 'px'; // ...this WRITE dirtied it last time } console.timeEnd('interleaved'); }); document.querySelector('#fast').addEventListener('click', () => { console.time('batched'); const widths = all.map((b) => b.offsetWidth); // all reads: one layout all.forEach((b, i) => { b.style.width = (widths[i] % 300) + 20 + 'px'; }); console.timeEnd('batched'); });

blocks.text: Click each button a few times and compare the timings in the Console. The exact numbers depend on your Mac and browser; the ratio is the lesson. Chrome's Performance panel shows the interleaved run as a wall of purple "Layout" blocks with a "Forced reflow" warning.
Watching the DOM: MutationObserver

A `MutationObserver` calls you back when nodes are added or removed, attributes change, or text changes, inside a subtree you choose. Callbacks are **batched and asynchronous**: the browser collects the records and delivers them as a microtask after the current script finishes, so a loop that adds 100 nodes produces one callback, not 100.

synchronous code finished
mutation: childList +2 -0 -
mutation: childList +0 -1 -
mutation: attributes +0 -0 data-state

blocks.text: Use it to react to content you do not control, such as a third-party widget; your own changes you already know about. (This playground's Elements pane uses one to know when to redraw.)
Seeing what is visible: IntersectionObserver

An `IntersectionObserver` tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or a scrolling container), computed by the browser during its rendering steps, without scroll listeners or layout reads in your code. It powers lazy loading, "load more" lists and "mark as read".

attrs.title: Load more hosts when the sentinel scrolls into view

blocks.code:
Scroll inside the box. More hosts load when the last line becomes visible.

    loading more…

    --- css #box { height: 150px; overflow: auto; border: 1px solid #c8d0d6; padding: 0 8px; font: 13px ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace; } --- js const list = document.querySelector('#list'); let n = 0; function addBatch() { const frag = document.createDocumentFragment(); for (let i = 0; i < 10 && n < 254; i++) { n++; frag.append(Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: `host-${String(n).padStart(3, '0')} 192.168.1.${n}` })); } list.append(frag); console.log('loaded up to', n); } const sentinel = document.querySelector('#sentinel'); const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => { if (!entries[0].isIntersecting) return; if (n >= 254) { io.disconnect(); sentinel.textContent = 'end of the /24'; return; } addBatch(); io.unobserve(sentinel); // callbacks fire on *changes*: if the sentinel is still io.observe(sentinel); // visible after this batch, re-observing reports it again }, { root: document.querySelector('#box'), rootMargin: '0px 0px 40px 0px' }); io.observe(sentinel);

blocks.name: new MutationObserver()
blocks.sum: Get batched, asynchronous callbacks when nodes, attributes or text change inside an observed subtree.
blocks.syntax: const mo = new MutationObserver((records, observer) => {...}); mo.observe(target, { childList, attributes, characterData, subtree, attributeFilter, attributeOldValue }); mo.disconnect(); mo.takeRecords()

how.text: You choose what to watch with the options object: `childList` (children added or removed), `attributes` (optionally limited by `attributeFilter`), `characterData` (text changes), and `subtree` to include all descendants. Each `MutationRecord` has `type`, `target`, `addedNodes`, `removedNodes`, `attributeName` and, if requested, `oldValue`.

Records are queued and delivered as a **microtask** after the current script, so the callback sees the final state of a burst of changes. `disconnect()` stops observing; `takeRecords()` empties the queue synchronously.

examples.desc: Log rows added to a table by someone else's script
examples.code: new MutationObserver((rs) => rs.forEach((r) => r.addedNodes.forEach((n) => console.log('added', n.textContent)))).observe(tbody, { childList: true });

examples.desc: Count changes by type
examples.code: new MutationObserver((rs) => console.log(Object.groupBy(rs, (r) => r.type))).observe(document.body, { childList: true, attributes: true, subtree: true });

gotchas: Changing the observed subtree inside the callback queues new records and can loop forever. Disconnect first, or guard with a flag.

blocks.name: new IntersectionObserver()
blocks.sum: Get a callback when observed elements start or stop intersecting the viewport or a scroll container.
blocks.syntax: const io = new IntersectionObserver((entries) => {...}, { root, rootMargin, threshold }); io.observe(el); io.unobserve(el); io.disconnect()

how.text: The browser computes intersections during its rendering steps, off your JavaScript, and calls back with `IntersectionObserverEntry` objects (`target`, `isIntersecting`, `intersectionRatio`, `boundingClientRect`). `root` is the scrolling ancestor (default: the viewport), `rootMargin` grows or shrinks it like CSS margins (start loading 200 px early), and `threshold` lists the visible fractions that trigger callbacks (`[0, 0.5, 1]`). It replaces scroll listeners that call `getBoundingClientRect()` on every frame.

examples.desc: Lazy-load images when they come close
examples.code: const io = new IntersectionObserver((es) => es.forEach((e) => { if (e.isIntersecting) { e.target.src = e.target.dataset.src; io.unobserve(e.target); } }), { rootMargin: '200px' });

examples.desc: Observe many elements at once

gotchas: For plain images, the HTML attribute `loading="lazy"` already does this without any script.

blocks.name: requestAnimationFrame()
blocks.sum: Run a function right before the browser's next repaint, once.

how.text: The callback runs in the rendering step of the event loop, just before style, layout and paint, usually 60 times a second (more on ProMotion displays) and **not at all** in background tabs. That makes it the right place for visual updates driven by JavaScript: you do your writes once per frame, aligned with the display, instead of whenever a timer or message happens to fire. The `timestamp` argument lets you animate by elapsed time instead of by frame count. For a continuous animation, call it again from inside the callback.

examples.desc: Coalesce many updates into one write per frame
examples.code: let queued = false; function schedule() { if (!queued) { queued = true; requestAnimationFrame(() => { queued = false; draw(); }); } }

examples.desc: Animate a meter towards a target value over time
examples.code: const start = performance.now(); requestAnimationFrame(function step(t) { const p = Math.min((t - start) / 500, 1); meter.style.transform = `scaleX(${p})`; if (p < 1) requestAnimationFrame(step); });

gotchas: It does not run in hidden tabs, so never use it for work that must continue there (polling, timers).

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **The script runs before the element exists.** `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'addEventListener')` in Chrome (Safari: `null is not an object`, Firefox: `btn is null`). Add `defer` or `type="module"`, or move the script to the end of `<body>`.
**Treating a NodeList as an array.** `querySelectorAll(...).map is not a function`. Use `[...list]` or `Array.from(list)`.
**Attaching listeners to elements that do not exist yet.** Rows rendered after the `forEach` have no listener. Delegate to the container.
**`innerHTML +=` in a loop.** Re-parses the whole container each time, drops listeners and form state, and is an XSS sink. Build nodes, append once.
**Forgetting `preventDefault()` on submit.** The page reloads and your `fetch` is cancelled mid-flight; in DevTools the request shows as "(canceled)".
**`dataset` and form values are strings.** `'false'` is truthy, `'8080' + 1` is `'80801'`. Use `input.valueAsNumber` for number inputs and compare strings explicitly.

blocks.title: Write debounce

task.text: Implement `debounce(fn, ms)`. It returns a function that, when called repeatedly, waits until `ms` milliseconds pass **without** another call and then calls `fn` once with the **latest** arguments. Give the returned function a `cancel()` method that drops a pending call. The check calls it with timers, so print nothing.

hints: `let timer;` in `debounce`, then inside the returned function `clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);`.
Build the function first (`const debounced = (...args) => {...}`), then add `debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timer);` and return it.

why.text: Each call clears the previous timer, so only the last one in a burst survives the quiet period, and because the arrow function captures `args` from that last call, `fn` sees the latest input. Functions are objects in JavaScript, so hanging `cancel` on the returned function is ordinary property assignment.

questions.q: What does `document.querySelectorAll('li')` return?

options.text: A live HTMLCollection that updates when items are added
A static NodeList snapshot, empty if nothing matches

questions.why: `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList`. It has `forEach` but not `map`; convert with `[...list]`. `getElementsByTagName` is the method that returns a live `HTMLCollection`.

questions.q: A device name comes from an API. Which line puts it on the page safely?
questions.why: `textContent` creates a text node and never parses markup, so `` stays visible text. The other three run the HTML parser and are XSS sinks.

questions.q: In a delegated listener on a `<ul>`, which event property is the `<ul>` itself?
questions.why: `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running (where you attached it). `target` is where the event started, often a child such as a `<b>` inside an `<li>`.

questions.q: An `<input value="192.168.1.50">` has been edited by the user to `10.0.0.9`. What does `input.getAttribute('value')` return?
questions.why: The attribute is the default value from the markup; the `value` property holds the current text. `form.reset()` restores the attribute's value.

questions.q: A `<table>` written without `<tbody>` has three `<tr>` rows. How many elements does `table.querySelectorAll(':scope > tr')` find?

options.text: 0, because the parser wrapped the rows in an inserted tbody
It throws, because :scope is invalid here

questions.why: Queries run against the parsed tree, and the HTML parser inserts a `<tbody>` around bare rows. `table.querySelectorAll('tr')` finds all three.

questions.q: You want one listener on a form to notice whenever any field inside it gains focus. Which event do you listen for?
questions.why: `focus` does not bubble, so a listener on the form never hears it from a child. `focusin` is the bubbling version.

terms.def: Document Object Model: the live tree of objects a browser builds from HTML, and the API for reading and changing it
Any object in the DOM tree: elements, text, comments and the document itself all inherit from Node
A node holding the characters inside an element, including the whitespace between tags
A list of nodes; static when returned by querySelectorAll, live when returned by childNodes
A live, element-only collection (children, getElementsByClassName) that updates as the tree changes
A name/value string pair written in the markup, read with getAttribute
A field on the JavaScript element object; some reflect attributes, others (value, checked) hold live state
Cross-site scripting: attacker-controlled data parsed as markup or code inside your page's origin
The path an event takes: capture down from window, the target, then bubbling back up
Handling events for many children with one listener on a common ancestor, using event.target and closest()
A parentless node used to build a subtree off-page and insert it in one operation
Forcing repeated synchronous layout by alternating DOM writes with reads of layout properties
Delaying a function until calls have stopped for a set time, so only the last call in a burst runs
The browser's built-in form checking (required, pattern, type) exposed through validity and setCustomValidity

blocks.text: XML is the format that quietly runs a large part of your Mac and the web: every `launchd` job, app preference and `Info.plist`, every RSS and Atom feed, every SVG icon, every `.docx` and `.xlsx` file, every sitemap, every Maven `pom.xml` and Android layout. In this chapter you will use the DOM skills from [the previous chapter](#dom) on XML documents: parse the practice server's `/data/devices.xml` and `/data/feed.rss`, query them with XPath, build new XML without opening an injection hole, transform it with XSLT, draw a device-status chart in SVG, and then move to Terminal to validate files with `xmllint` and read and convert property lists with `plutil`. You will also break a document on purpose with one unescaped `&`, which is how most people meet XML's strictness for the first time.
What XML is, and what it is not

**XML** (Extensible Markup Language) is a W3C syntax, first published in 1998 and current as XML 1.0 Fifth Edition (2008), for writing a **tree of named elements** as text. It has no built-in tags. A *vocabulary* defines them: RSS says `<item>` and `<pubDate>`, SVG says `<rect>` and `<circle>`, Apple's plist format says `<dict>` and `<key>`. XML itself only fixes the grammar: how tags, attributes, text and comments are written and how they nest.

The defining property is **strictness**. The XML specification requires a parser to stop at the first *well-formedness* error and report it ("draconian" error handling). HTML went the other way: the HTML standard tells the parser exactly how to repair any input, so a browser never refuses a page. Feed the same broken markup to both parsers:

blocks.out:
bold both italic

true error on line 1 at column 23: Opening and ending tag mismatch: i line 1 and b

blocks.text: The HTML parser closed and reopened `` to make a valid tree (the "adoption agency" algorithm). The XML parser refused at column 23, the `` that closes the wrong element. The message above is Chrome's and Safari's wording (both use libxml2-derived parsers); Firefox reports the same error as `XML Parsing Error: mismatched tag`.

XML is not a database, not a programming language and not a data type system: everything in it is text until a schema or your code says otherwise. It is also not HTML. XHTML is HTML written under XML rules, but browsers only apply those rules when the server sends `Content-Type: application/xhtml+xml`; served as `text/html`, the same file goes through the forgiving HTML parser (see [HTML](#html)).
Anatomy of an XML document

blocks.code:
⟪c:<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>⟫           ◀ declaration: optional, first
 ⟪m:<?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" href="d.xsl"?>⟫  ◀ processing instruction
 ⟪d:<!-- exported by the router at 10:00 -->⟫         ◀ comment

   <⟪b:device⟫ ⟪y:id⟫="⟪g:1⟫" ⟪y:type⟫="⟪g:router⟫">                  ◀ attributes: name="value"
     <⟪b:name⟫>router</⟪b:name⟫>                          ◀ element with text content
     <⟪b:note⟫>⟪r:R&D⟫: port ⟪r:<⟫443⟪r:>⟫</⟪b:note⟫>       ◀ entity references
     <⟪b:raw⟫>⟪m:<![CDATA[ a < b && c ]]>⟫</⟪b:raw⟫>          ◀ CDATA: no escaping inside
     <⟪b:backup⟫/>                                    ◀ empty element, self-closed
   </⟪b:device⟫>

blocks.text: A document is **well-formed** when it follows the grammar. The rules that catch people:

items.text: Exactly **one root element** wraps everything.
Every start tag has a matching end tag, or is self-closed: `<backup/>`.
Elements **nest properly**: ``, never ``.
Names are **case-sensitive**: `<Name>...</name>` is an error.

Attribute values are **always quoted** (single or double quotes), an attribute appears at most once per element, and HTML's bare attributes are illegal: `<input disabled>` must be `disabled="disabled"`.
`<` and `&` never appear raw in text or attribute values.

Names start with a letter or `_` and may contain letters, digits, `-`, `.` and `_`. Names beginning with `xml` in any case are reserved. A `:` is legal but means a namespace prefix (see [Namespaces](#namespaces)).
The XML declaration, if present, is the very first thing in the file: not even a blank line or a space may come before it.
Comments cannot contain `--`, and cannot appear inside a tag.

blocks.text: Escaping: five entities and character references

XML predefines exactly five **entity references**. Anything else, including HTML favourites like ` ` and `©`, is an error unless a DTD declares it. For any other character, use a numeric **character reference** with the Unicode code point in decimal or hex.

blocks.text: A **CDATA section** (`<![CDATA[ ... ]]>`) holds text that the parser does not scan for markup, so `<` and `&` inside it need no escaping; the only thing it cannot contain is `]]>`. It is handy for embedded code or HTML snippets and changes nothing about the data: to a program, CDATA is just text. **Processing instructions** (`<?target data?>`) carry instructions for a specific application, like `xml-stylesheet` for a browser or an XSLT engine. The XML declaration looks like one but is not a node in the tree.

blocks.out:
7 xml-stylesheet
8 #comment
1 network
xml-stylesheet "type=\"text/xsl\" href=\"devices.xsl\""
4 #cdata-section "uses <b> & <i> freely"
0 <device id="1"><name>router</name><note><![CDATA[uses <b> & <i> freely]]></note><backup/></device>

blocks.text: The document node has three children: the processing instruction (`nodeType` 7), the comment (8) and the root element (1). The declaration is gone: it told the parser the version and encoding and was consumed. The CDATA section is a node of type 4, and its `textContent` is plain text.
Elements or attributes?

Both can hold a value, and vocabularies differ. A rule of thumb that ages well: **attributes for metadata about an element** (identifiers, types, units, flags: `id="1"`, `proto="tcp"`), **elements for content** and for anything that can repeat, has structure of its own, or might need markup inside it (`<port>` appears several times; a `<description>` might contain `<b>`). Attributes cannot repeat, cannot nest and have no order.
Whitespace

Unlike HTML rendering, XML keeps whitespace: the newlines and indentation between tags are text nodes in the tree, exactly as you saw in [the DOM chapter](#dom/tree). Pretty-printing a document (`xmllint --format`) therefore changes it, slightly. Programs that read data-style XML usually ignore whitespace-only text; document-style XML (DocBook, XHTML) can declare `xml:space="preserve"` where it matters.
Namespaces

Vocabularies collide. `<title>` means a page title in XHTML, a tooltip in SVG, and a feed or entry title in Atom. As soon as one document mixes vocabularies (SVG inside XHTML, extension elements inside an Atom feed), a name alone is ambiguous. **XML Namespaces** fix this by pairing every element name with a namespace **URI**.

items.text: `xmlns="URI"` declares the **default namespace** for that element and its descendants: unprefixed element names belong to it.
`xmlns:lab="URI"` binds the **prefix** `lab` to a URI; `<lab:severity>` is then the element `severity` in that namespace.

The URI is an identifier, compared as a string. Nothing fetches it, and it does not have to resolve to a web page. Prefixes are local nicknames: `<a:entry xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">` and `<entry xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">` are the same element.
**Unprefixed attributes are in no namespace**, even inside a default namespace. Only prefixed attributes such as `xlink:href` or `xml:lang` belong to one.

blocks.text: Well-known URIs: XHTML `http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml`, SVG `http://www.w3.org/2000/svg`, XLink `http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink`, Atom `http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom`, XSLT `http://www.w3.org/1999/XSL/Transform`, XML Schema `http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema`.

The line that prints `0` is the most common XPath bug in existence. In XPath 1.0 an unprefixed name in an expression means "no namespace", so `//entry` does not match Atom's `entry`, which lives in the Atom namespace. Bind a prefix with a **namespace resolver** function (third argument of `document.evaluate`) and write `//a:entry`, or match on `local-name()` when you do not care. CSS selectors in `querySelector` are more relaxed: a type selector without a namespace matches elements in any namespace, which is why `entry title` found the entry's title.
Well-formed versus valid: DTD and XML Schema

**Well-formed** means the syntax is right. **Valid** means the document also follows a **schema**: which elements may appear, in what order, with which attributes, holding which kinds of values. Browsers only check well-formedness; validation is a separate step you run with a tool.

items.text: A **DTD** (Document Type Definition) is the original schema language, inherited from SGML. It is referenced from a `<!DOCTYPE>` line and can also declare entities. Every Apple plist starts with `<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">`. DTDs know nothing about data types or namespaces.

**XML Schema** (XSD, a W3C Recommendation, versions 1.0 and 1.1) is itself written in XML and has data types (`xs:unsignedShort`, `xs:boolean`, patterns, enumerations). SOAP, Office Open XML and most enterprise formats use it.
**RELAX NG** is a simpler, more readable alternative; **Schematron** adds rule-based checks ("a server must have at least one port").

blocks.text: Here is an XSD for the practice server's device inventory. It says a network holds one or more devices, each with a name, an IPv4-looking address and any number of ports; a port is a number from 0 to 65535 with a `proto` of `tcp` or `udp`.

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:element name="network">
    <xs:complexType>
      <xs:sequence>
        <xs:element name="device" maxOccurs="unbounded">
          <xs:complexType>
            <xs:sequence>
              <xs:element name="name" type="xs:string"/>
              <xs:element name="ip" type="ipv4"/>
              <xs:element name="port" minOccurs="0" maxOccurs="unbounded">
                <xs:complexType>
                  <xs:simpleContent>
                    <xs:extension base="xs:unsignedShort">
                      <xs:attribute name="proto" use="required">
                        <xs:simpleType>
                          <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
                            <xs:enumeration value="tcp"/>
                            <xs:enumeration value="udp"/>
                          </xs:restriction>
                        </xs:simpleType>
                      </xs:attribute>
                    </xs:extension>
                  </xs:simpleContent>
                </xs:complexType>
              </xs:element>
            </xs:sequence>
            <xs:attribute name="id" type="xs:positiveInteger" use="required"/>
            <xs:attribute name="type" type="xs:string" use="required"/>
            <xs:attribute name="online" type="xs:boolean" use="required"/>
          </xs:complexType>
        </xs:element>
      </xs:sequence>
      <xs:attribute name="name" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:attribute name="subnet" type="xs:string"/>
    </xs:complexType>
  </xs:element>
  <xs:simpleType name="ipv4">
    <xs:restriction base="xs:string">
      <xs:pattern value="\d{1,3}(\.\d{1,3}){3}"/>
    </xs:restriction>
  </xs:simpleType>
</xs:schema>

blocks.text: `broken.xml` is perfectly **well-formed** (any XML parser reads it) and still **invalid**. That is the whole difference. Each error names the file, line, element and the schema rule (a *facet*) that failed, and the exit status is non-zero, so the check slots into scripts and CI with `&&`. Messages and exit codes come from the libxml2 version on your Mac; run `xmllint --version` to see it.

blocks.name: xmllint
blocks.sum: Check, pretty-print, validate and query XML (and parse HTML) from the command line.

how.text: `xmllint` is the command-line front end to **libxml2**, the C library behind much of the XML handling on macOS and Linux. With no options it parses the file and prints it back, so its first use is as a well-formedness checker: any error is printed with the line, a caret under the column, and a non-zero exit status. `-` reads standard input, which makes it a pipeline stage.

`--format` re-indents the output, `--noout` suppresses it (you only want errors), `--schema` validates against an XSD, `--dtdvalid` against an external DTD and `--valid` against the DTD the document declares. `--html` switches to libxml2's HTML parser, which predates HTML5 and complains about tags like `<main>` on stderr; it still builds a tree you can query.

Substitute entity references with their values. Expands external entities too: never use it on untrusted files.

blocks.text: For a new web API, JSON wins: it maps straight onto JavaScript and Python data, it is smaller, and `res.json()` is one call. XML still wins, or is simply what you must speak, in these places:

items.text: **Documents with mixed content**, where markup sits inside running text: DocBook, DITA, XHTML, TEI, legal and publishing formats, and the office formats (`.docx`, `.xlsx`, `.pptx` are zip files of XML; LibreOffice's ODF too).
**Established standards**: RSS and Atom feeds, SVG graphics, `sitemap.xml` for search engines, GPX tracks and KML maps, SAML single sign-on, XMPP chat, SOAP and WSDL services, MusicXML.
**Configuration ecosystems**: Apple property lists, Android layouts and manifests, Maven `pom.xml`, .NET `.csproj`, many Java application servers.
**When validation and transformation tooling matters**: a schema that rejects bad data at the door, and XSLT or XQuery pipelines that publishers have run for decades.

blocks.text: Pick any `.docx` on your Mac and run `unzip -l {{docx}}`. You will see `word/document.xml`, `word/styles.xml` and friends. `unzip -p {{docx}} word/document.xml | xmllint --format - | head -40` shows the text wrapped in `<w:p>` (paragraph) and `<w:r>` (run) elements in the `w:` namespace.
Parsing XML in the browser

`DOMParser` turns a string into a document. With the MIME type `application/xml` (or `text/xml`, `image/svg+xml`, `application/xhtml+xml`) it runs the XML parser and returns an `XMLDocument`; with `text/html` it runs the HTML parser. It never throws on bad input. Instead, the result contains a `<parsererror>` element, whose position and wording differ between engines (Chrome puts it inside the partial document, Firefox makes it the root), so the portable test is "is there a `parsererror` element anywhere?".

Everything from [the DOM chapter](#dom) works on the result, with three differences: matching is **case-sensitive** (`<Device>` is not `<device>`), there is no HTML-only API (`innerText`, `dataset` and the form properties belong to `HTMLElement`; XML elements are plain `Element`s), and the tree keeps every whitespace text node.

`querySelector('Device')` found nothing: XML is case-sensitive. `XMLSerializer` turned the modified element back into text, keeping the original indentation whitespace inside it. Use `serializeToString(doc)` for a whole document; it does not add an XML declaration, so prepend one yourself when the consumer needs it.

blocks.name: DOMParser.parseFromString()
blocks.sum: Parse a string of XML, SVG or HTML into a new Document object.

how.text: The MIME type picks the parser. The XML types run a namespace-aware XML parser and return an `XMLDocument`; `text/html` runs the HTML parser (scripts inside are marked not to run). The new document is not attached to the page and has no rendering, so parsing is safe for display purposes, and you query it with the usual DOM methods.

The XML parser never throws. On a well-formedness error it returns a document containing a `<parsererror>` element with an engine-specific message, and in Chrome a partial tree up to the error. Always test for it before trusting the result.

blocks.name: XMLSerializer.serializeToString()
blocks.sum: Turn a DOM node or document back into XML text, with correct escaping.

how.text: Walks the subtree and writes XML: `&`, `<` and `>` in text become entity references, quotes in attribute values become `"`, empty elements are written self-closed (`<backup/>`), and namespace declarations are added where needed so the output parses back to the same tree. It does not emit an XML declaration and does not pretty-print; whitespace text nodes are written exactly as they are.
Serializing an HTML element gives XHTML-style output with the XHTML namespace on the top element, which is how you produce XML from an HTML page (for example an inline `<svg>` saved as a file).

The NS variant ignores prefixes and compares the namespace URI and local name, which is the robust choice when documents may use different prefixes (or a default namespace) for the same vocabulary. `'*'` is a wildcard for either part.
Both return a **live** `HTMLCollection`. In HTML documents tag names match case-insensitively; in XML documents, exactly.

blocks.text: XPath in depth

CSS selectors can find elements by name, class, attribute and position, and since `:has()` even by their descendants. **XPath** 1.0 (W3C, 1999) goes further: it navigates in every direction (parents, ancestors, preceding siblings), selects attributes and text nodes as results, filters on text content, and computes numbers, strings and booleans. Browsers implement XPath 1.0 only (2.0 and 3.1 exist in tools such as Saxon). It works on HTML pages too, which is why DevTools has `$x()`.

An XPath expression is usually a **location path**: steps separated by `/`, each step written `axis::node-test[predicate]`. A path starting with `/` begins at the document root; otherwise it starts at the **context node** you pass in.

predicate: keep only devices whose online attribute equals 'true'
their port children

select the text node inside each port, not the element

blocks.name: document.evaluate()
blocks.sum: Evaluate an XPath 1.0 expression against a document or node and return an XPathResult.
blocks.syntax: document.evaluate(expression, contextNode, namespaceResolver | null, XPathResult.TYPE, null) -> XPathResult

how.text: Compiles the expression and runs it with `contextNode` as the starting point for relative paths. The `namespaceResolver` is a function from prefix to URI (or `null` when the document uses no namespaces); without it, prefixed names throw and unprefixed names only match elements in **no** namespace. The result type constant decides what you read back: a number, string, boolean, an iterator, a snapshot or a single node.
Call it on the document that owns the nodes: `xmlDoc.evaluate(...)` for a parsed XML document, `document.evaluate(...)` for the page. `$x()` in DevTools wraps it and returns an array.

blocks.text: Fetch and render: an RSS feed

**RSS 2.0** is a small vocabulary from the early 2000s: an `<rss>` root, one `<channel>` with a `title`, `link` and `description`, and one `<item>` per entry with `title`, `link`, `description`, `pubDate`, `guid` and `category`. Dates use the old e-mail format of RFC 822 (`Mon, 05 Oct 2026 09:12:00 GMT`), which JavaScript's `Date` parses. **Atom** (RFC 4287) is the stricter successor: namespaced, with `<feed>`, `<entry>` and RFC 3339 dates (`2026-10-05T09:12:00Z`). Feed readers handle both; your router, CI server and home-automation box often publish one.
The practice server's `/data/feed.rss` holds two lab events. Fetch, parse, render with `textContent`:

blocks.page: Lab Status
blocks.out:
Lab Status | application/rss+xml
[
  '2026-10-05 [alert] nas went offline',
  '2026-10-04 [info] pi updated to 6.12'
]

blocks.text: Two habits in that code matter beyond RSS. Dates are printed with `toISOString()`, so the output is the same in every time zone (use `toLocaleString()` with explicit options when you display dates to people). And every piece of feed text goes in through `textContent` and `append`: a feed is **untrusted input**. RSS `<description>` elements routinely carry escaped HTML, and rendering that with `innerHTML` turns anyone who can publish to the feed into someone who can run script on your page ([XSS](#dom/xss)).
Building XML safely

Generating XML with template strings works until a value contains a special character, and then it fails in one of two ways. Either the output is no longer well-formed, or, worse, it is well-formed and **means something else**: an XML injection.

The second document parsed without complaint and now contains an `<admin>true</admin>` element the program never meant to write. If a server trusts that file, a device name just granted admin rights. The fix is the same as for HTML: let a library do the escaping. Build the tree with DOM methods and serialize it; text and attribute values are escaped automatically, so no input can change the structure:

blocks.out:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<network name="R&D "lab""><device id="3" online="true"><name>pi</name><ip>192.168.1.50</ip></device><device id="6" online="true"><name>homeassistant</name><ip>192.168.1.90</ip></device><device><name>cam</name><admin>true</admin></name></device></network>
3 0 cam</name><admin>true</admin>

blocks.text: The hostile name round-trips as data: no `<admin>` element exists, and reading it back gives the exact original string. Where no DOM is available (a Node script, a shell generator), escape every value, replacing `&` **first**:
In Python, `xml.etree.ElementTree` does the same job ([Python's version](#xml/mac) is below), and in Node the capstone builds its XML export with exactly this escaping function.

blocks.name: document.implementation.createDocument()
blocks.sum: Create a new, empty XML document with a root element, to build with DOM methods and serialize.

how.text: Returns a standalone `XMLDocument` whose root element has the given name (in the given namespace, or none with `null`). Its `createElement` creates elements in no namespace, exactly what a plain data vocabulary wants; use `createElementNS` for namespaced ones. Text you assign with `textContent` and values you pass to `setAttribute` are stored as data, so the serializer escapes them and no value can inject markup.
`doc.createComment()`, `createCDATASection()` and `createProcessingInstruction()` add the other node types when a format needs them.

blocks.text: XSLT in one example

**XSLT** 1.0 (XSL Transformations, W3C 1999) is a language, written in XML, for transforming XML into XML, HTML or text. A stylesheet is a set of **templates**; each `match`es nodes with an XPath pattern and says what to output for them. The processor walks the input tree and applies the best-matching template to each node. Publishers still run large XSLT pipelines, and it is how a raw RSS or sitemap file can look like a styled page when opened directly in a browser (through an `<?xml-stylesheet?>` instruction).

blocks.code: Network ()

blocks.text: `match="/network"` fires once for the root element and writes the table; `apply-templates select="device"` hands each device, sorted by name, to the second template; `{@type}` inside an attribute is an *attribute value template* that inserts the XPath result. macOS includes `xsltproc` (libxslt) in `/usr/bin`:

blocks.code:
$ xsltproc devices.xsl devices.xml
Network home (192.168.1.0/24)
nas 192.168.1.60 1
pi 192.168.1.50 2
router 192.168.1.1 2

blocks.text: Browsers have shipped an XSLT 1.0 engine (`XSLTProcessor` and `<?xml-stylesheet?>`) for twenty years, but it is being removed for security and maintenance reasons. Chrome deprecated it in 2025; per Chrome's "Removing XSLT" page, XSLT stops working in Chrome 158 (Stable on 17 November 2026) for everyone except sites in an origin trial or browsers under an enterprise policy, and those escape hatches end with Chrome 176 (August 2027). Firefox and WebKit have signalled support for removing it as well. Run XSLT on a server or with `xsltproc` instead, or rewrite small transforms as JavaScript DOM code.
The playground below uses `XSLTProcessor` when your browser still has it and says so when it does not:

port(s) `; async function run() { const note = document.querySelector('#note'); if (typeof XSLTProcessor === 'undefined') { note.textContent = 'This browser no longer has XSLTProcessor. Use xsltproc in Terminal instead.'; console.warn('XSLTProcessor is not available'); return; } const parser = new DOMParser(); const xml = parser.parseFromString(await (await fetch('/data/devices.xml')).text(), 'application/xml'); const proc = new XSLTProcessor(); proc.importStylesheet(parser.parseFromString(xsl, 'application/xml')); document.querySelector('#out').replaceChildren(proc.transformToFragment(xml, document)); note.textContent = 'Transformed by the browser\'s built-in XSLT 1.0 engine.'; console.log('rows:', document.querySelectorAll('#out tr').length); } run();

blocks.name: XSLTProcessor.transformToFragment()
blocks.sum: Apply an XSLT 1.0 stylesheet to an XML document in the browser and get the output as a DocumentFragment.
blocks.syntax: const p = new XSLTProcessor(); p.importStylesheet(xslDoc); p.setParameter(null, name, value); p.transformToFragment(xmlDoc, document) -> DocumentFragment

how.text: `importStylesheet` compiles a parsed XSLT document; `setParameter` fills `<xsl:param>` values; `transformToFragment` runs the transform and returns nodes owned by the target document, ready to `append`. `transformToDocument` returns a whole new document instead. With `<xsl:output method="html"/>` the result is parsed as HTML (so tables gain a `tbody`, for example).
Being removed from browsers (see the warning above). Feature-test with `typeof XSLTProcessor !== 'undefined'` and keep a fallback.

blocks.text: SVG: XML you can script

**SVG** (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML vocabulary for 2-D drawings, rendered natively by every browser. Inside an HTML page you can write `<svg>` inline, and the HTML parser puts it and its children in the SVG namespace automatically. The `viewBox="0 0 360 150"` attribute defines the drawing's own coordinate system (x to the right, y **down**), which the browser scales to whatever size the element gets, so charts stay sharp at any zoom.
From JavaScript, SVG elements must be created **in the SVG namespace**:

blocks.page: Only one circle appears: the one created with createElementNS.
blocks.out:
http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml HTMLUnknownElement
http://www.w3.org/2000/svg SVGCircleElement
http://www.w3.org/2000/svg 0 0 100 40 2
object 14 14

blocks.text: Both elements are in the tree (`querySelectorAll` counts 2), but only the namespaced one draws. The `wrong` one is an unknown HTML element that happens to be called `circle`. The last line shows the other SVG difference: geometry properties such as `r` are animated-value objects (`r.baseVal.value`), so set and read them with `setAttribute` and `getAttribute`. Styling properties (`fill`, `stroke`, `opacity`) can come from CSS classes, and CSS wins over the presentation attributes of the same name.

'up' : 'down' }); dot.append(el('title', {}, `${d.name} ${d.ip} (${d.online ? 'online' : 'offline'})`)); g.append(dot, el('text', { y: 32, class: 'label' }, d.name.slice(0, 10))); svg.append(g); }); status.load.forEach((v, i) => { const w = v * 250; svg.append( el('text', { x: 35, y: 100 + i * 18, class: 'label' }, ['1 min', '5 min', '15 min'][i]), el('rect', { x: 70, y: 90 + i * 18, width: w, height: 12, rx: 2, class: 'bar' }), el('text', { x: 76 + w, y: 100 + i * 18, class: 'value' }, v.toFixed(2)), ); }); } document.querySelector('#toggle').addEventListener('click', async () => { const nas = await (await fetch('/api/devices/4')).json(); await fetch('/api/devices/4', { method: 'PATCH', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ online: !nas.online }) }); draw(); }); draw();

blocks.name: document.createElementNS()
blocks.sum: Create an element in a specific XML namespace, such as SVG or MathML.

how.text: An element's identity is its namespace plus local name. `createElement` always creates HTML elements in an HTML document, so `createElement('rect')` yields an `HTMLUnknownElement` that the SVG renderer ignores. `createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'rect')` creates a real `SVGRectElement`. Children of an SVG element must be SVG elements too, including `text`, `g` and `title`.
Attributes on SVG elements are set with plain `setAttribute`; only namespaced attributes (rare today, such as the old `xlink:href`) need `setAttributeNS`.
