blocks.name: express.static()
blocks.sum: Middleware that serves files from a folder, with content types, caching headers and traversal protection.

how.text: For GET and HEAD requests it maps the URL path onto the folder, refuses paths that escape it, sets `Content-Type` from the extension plus `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and `Accept-Ranges`, and streams the file. If no file matches it calls `next()`, so your routes still run. Dotfiles such as `.env` are ignored by default. Give it an absolute path (from `import.meta.dirname`), or it depends on the folder you started from.

examples.desc: Serve public/ next to the code
Check content types of everything you serve

blocks.name: Express error handler
blocks.sum: Middleware with four parameters that receives errors from any earlier layer and sends one consistent response.
blocks.syntax: app.use((err, req, res, next) => { res.status(500).json({ error: '...' }); })

how.text: Express recognises error handlers by `fn.length === 4`, so keep all four parameters even if `next` is unused. Register it last. Map known error types to client errors (`entity.parse.failed` to 400, `entity.too.large` to 413) and everything else to 500, logging the stack on the server and sending no internal details to the client. With `NODE_ENV=production`, Express's built-in fallback also hides stack traces.

examples.desc: Known errors to 4xx, the rest to 500
Provoke a parse error and see the clean JSON answer

blocks.text: Configuration: environment variables and .env

Configuration that differs between machines (port, bind address, data folder, API tokens) belongs in environment variables, read through `process.env`. Typing them before every command gets old, so projects keep them in a `.env` file, and Node reads it natively: `--env-file` since Node 20.6 and `process.loadEnvFile()` since 20.12, so the old `dotenv` package is no longer needed.

blocks.code:
$ printf 'PORT=8080\n# comments are allowed\nLAB_TOKEN=change-me\n' > .env
$ node --env-file=.env express-server.js
listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080
$ node --env-file=.env -p 'process.env.LAB_TOKEN'
change-me
$ node -p 'process.loadEnvFile(); process.env.PORT'
8080
$ node --env-file=missing.env -p 1; echo "status $?"
node: missing.env: not found
status 9

blocks.text: Variables already set in the real environment win over the file, so `PORT=9000 node --env-file=.env ...` uses 9000. `--env-file-if-exists=.env` (Node 22.9+) tolerates a missing file; in code, wrap `process.loadEnvFile()` in `try` and ignore `ENOENT`, as the capstone's `server.js` does.

blocks.title: .env stays out of git and out of the browser

blocks.text: Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before the first commit, and commit a `.env.example` with dummy values instead. Anything a browser downloads (every file in `public/`, every JavaScript bundle) is public: a token there is readable in DevTools by anyone who opens the page. Secrets stay on the server, which uses them on the client's behalf.

blocks.name: node --env-file
blocks.sum: Load KEY=value lines from a file into process.env before the script starts (process.loadEnvFile() does it from code).

how.text: Lines are `KEY=value`; `#` starts a comment; values may be quoted. Existing environment variables are not overwritten. A missing file is a fatal error (exit status 9) with the flag, and an `ENOENT` exception from `process.loadEnvFile()`. Several `--env-file` flags may be given; later files override earlier ones.

examples.desc: Load .env when present, from code

blocks.text: CORS from the server's side

In [How the web works](#web-intro) you met the **same-origin policy**: a page from `http://localhost:8000` may send a request to `http://localhost:3000` (a different port is a different origin), but the browser will not let the page's JavaScript **read** the response unless the server says it may, with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. CORS is enforced by browsers only. `curl`, Python and Node's `fetch` ignore it, which is why an API "works in curl but not in the page".

For requests that could change data or use non-simple headers (a `PUT`, a `DELETE`, a `POST` with `Content-Type: application/json`), the browser first sends a **preflight**: an `OPTIONS` request asking permission. The CORS middleware in `express-server.js` answers both kinds:

blocks.code:
$ curl -si -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/echo -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8000' \
    -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type'
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
X-Powered-By: Express

blocks.text: CORS is **not authentication**: anyone with `curl` can still call your API. `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` suits public read-only data; for an API that changes things, list the origins you serve. A page and API from the same server, as in the capstone, need no CORS headers at all.

The playground below has the two practice hosts from earlier chapters: `cors.example` sends the header, `nocors.example` does not. Click both buttons and compare the Console with the response headers in the Network pane.

blocks.code:
Same data, two hosts. Only one sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin.


--- js
const out = document.querySelector('#out');
async function load(host) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`https://${host}/api/status`);
    const data = await res.json();
    out.textContent = `${host}: ${res.status}, ${data.devices} devices`;
  } catch (err) {
    out.textContent = `${host}: ${err.name}: ${err.message}`;
  }
}
document.querySelector('#ok').addEventListener('click', () => load('cors.example'));
document.querySelector('#blocked').addEventListener('click', () => load('nocors.example'));

blocks.name: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
blocks.sum: Response header that tells a browser which page origin may read the response.
blocks.syntax: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://dashboard.example | *      (+ Vary: Origin when it depends on the request)

how.text: The browser compares the page's origin with this header after the response arrives; on a mismatch it hides the response from JavaScript and `fetch` rejects with `TypeError: Failed to fetch`. Preflighted requests also need `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` on the `OPTIONS` answer, and `Access-Control-Max-Age` lets the browser cache that permission. Cookies or HTTP auth additionally need `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and then `*` is not allowed. When the value is chosen per request, send `Vary: Origin` so caches keep the variants apart.

examples.desc: Allow one origin, answer preflights
Simulate a browser preflight with curl and show only the CORS headers
examples.code: curl -si -X OPTIONS -H 'Origin: http://localhost:8000' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' http://localhost:3000/api/echo | grep -i '^access-control'

gotchas: CORS errors appear only in the browser console, never in curl. When the page fails and curl works, look for the missing header on the response, or the failed `OPTIONS` request, in the Network panel.

blocks.text: Debugging Node

`console.log` debugging works, but Node speaks the same debugging protocol as Chrome, so you get breakpoints, stepping and scope inspection with the DevTools you already know from [DevTools](#devtools).

blocks.code:
$ node --inspect express-server.js
Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/18996b7d-8b9b-4098-a183-89dfb5a4f6da
For help, see: https://nodejs.org/en/docs/inspector
listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000

items.text: Open `chrome://inspect` in Chrome and click **Open dedicated DevTools for Node** (or **inspect** under Remote Target).
In Sources, open `express-server.js` and click the line number inside the `/api/ports/:port` handler to set a breakpoint.
Run `curl -s http://localhost:3000/api/ports/22` in the other tab. curl waits, and DevTools stops on your line: hover `req.params`, look at Scope, step with F10, resume with F8.
Use `node --inspect-brk` to stop on the first line, when the bug happens during startup. A `debugger;` statement in the code acts as a breakpoint whenever a debugger is attached.

blocks.text: In VS Code, open a **JavaScript Debug Terminal** from the Command Palette and run `node server.js` (or `npm run dev`) in it: breakpoints set in the editor work with no configuration. PyCharm's Pro subscription adds Node.js run configurations with the same debugger; the free tier does not have them.
Anyone who can reach the inspector port can run arbitrary code inside your process. `--inspect` binds to `127.0.0.1:9229` by default; never use `--inspect=0.0.0.0` on a network you do not control.

blocks.name: node --inspect
blocks.sum: Start Node with the V8 inspector open so Chrome DevTools, VS Code or PyCharm can attach a debugger.

how.text: Node opens a WebSocket on port 9229 that speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, and lists debuggable targets at `http://127.0.0.1:9229/json/list`. A debugger that connects can set breakpoints, step, evaluate expressions in paused frames, and record CPU and heap profiles. `--inspect-brk` pauses before the first line; `--inspect-wait` waits for a debugger without pausing.

blocks.text: Testing with node:test, and fetch in Node

Node ships a test runner (`node:test`) and an assertion library (`node:assert`), so a project needs no test framework. `node --test` finds files named like `*.test.js`, `*-test.js`, `test-*.js` or anything under a `test/` folder, runs each in its own process and reports. An HTTP server is tested the honest way: start it on port 0, talk to it with `fetch`, close it.

`fetch` is global in Node since version 18 (stable since 21) and is the same WHATWG API as in the browser, minus the browser's rules: no CORS, no cookie jar, any header allowed. Here it runs against the practice server:

blocks.name: node --test
blocks.sum: Run test files with Node's built-in test runner.

how.text: Without arguments, it searches the project (skipping `node_modules`) for `**/*.test.{js,mjs,cjs}`, `**/*-test.*`, `**/*_test.*`, `**/test-*.*` and everything under `test/` folders, runs each file in a child process (several at once), and exits 1 if any test failed, so `npm test && deploy` is safe. Inside files, `test()` or `describe()`/`it()` define tests; `before`, `after`, `beforeEach`, `afterEach` are hooks; an async test passes when its promise resolves. Tests in one file run in order.

blocks.name: node:assert
blocks.sum: Assertion functions that throw an AssertionError with a readable diff when a check fails.
blocks.syntax: import assert from 'node:assert/strict';  assert.equal(a, b)  assert.deepEqual(a, b)  assert.match(str, re)  await assert.rejects(promise)

how.text: Import the `strict` variant, where `equal` means `===` and `deepEqual` compares structure strictly (types, prototypes) instead of with `==`. `assert.throws(fn, /msg/)` and `await assert.rejects(promise)` check failures; `assert.ok(value, message)` checks truthiness. Every function takes an optional last argument, a message for the failure report.

examples.desc: The checks you will use most
Assertions also work as cheap checks in one-liners: exit status 1 on failure

blocks.name: fetch() (Node)
blocks.sum: The browser's fetch API, built into Node: send HTTP requests and read responses with promises.
blocks.syntax: const res = await fetch(url, { method, headers, body, signal })    res.ok  res.status  res.headers.get()  await res.json()

how.text: Node's `fetch` is implemented by the undici HTTP client. It resolves as soon as the status and headers arrive, and the body is read with `res.json()`, `res.text()` or as a stream (`res.body`). HTTP errors (404, 500) do **not** reject; only network failures and aborts do, so check `res.ok`. Pass `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` as `signal` for a deadline. Connections are kept alive and reused between calls to the same host.

examples.desc: Status, a header and the JSON body
A health check you can schedule: exit status 1 when the API is not OK
examples.code: node -e "fetch('http://localhost:3000/api/status').then((r) => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1), () => process.exit(1))" && echo up || echo DOWN

head: Symptom
Cause
Fix
rows: `ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope`

another process owns the port, often your own earlier server

blocks.text: Practice
Do these in `~/lab/node`. Every Terminal exercise ends with something you can check, usually a `curl` or a test run.

blocks.title: The core of a top-talkers tool

task.text: Write `topClients(text, n)`. `text` is a web log (combined format, one request per line, the client IP is the first field). Return an array of `[ip, count]` pairs, busiest first, at most `n` of them. Break ties by IP in ascending string order, and ignore blank lines. The starter prints the result for a five-line sample.

hints: Split the text on newlines, take everything before the first space, and count with a `Map`.
`[...map]` turns a Map into `[key, value]` pairs; sort with `(a, b) => b[1] - a[1] || a[0].localeCompare(b[0])`.

why.text: The Map keeps one counter per key in insertion order, and the comparator sorts by count first and falls back to the IP only when counts tie, because `0 || x` evaluates to `x`. This pure function is the part worth testing; the next exercise wraps it in stdin and stdout.

blocks.title: top.js in a zsh pipeline

task.text: Turn the previous function into `top.js`: it reads a log on **stdin**, takes an optional count argument (default 10), and prints `count ip` lines right-aligned like `uniq -c`. Exit with status 2 and a usage line on stderr when the argument is not a positive integer, and do not crash when piped into `head`. Then use it:

task.code:
cat ~/lab/access.log | node top.js 5
node top.js 3 < ~/lab/access.log | awk '{print $2}'
node top.js zero < ~/lab/access.log; echo "status $?"

hints: Combine `readline.createInterface({ input: process.stdin })` from `codes.js` with your `topClients` logic, counting line by line.
`String(count).padStart(7)` mimics the width of macOS `uniq -c`.

why.text: The script obeys the pipeline contract from [Pipes](#pipes): data in on stdin, results on stdout, the usage message on stderr, a meaningful exit status. On this log it prints `23 45.33.32.156`, `18 185.220.101.4`, `15 203.0.113.7`, `12 198.51.100.23`, then `10 172.16.5.9`; the shell version may print `198.51.100.8` fifth instead, because two IPs tie at 10 and `sort -rn` breaks ties differently. That is why the check compares only four lines.

blocks.verify: diff <(node top.js 4 < ~/lab/access.log) <(awk '{print $1}' ~/lab/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -4) && echo OK

blocks.title: A devices API on node:http

task.text: Write `devices-http.js`, a JSON API with no dependencies that keeps three devices in memory (`router 192.168.1.1 router`, `pi 192.168.1.50 server`, `nas 192.168.1.60 storage`) and supports:

items.text: `GET /api/devices` (optional `?type=server` filter) answering 200 with an array;
`GET /api/devices/:id` answering 200, or 404 with `{"error":"device 9 not found"}`;
`POST /api/devices` with a JSON `{ name, ip, type? }`: 201 with a `Location` header and the new device; 400 for broken JSON; 422 for a missing name or an invalid IPv4 address;
JSON 404 for anything else.

task.text: Start it on port 3000 and test every case with `curl -i`.

hints: Reuse `send()`/`readBody()` ideas from `app.js`. Match `/api/devices/(\d+)` with a regex and compare `Number(match[1])` with the ids.

why.text: The verify commands print `{"id":4,"name":"printer","ip":"192.168.1.70","type":"unknown"} 201` and `{"error":"device 9 not found"} 404`. 400 means the body cannot be parsed; 422 means it parsed but breaks the rules, the convention the capstone and the practice server share.

blocks.verify: curl -s -X POST localhost:3000/api/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"printer","ip":"192.168.1.70"}' -w ' %{http_code}\n'; curl -s localhost:3000/api/devices/9 -w ' %{http_code}\n'

blocks.title: Port it to Express

task.text: Rewrite the API as `devices-express.js` with Express 5: same routes, same status codes, same JSON errors, plus a 415 when a POST body is not JSON. Use `express.json()`, `req.params`, `req.query`, `res.status().location().json()`, a JSON 404 handler and an error handler that turns `entity.parse.failed` into 400. Make the `listen` callback report a busy port. Run the same curl checks as before, then start a second copy and confirm it exits with status 1.

hints: `req.is('application/json')` is false when the client did not send that Content-Type.
The listen callback receives the error in Express 5: `app.listen(3000, '127.0.0.1', (err) => { if (err) ... })`.

why.text: Half the length, and every remaining line is about devices. With the first copy running, the second prints `cannot listen: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:3000` and exits 1; with `() => console.log(...)` it would claim to listen and exit 0.

blocks.verify: node devices-express.js; echo "second copy exited with $?"

blocks.title: Break it: forget express.json()

task.text: In `devices-express.js`, comment out `app.use(express.json());`, restart, and POST a valid device with curl. Read the HTTP status, then read the server tab. Restore the line. Then remove the 415 guard instead and POST a form body (`curl -d 'name=pi&ip=192.168.1.50'`). Explain both failures in one sentence each.

hints: Look for the word `undefined` in the server's stack trace.
blocks.solution:
sed -i '' 's|^app.use(express.json());|// app.use(express.json());|' devices-express.js
node devices-express.js
# in the other tab:
curl -si -X POST localhost:3000/api/devices -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"printer","ip":"192.168.1.70"}' | head -1
# server tab shows: TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'name' of 'req.body' as it is undefined.
sed -i '' 's|^// app.use(express.json());|app.use(express.json());|' devices-express.js

why.text: Without the parser nobody reads the body stream, `req.body` stays `undefined`, destructuring it throws a TypeError, and the error handler turns that into `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error`. The form body fails the same way even with the parser present, because `express.json()` only handles `application/json`; that is why the 415 guard exists. The client sees a generic 500 while the stack trace stays in the server log, which is the behaviour you want in production.

blocks.title: Test the devices API with node --test

task.text: Make the Express API testable: copy `devices-express.js` to `devices-app.js`, replace the `app.listen(...)` call with `export default app;`, and write `test/devices.test.js` that starts it on port 0 and checks, with `fetch`: the seed list, the `?type=` filter, a JSON 404, a successful POST (201, `Location`, then readable by id), the two 422 cases, and 400/415. Run `npm test` and make all tests green.

hints: `server = app.listen(0, '127.0.0.1'); await once(server, 'listening');` with `once` from `node:events`.
Group with `describe('POST', () => { it(...) })` so the report reads like a specification.

why.text: Six tests in two suites pass in about 300 ms. Exporting the app instead of starting it lets the test own the server's lifetime and port, so it never collides with a server you left running on 3000. The capstone does the same with a factory function.

questions.q: Your `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Which file is loaded as CommonJS?
questions.why: The nearest `package.json` sets the default for `.js` files (ES modules here). `.cjs` always means CommonJS and `.mjs` always means ES module.

questions.q: A user can choose which file `lines.js` counts. Which call is safe against shell injection?
questions.why: `execFile` runs the program directly with an argument array; no shell parses the value. Quoting inside an `exec` string fails as soon as the value contains a quote character.

questions.q: In Express, which function signature makes middleware an error handler?
questions.why: Express counts the parameters. Four means error handler: skipped normally, called after a throw, `next(err)` or (Express 5) a rejected promise.

questions.q: Your page at http://localhost:8000 fetches http://localhost:3000/api/status. curl works, the page logs "TypeError: Failed to fetch". What does the API response lack?
questions.why: Different ports are different origins. The browser hides the response from the page unless the server allows that origin; curl applies no such rule.

questions.q: `package.json` says `"express": "^5.1.0"`. Which version can `npm update` install?
questions.why: A caret range accepts any version at least 5.1.0 with the same major version: below 6.0.0 and not below 5.1.0.

questions.q: Which command restarts your server automatically when `app.js`, imported by `server.js`, changes?
questions.why: `node --watch` watches the module graph of the entry script; the `dev` script in this chapter runs exactly that.

blocks.text: Glossary and next steps
Next: put the whole stack together in [Capstone: a LAN dashboard, front to back](#web-capstone).

terms.def: A JavaScript runtime built on V8 and libuv that runs JavaScript outside the browser with access to files, processes and the network
The C library that gives Node its event loop, asynchronous I/O and thread pool
Read-eval-print loop: the interactive prompt you get by running `node` without arguments
Node's original module system: `require()` and `module.exports`, loaded synchronously
The standard JavaScript module system (`import`/`export`), the default for new Node code with `"type": "module"`
A Node object that calls registered listener functions synchronously when it emits a named event
An object that moves data in chunks (Readable, Writable, Transform) with back-pressure, so memory stays bounded
"Broken pipe": the error from writing to a pipe whose reader has closed it
Running attacker-controlled text as shell code because data was pasted into a command string
A function `(req, res, next)` in a chain that may end the response or pass the request on with `next()`
The file recording the exact version and integrity hash of every installed package
Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, where only a major change may break compatibility
The `OPTIONS` request a browser sends to ask a server's permission before a cross-origin request that is not simple
A file of `KEY=value` lines loaded into environment variables, kept out of version control

chapters.title: Capstone: netkit
chapters.sub: Build one tested, installable command that combines subnet maths, ping, DNS, port scan and log analysis
goals: Structure a Python project as an installable package with a src layout and pyproject.toml
Build a multi-command CLI with argparse subcommands and shared options
Separate parsing, networking and presentation so each piece can be tested alone
Write pytest tests for pure functions, a real loopback socket and the CLI itself
Make a tool behave in pipelines with exit codes, quiet mode, stdin and JSON or CSV output
Review your own code against a rubric

blocks.text: You will build `netkit`, one command with five subcommands: `subnet` (from [Addressing](#addressing)), `ping` (from [Reachability](#net-reach)), `dns` (from [DNS](#dns)), `scan` (from [Python for networking](#py-net) and [Ports](#ports)) and `logs` (from [Python files](#py-files) and the loganalyzer). Each one started as a shell pipeline or a script. Here they become a single package with a shared output layer, tests and an installable entry point, so that `netkit scan 127.0.0.1 -p 8000-9000 -f json | jq` just works.

This is a long build. Plan two hours, commit to git after every step ([Thinking](#thinking) covers the commands), and run the checkpoint at the end of each step before continuing. When a test fails, read the failure before you change anything.
What you are building

blocks.code:
netkit subnet|ping|dns|scan|logs  [-f table|json|csv] [-q] [-v]
                                  │
                         cli.py   │  argparse subparsers, exit codes, logging
        ┌────────────┬────────────┼────────────┬─────────────┐
        ▼            ▼            ▼            ▼             ▼
    subnet.py     ping.py     dnscheck.py    scan.py       logs.py       "doing" layer:
    ipaddress     subprocess  socket, dig    socket,       re, Counter   one module per command,
                  + regex                    threads                     no printing, no argv
        └────────────┴─────┬──────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘
                           ▼
                      models.py   (dataclasses: ScanResult, PingStats)
                           ▼
                      output.py   rows (list of dicts) ──▶ table | csv | json   "presentation" layer

blocks.text: The rule that makes this testable: **modules return data, `cli.py` prints it.** A function that calls `print()` can only be tested by capturing output. A function that returns a list of dicts can be tested with one `assert`. The only module that touches `sys.argv`, `sys.stdin`, `print` or `sys.exit` is `cli.py`.
The command contract
Write down how the tool behaves before you write it. These rules are what make a program a good citizen in [pipelines](#pipes):

head: Rule
Behavior
rows: written to **stdout**, nothing else on stdout
print nothing at all; the exit status is the answer
the command did its job and the answer is "good"
the command ran and the answer is "bad" (no open ports, packet loss, bad input line, unparsable log)
the command was used wrongly or refused (bad option, refused target, unreadable file)
`subnet` and `logs` read stdin when no argument is given

blocks.text: In zsh, `netkit ping {{host}} --max-avg 50 || echo slow` only works if the program reports failure through its exit status. `grep` set this convention (0 found, 1 not found, 2 error), and tools that follow it compose with `&&`, `||`, `if` and `set -e` without any parsing.
The package layout

blocks.code:
netkit/                       project root (a git repository)
├── pyproject.toml            name, version, dependencies, the `netkit` command
├── README.md
├── src/
│   └── netkit/               the importable package
│       ├── __init__.py       version
│       ├── __main__.py       lets you run:  python3 -m netkit
│       ├── cli.py            argparse + exit codes + logging
│       ├── models.py         dataclasses
│       ├── output.py         table / csv / json
│       ├── subnet.py  ping.py  dnscheck.py  scan.py  logs.py
└── tests/
    ├── test_subnet.py  test_ping.py  test_scan.py  test_logs.py  test_cli.py

blocks.text: The `src/` layout puts the package one level down. Tests then import the **installed** package, not whatever happens to be in the current directory, which catches missing files and wrong imports before users do.

blocks.name: netkit
blocks.sum: The command you build in this chapter: five subcommands behind one entry point.

how.text: Each subcommand is an `argparse` sub-parser that shares `-f/--format`, `-q/--quiet` and `-v/--verbose` through a parent parser. `cli.main(argv)` builds the parser, runs one function per command and returns an exit status, and `sys.exit(main())` hands that to the shell. Options for the shared group go **after** the subcommand: `netkit subnet -f json 10.0.0.0/8`.

examples.desc: Describe a network
Scan your own Mac and keep only the open ports as JSON
Open ports as a plain list for a loop
Top client addresses from a log, as CSV for sort or awk

blocks.text: Design decisions worth understanding
Every choice in `netkit` has a reason, and each reason applies to the next tool you write.
Rows of dicts as the common currency

Every command returns `list[dict]` with identical keys per row. A table needs column headers and aligned cells, CSV needs a header row and one value per column, and JSON needs serializable values. All three are views of the same rows, so `output.render` is 25 lines instead of five formatters. The cost is that nested data must be flattened first, which is why `logs` emits `section,key,value` rows instead of a nested dict. That shape is also friendlier to `awk`, as the pipe examples show.
Dataclasses for results, dicts for output

`ScanResult` and `PingStats` are frozen dataclasses: typed, immutable, with a free `__repr__` and `__eq__`. Tests compare them directly (`assert result == ScanResult(...)`). The `as_row()` method is the only bridge to the presentation layer. If you later add an HTML report or a database writer, you add a new consumer and leave the producers alone.
Subprocess for ping and dig, sockets for scan

Use the operating system's own tool when it does a privileged or complicated job well (`ping` needs special permission for ICMP; `dig` implements the whole DNS protocol, including TCP fallback). Use the standard library when it is simple and gives you control (a TCP connect test is four lines of `socket`). The price of a child process is parsing its text, which is why `parse_ping` is a separate, tested function, and why `dnscheck` reports a clear error when `dig` is missing.
Threads in scan, not in ping

A scan makes hundreds of independent, short, waiting operations, so a thread pool pays off at once. `ping` over several hosts could use threads as well, but a ping already waits one second per packet, and parallelism there changes the output order and the load on your network. Add it only when you measure a need.
Errors: expected versus unexpected

`cli.py` catches the exceptions it **expects** from users and the world: `ValueError` from bad input, `OSError` from missing files and refused sockets, `RuntimeError` from a missing `ping`. It turns each into one log line and an exit status. It does not catch `Exception`, because a `TypeError` or `KeyError` is a bug in your code, and the traceback is exactly what you want to see while developing. Swallowing those would hide the evidence.

`logging.basicConfig` does nothing if the root logger already has handlers. pytest installs its own handlers, so without `force=True` the error messages would never reach `capsys` and the CLI tests that check stderr would fail. The same call works in normal runs.
Working in PyCharm
Open `~/lab/netkit` as a project and choose the existing `.venv` interpreter (Settings, Project, Python Interpreter, Add Interpreter, Existing). Then:

items.text: Mark `src` as a **Sources Root** (right-click the folder, Mark Directory as) so the editor resolves `import netkit`.

Right-click `tests/` and choose Run `pytest in tests`. PyCharm lists each test and shows the failing assertion with a diff. If it offers unittest instead, set Settings, Tools, Python Integrated Tools, Default test runner, to pytest.

Create a Run configuration of type Python with **Module name** `netkit` and **Parameters** `scan 127.0.0.1 -p 8000-8003`. This runs `python -m netkit`, which is what `__main__.py` is for. Click the gutter beside a line in `scan.py` to set a breakpoint, and run that configuration with Debug.
Use the Terminal tool window for `pytest -q` and the `netkit` command; it activates `.venv` for you.

Step 2: Subnet maths, output formats and a first command
Start from the two pure modules. Both run in the page, so test them here first, then save only the part **above** the demo marker as the file named in the first line.

First `src/netkit/subnet.py`. `describe` turns text such as `192.168.1.23/26` into a dict of facts, relying on `ipaddress` as in [Addressing](#addressing). `net.hosts()` excludes network and broadcast addresses; a /31 point-to-point link (RFC 3021) has two usable addresses, a case the tests will pin down.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/subnet.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Subnet maths on top of the standard ipaddress module."""
import ipaddress


def describe(text):
    """Return a dict describing an address with prefix, e.g. 192.168.1.23/26.

    Raises ValueError for text that is not a valid IPv4 or IPv6 interface.
    """
    iface = ipaddress.ip_interface(text)
    net = iface.network
    usable = net.num_addresses - 2 if net.version == 4 and net.prefixlen < 31 else net.num_addresses
    hosts = list(net.hosts()) if net.num_addresses <= 2**16 else []
    return {
        "address": str(iface.ip),
        "network": str(net.network_address),
        "prefix": net.prefixlen,
        "netmask": str(net.netmask),
        "broadcast": str(net.broadcast_address) if net.version == 4 else "",
        "first_host": str(hosts[0]) if hosts else "",
        "last_host": str(hosts[-1]) if hosts else "",
        "usable_hosts": usable,
        "private": net.is_private,
    }


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
for text in ["192.168.1.23/26", "10.0.0.0/31"]:
    d = describe(text)
    print(d["network"], d["broadcast"], d["first_host"], d["last_host"], d["usable_hosts"])
try:
    describe("300.1.1.1/24")
except ValueError as exc:
    print("ValueError:", exc)

blocks.text: Next `src/netkit/output.py`. Every command produces a **list of dicts** (rows with the same keys) and this one function turns them into a table, CSV or JSON. The table widths are computed from the data, so no column is truncated.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/output.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Render a list of dict rows as a table, CSV or JSON."""
import csv
import io
import json


def render(rows, fmt="table"):
    """Return text for rows (a list of dicts with the same keys)."""
    if fmt == "json":
        return json.dumps(rows, indent=2)
    if not rows:
        return ""
    keys = list(rows[0])
    if fmt == "csv":
        buf = io.StringIO()
        writer = csv.DictWriter(buf, fieldnames=keys, lineterminator="\n")
        writer.writeheader()
        writer.writerows(rows)
        return buf.getvalue().rstrip("\n")
    widths = {k: max(len(k), *(len(str(r[k])) for r in rows)) for k in keys}
    head = "  ".join(k.upper().ljust(widths[k]) for k in keys)
    body = ["  ".join(str(r[k]).ljust(widths[k]) for k in keys).rstrip() for r in rows]
    return "\n".join([head.rstrip(), *body])


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
rows = [{"host": "192.168.1.1", "port": 22, "state": "open"},
        {"host": "192.168.1.10", "port": 8080, "state": "open"}]
print(render(rows))
print()
print(render(rows, "csv"))
print()
print(render(rows, "json"))

"""Command-line entry point (first version: subnet only)."""
import argparse
import sys

from netkit import __version__
from netkit.output import render
from netkit.subnet import describe


def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="netkit", description="Small network toolkit.")
    p.add_argument("--version", action="version", version=f"netkit {__version__}")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)
    s = sub.add_parser("subnet", help="describe CIDR networks")
    s.add_argument("cidr", nargs="+", help="e.g. 192.168.1.23/26")
    s.add_argument("-f", "--format", choices=["table", "json", "csv"], default="table")
    return p


def main(argv=None):
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    rows = [describe(c) for c in args.cidr]
    print(render(rows, args.format))
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

Step 3: ping and latency

`ping.py` runs the system `ping` as a child process and parses its summary. The parser is a separate pure function, `parse_ping`, so tests feed it saved text from both macOS and Linux and never need a network. The models go in their own file:

blocks.code:
"""Run the system ping and turn its text into numbers."""
import re
import subprocess
import sys

from netkit.models import PingStats

COUNTS_RE = re.compile(r"(\d+) packets transmitted, (\d+)(?: packets)? received")
LOSS_RE = re.compile(r"([\d.]+)% packet loss")
RTT_RE = re.compile(r"=\s*([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)/([\d.]+)")


def parse_ping(host, text):
    """Parse macOS or Linux ping output. Return PingStats, or None if no summary."""
    counts = COUNTS_RE.search(text)
    loss = LOSS_RE.search(text)
    if not counts or not loss:
        return None
    sent, received = int(counts.group(1)), int(counts.group(2))
    rtt = RTT_RE.search(text)
    lo, avg, hi = (float(x) for x in rtt.groups()) if rtt else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
    return PingStats(host, sent, received, float(loss.group(1)), lo, avg, hi)


def ping(host, count=4, timeout=10.0):
    """Ping host `count` times. Raises RuntimeError if ping is missing or fails to run."""
    cmd = ["ping", "-c", str(count), host]
    try:
        proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout + count)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        raise RuntimeError("the ping command was not found") from None
    except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
        raise RuntimeError(f"ping {host} timed out") from None
    stats = parse_ping(host, proc.stdout)
    if stats is None:
        message = (proc.stderr or proc.stdout).strip().splitlines()
        raise RuntimeError(message[-1] if message else f"no ping summary for {host}")
    return stats

blocks.text: Look at the three regular expressions. macOS prints `4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 25.0% packet loss`; Linux prints `4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss`. The `(?: packets)?` group makes the word optional. When every packet is lost there is no `round-trip` line, which the parser handles by returning zeros instead of failing.
**Checkpoint 3.** Try it directly from Python (the CLI gets the command in Step 7). Use a host you own, such as your router or `127.0.0.1`:

$ python3 -c "from netkit.ping import ping; print(ping('127.0.0.1', 3))"
PingStats(host='127.0.0.1', sent=3, received=3, loss_pct=0.0, min_ms=0.052, avg_ms=0.081, max_ms=0.126)

blocks.title: Why a child process and not raw ICMP

blocks.text: Sending ICMP from Python needs a raw socket and root. The system `ping` is already set up to do that safely (it is setuid or uses a privileged socket), so the program calls it with a **list** of arguments, never `shell=True`, and a `timeout`.
Step 4: dns

`dnscheck.py` has two ways to resolve. With no `--server`, it uses `socket.getaddrinfo`, the same resolution path as your browser, so it includes `/etc/hosts` and VPN rules. With `--server`, it runs `dig +short @server name type` and returns the answer lines. The `compare` function asks several servers and reports whether they agree, which is the heart of the DNS-hijack check from [DNS](#dns).

`+time` and `+tries=1` keep `dig` from retrying for 15 seconds on an unreachable resolver. `sorted` makes answer order irrelevant, because DNS round-robin changes the order of records between queries and would otherwise look like a disagreement.
**Checkpoint 3b.**

blocks.text: Step 5: the port scanner

`scan.py` is the scanner from [Python for networking](#py-net), reorganized so that it returns `ScanResult` objects and enforces the address rule in one place (`scan` raises `PermissionError` for public addresses unless `allow_public=True`).
Differences from `portscan.py`: it reads a short banner from open ports, it returns data instead of printing, and the safety check is a named function (`is_allowed`) the tests can call.

The command-line flag `--allow-public` exists for a host you own that sits on a public address, such as your own VPS, or one you have written permission to test. Do not remove the private-address check, and do not make `--allow-public` the default. Treat it like `rm -rf`: the safe default should need no thought.

blocks.text: Step 6: log analysis

`logs.py` is the combined-format parser from [Python files](#py-files), trimmed to what the CLI needs: it returns plain data, and it takes any iterable of lines, so a file, stdin and a test list all work. It runs in the page, so try it here first.

blocks.code:
# src/netkit/logs.py  (save everything above the "demo" line)
"""Summarize a combined-format web access log."""
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

LOG_RE = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<ip>\S+) \S+ \S+ \[(?P<time>[^\]]+)\] '
    r'"(?P<method>[A-Z]+) (?P<path>\S+)[^"]*" (?P<status>\d{3}) (?P<bytes>\d+|-)'
)


def parse_line(line):
    """Return a dict for one log line, or None if it does not match."""
    m = LOG_RE.match(line)
    if not m:
        return None
    rec = m.groupdict()
    rec["status"] = int(rec["status"])
    rec["bytes"] = 0 if rec["bytes"] == "-" else int(rec["bytes"])
    return rec


def summarize(lines, top=5):
    """One pass over any iterable of lines. Returns a dict of plain data."""
    clients, codes, sent = Counter(), Counter(), defaultdict(int)
    total = bad = 0
    for line in lines:
        if not line.strip():
            continue
        rec = parse_line(line)
        if rec is None:
            bad += 1
            continue
        total += 1
        clients[rec["ip"]] += 1
        codes[rec["status"]] += 1
        sent[rec["ip"]] += rec["bytes"]
    return {
        "requests": total,
        "unparsable": bad,
        "top_clients": clients.most_common(top),
        "status": sorted(codes.items()),
        "bytes_by_client": sorted(sent.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])[:top],
    }


# ---- demo: do not save below this line ----
SAMPLE = [
    '203.0.113.7 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "curl/8.7"',
    '203.0.113.7 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:09 +0000] "GET /missing HTTP/1.1" 404 - "-" "curl/8.7"',
    '198.51.100.8 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:15:00 +0000] "POST /api HTTP/1.1" 500 120 "-" "x"',
    "garbage",
]
s = summarize(SAMPLE, top=2)
print(s["requests"], s["unparsable"], s["top_clients"], s["status"])

blocks.text: Save the module part as `src/netkit/logs.py`. A line that does not match is counted in `unparsable` instead of crashing the run. The function also never holds the whole file in memory, only counters, so it handles a multi-gigabyte log.
Step 7: the full command line

Replace `src/netkit/cli.py` with the finished version. Read the structure before typing it: `build_parser` declares the interface, one `cmd_*` function per subcommand does the work and returns an exit status, and `main` ties them together with logging.

blocks.code:
"""Command-line entry point: netkit subnet|ping|dns|scan|logs."""
import argparse
import logging
import sys

from netkit import __version__, dnscheck, logs, ping as pingmod, scan as scanmod, subnet
from netkit.output import render

log = logging.getLogger("netkit")

OK, FAILED, USAGE = 0, 1, 2


def build_parser():
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="netkit", description="Small network toolkit.")
    p.add_argument("--version", action="version", version=f"netkit {__version__}")
    common = argparse.ArgumentParser(add_help=False)
    common.add_argument("-f", "--format", choices=["table", "json", "csv"], default="table")
    common.add_argument("-q", "--quiet", action="store_true", help="print nothing, use the exit status")
    common.add_argument("-v", "--verbose", action="store_true", help="log details to stderr")
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    s = sub.add_parser("subnet", parents=[common], help="describe CIDR networks")
    s.add_argument("cidr", nargs="*", help="e.g. 192.168.1.23/26 (reads stdin when omitted)")

    s = sub.add_parser("ping", parents=[common], help="latency and loss through the system ping")
    s.add_argument("host", nargs="+")
    s.add_argument("-c", "--count", type=int, default=4)
    s.add_argument("--max-avg", type=float, metavar="MS", help="exit 1 if the average RTT exceeds MS")

    s = sub.add_parser("dns", parents=[common], help="resolve names, optionally compare servers")
    s.add_argument("name", nargs="+")
    s.add_argument("-t", "--type", default="A", help="record type for --server queries")
    s.add_argument("-s", "--server", action="append", help="resolver to ask via dig (repeatable)")

    s = sub.add_parser("scan", parents=[common], help="TCP connect scan of your own hosts")
    s.add_argument("host")
    s.add_argument("-p", "--ports", default="1-1024")
    s.add_argument("--timeout", type=float, default=0.5)
    s.add_argument("--workers", type=int, default=100)
    s.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="also list closed ports")
    s.add_argument("--allow-public", action="store_true",
                   help="I own this host or have written permission to test it")

    s = sub.add_parser("logs", parents=[common], help="summarize a web access log")
    s.add_argument("file", nargs="?", default="-", help="log file, or - for stdin")
    s.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=5)
    return p


def say(args, text):
    if text and not args.quiet:
        print(text)


def cmd_subnet(args):
    items = args.cidr or [ln.strip() for ln in sys.stdin if ln.strip()]
    rows, bad = [], 0
    for item in items:
        try:
            rows.append(subnet.describe(item))
        except ValueError as exc:
            log.error("%s", exc)
            bad += 1
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return FAILED if bad else OK


def cmd_ping(args):
    rows, worst = [], OK
    for host in args.host:
        try:
            stats = pingmod.ping(host, args.count)
        except RuntimeError as exc:
            log.error("%s", exc)
            worst = FAILED
            continue
        rows.append(stats.as_row())
        if stats.received == 0 or (args.max_avg and stats.avg_ms > args.max_avg):
            worst = FAILED
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return worst


def cmd_dns(args):
    rows, agree = [], True
    try:
        for name in args.name:
            if args.server:
                found, same = dnscheck.compare(name, args.type, args.server)
                rows += found
                agree = agree and same
            else:
                rows.append({"name": name, "type": "A/AAAA", "server": "system",
                             "answer": " ".join(dnscheck.lookup_system(name))})
    except (LookupError, RuntimeError) as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return FAILED
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    if not agree:
        log.warning("servers disagree")
    return OK if agree else FAILED


def cmd_scan(args):
    try:
        ports = scanmod.parse_ports(args.ports)
        results = scanmod.scan(args.host, ports, args.timeout, args.workers, args.allow_public)
    except PermissionError as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    except (ValueError, OSError) as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    shown = [r for r in results if args.all or r.state == "open"]
    if shown or args.format != "table":
        say(args, render([r.as_row() for r in shown], args.format))
    else:
        say(args, f"no open ports among {len(ports)} scanned")
    return OK if any(r.state == "open" for r in results) else FAILED


def cmd_logs(args):
    try:
        if args.file == "-":
            summary = logs.summarize(sys.stdin, args.top)
        else:
            with open(args.file, encoding="utf-8", errors="replace") as fh:
                summary = logs.summarize(fh, args.top)
    except OSError as exc:
        log.error("%s", exc)
        return USAGE
    rows = [{"section": "requests", "key": "total", "value": summary["requests"]},
            {"section": "requests", "key": "unparsable", "value": summary["unparsable"]}]
    for ip, n in summary["top_clients"]:
        rows.append({"section": "top_clients", "key": ip, "value": n})
    for code, n in summary["status"]:
        rows.append({"section": "status", "key": code, "value": n})
    for ip, n in summary["bytes_by_client"]:
        rows.append({"section": "bytes_by_client", "key": ip, "value": n})
    say(args, render(rows, args.format))
    return OK if summary["requests"] else FAILED


COMMANDS = {"subnet": cmd_subnet, "ping": cmd_ping, "dns": cmd_dns, "scan": cmd_scan, "logs": cmd_logs}


def main(argv=None):
    args = build_parser().parse_args(argv)
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG if args.verbose else logging.WARNING,
                        format="netkit: %(levelname)s: %(message)s", stream=sys.stderr, force=True)
    try:
        return COMMANDS[args.command](args)
    except BrokenPipeError:
        return OK
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        return 130

blocks.text: Points to study:

items.text: `common` is a **parent parser** with `add_help=False`. Every subcommand inherits `-f`, `-q` and `-v` from it, so you declare them once.
`logging.basicConfig(..., stream=sys.stderr, force=True)` sends diagnostics to stderr. `log.error(...)` replaces the traceback you saw in Step 2.
`cmd_scan` returns `USAGE` (2) for refused targets and bad ports, `FAILED` (1) when no port is open, and `OK` (0) otherwise.
`except BrokenPipeError` handles `netkit ... | head -1`: when `head` exits early, the next `print` would raise. Returning cleanly is the correct behaviour for a filter.
`args.cidr or [... sys.stdin ...]` lets `subnet` read one CIDR per line from a pipe.

Step 8: tests

A test is a small program that fails loudly when the code is wrong. Install is already done (`.[dev]` included pytest). The tests have three flavours: pure functions with plain `assert`, the scanner against a **real loopback listener** in a thread (a socket test with no external network), and the CLI through `cli.main([...])` with `capsys` capturing output.

blocks.name: pytest.monkeypatch
blocks.sum: Temporarily replace an attribute, function or environment variable inside one test.
blocks.syntax: def test_x(monkeypatch, capsys): monkeypatch.setattr(target, value) ; monkeypatch.setenv(name, value)

how.text: `monkeypatch` is a **fixture**: pytest creates it for any test function that names it as a parameter, and undoes every change when the test ends. `capsys` is another: it captures what the code wrote to stdout and stderr, available through `capsys.readouterr()`. Replacing `sys.stdin` with `io.StringIO("...")` is how you test a command that reads a pipe.

examples.desc: Run one test file, verbose
List test names only

blocks.name: pytest.mark.parametrize
blocks.sum: Run one test function once for each of several inputs.

how.text: Each value becomes its own test case with its own pass or fail line, so a failure on `"70000"` does not hide the result for `"0"`. Pass several parameter names as one comma-separated string, with a list of tuples.

import pytest

from netkit.subnet import describe


def test_slash26():
    d = describe("192.168.1.23/26")
    assert d["network"] == "192.168.1.0"
    assert d["broadcast"] == "192.168.1.63"
    assert d["usable_hosts"] == 62
    assert d["first_host"] == "192.168.1.1"
    assert d["last_host"] == "192.168.1.62"


def test_slash31_has_two_usable():
    assert describe("10.0.0.0/31")["usable_hosts"] == 2


def test_private_flag():

    assert describe("8.8.8.9/24")["private"] is False

MAC = """PING example.com (93.184.216.34): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 93.184.216.34: icmp_seq=0 ttl=56 time=11.4 ms

--- example.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 25.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.2/12.8/15.0/1.6 ms
"""

LINUX = """--- example.com ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3004ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 11.2/12.8/15.0/1.6 ms
"""


def test_mac_format():

    assert (s.sent, s.received, s.loss_pct) == (4, 3, 25.0)
    assert s.avg_ms == 12.8


def test_linux_format():

    assert s.max_ms == 15.0


def test_total_loss_has_no_rtt_line():

def test_garbage_returns_none():

GOOD = '203.0.113.7 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 5120 "-" "curl/8.7"'

import pytest

from netkit import cli


def test_subnet_json(capsys):

    assert len(capsys.readouterr().out.strip().splitlines()) == 3   # header + 2 rows


def test_subnet_bad_input_exit_1(capsys):

    assert "nonsense" in capsys.readouterr().err


def test_quiet_prints_nothing(capsys):
    assert cli.main(["subnet", "-q", "10.0.0.0/8"]) == 0
    assert capsys.readouterr().out == ""


def test_scan_refuses_public(capsys):
    assert cli.main(["scan", "93.184.216.34", "-p", "80"]) == 2
    assert "not loopback or private" in capsys.readouterr().err


def test_logs_from_stdin(monkeypatch, capsys):
    line = '192.0.2.1 - - [07/Oct/2026:09:14:08 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 10 "-" "x"\n'
    monkeypatch.setattr("sys.stdin", io.StringIO(line))
    assert cli.main(["logs", "-f", "json"]) == 0
    assert json.loads(capsys.readouterr().out)[0]["value"] == 1


def test_missing_subcommand_is_usage_error():
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit) as exc:
        cli.main([])
    assert exc.value.code == 2

blocks.text: Two details are deliberate. The subnet test uses `8.8.8.9/24` as a public example because Python (correctly) treats the documentation range `203.0.113.0/24` as private-use. And the scan test for a closed port opens a socket on port 0, reads the port the kernel chose, and closes it again, which guarantees a closed port with no guessing.

In `subnet.py` change `net.num_addresses - 2` to `net.num_addresses - 1`. Run `pytest -q` and read the output: pytest shows the assertion, both values, and the line. Fix the code, not the test. This is the whole point of the suite: the next time you touch `describe`, you will know within a second whether you broke it.
Step 9: README and release check
A README answers four questions: what is this, how do I install it, how do I use it, how do I run the tests. Write `README.md`:

blocks.code:
# netkit

Small network toolkit: subnet maths, ping, DNS, TCP port scan and web-log summary.

## Install

    python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
    pip install -e '.[dev]'

## Use

    netkit subnet 192.168.1.23/26
    netkit ping 192.168.1.1 -c 3 --max-avg 50
    netkit dns example.com -s 1.1.1.1 -s 9.9.9.9
    netkit scan 127.0.0.1 -p 1-10000
    netkit logs access.log --top 5 -f json

Results go to stdout, diagnostics to stderr. Exit status: 0 good, 1 bad result, 2 misuse.
`-f` selects table, json or csv; `-q` prints nothing.

## Safety

`scan` refuses addresses that are not loopback, private or link-local unless you pass
`--allow-public`. Scan only machines you own or have written permission to test.

## Test

    pytest -q

blocks.text: How to review your own code
Reading your own code a day later is a skill. Take 20 minutes, print or open each file, and score it against this rubric. Fix anything below a 2.

head: Area
rows: some commands crash on bad input
handles bad input, exit codes inconsistent
every failure path has a message and the right exit code
only `cli.py` prints, reads argv and exits
guard exists but can be skipped silently
guard default-on, bypass explicit and documented
bad input, boundaries (/31, empty log, 0 packets) and one real socket
a stranger can guess what a function does
catches the specific exception and logs why

blocks.text: Then do the cold-read test: open `cli.py` and explain aloud what `netkit logs -` does, step by step, without running it. Wherever you hesitate, the code is unclear. Add a comment or rename something. Then use a linter once: `pip install ruff && ruff check src tests` (see [Python modules](#py-modules)) and look at what it finds.
Recipe: add a subcommand
Adding `netkit hash FILE` (print the SHA-256 of a file) shows how little the structure asks of you. The same six moves apply to every follow-on project below.

items.text: **Write the pure function first**, in a new module, returning data: `def digest(path): ...` returning `{"file": path, "sha256": hexstring}`. Read the file in 64 KiB chunks with `hashlib.sha256().update(chunk)` so a large file does not fill memory.
**Test it**: create a file under pytest's `tmp_path` fixture containing `b"abc"` and assert the known digest `ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad`.
**Declare the interface** in `build_parser`: `s = sub.add_parser("hash", parents=[common], help="SHA-256 of files")` and `s.add_argument("file", nargs="+")`.
**Write `cmd_hash(args)`**: call the function for each file, collect rows, `say(args, render(rows, args.format))`, return `OK`, or `USAGE` with a `log.error` when a file cannot be read.
**Register it** in the `COMMANDS` dictionary.
**Test the command** with `cli.main(["hash", str(path), "-f", "json"])` and `capsys`.

blocks.text: Compare your result with the system tool: `shasum -a 256 FILE` must print the same digest. If the two disagree, one of them is wrong, and `shasum` is not the one to suspect first.

Implement `hash` in 20 minutes. If step 3 raises `error: argument command: invalid choice`, you forgot to reinstall or to register the command. Use `git diff` before committing and read your own change as a reviewer would.
Follow-on projects
Each of these reuses the same ideas. Pick one, write its contract (inputs, outputs, exit codes) before any code, and add it to `netkit` as a new subcommand or as a separate tool.

head: Project
Spec
Stretch goals
rows: `netkit tail FILE --alert 'status=5\d\d' --every 10`: follow a growing file (like `tail -f`), count matches per window, print a line to stderr when the count passes a threshold
handle log rotation (inode change); send a macOS notification with `osascript -e 'display notification ...'`
`netkit watch URLS.txt --interval 30`: check each URL with `http.client`, record status and time in SQLite (`sqlite3`), print a summary of the last hour
percentile response times; mark a site down only after 3 failures; `--since 24h` report
`netkit arpwatch`: run `arp -an` every 30 seconds, keep a JSON file of known MAC addresses, print new devices and IP changes
resolve MAC vendors from an OUI table; flag one MAC claiming two IPs
`netkit dns --server` already compares resolvers. Add a watch mode that checks a list of names every few minutes against 3 resolvers and logs any disagreement
ignore CDN names that legitimately differ; compare TTLs; alert on private IPs returned for public names
serve `netkit` results over HTTP with `http.server`: `GET /subnet?cidr=10.0.0.0/8` returns JSON

task.text: In a brand-new virtual environment outside the project (`/tmp/nk-fresh`), install the project with `pip install ~/lab/netkit` (no `-e`) and run `netkit --version`. Then run `pip show -f netkit | head -20` and find where the files were copied.

hints: A normal install copies the package into `site-packages` instead of linking to your source folder.

python3 -m venv /tmp/nk-fresh
/tmp/nk-fresh/bin/pip install ~/lab/netkit
/tmp/nk-fresh/bin/netkit --version
/tmp/nk-fresh/bin/pip show -f netkit | head -20

why.text: The editable install points at your source, so a file you forgot to list in `pyproject.toml` still works for you. A normal install copies only what is declared, which is how you discover that gap before somebody else does.

blocks.title: Linux ping format

task.text: Write `parse_summary(text)` returning `(sent, received)` as ints from either macOS (`4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, ...`) or Linux (`4 packets transmitted, 4 received, ...`) text.

why.text: An optional non-capturing group, `(?: packets)?`, absorbs the word that only one platform prints. Tests with saved text from each platform keep both formats working.

blocks.check:
mac = "4 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 25.0% packet loss"
linux = "4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3004ms"
assert parse_summary(mac) == (4, 3), "macOS format"
assert parse_summary(linux) == (4, 4), "Linux format"

blocks.title: Break a test on purpose

task.text: In `subnet.py` change `net.num_addresses - 2` to `net.num_addresses - 1`. Run `pytest -q`, read which tests fail and what values they report, restore the line, and run `pytest -q` again until it is green.

hints: `pytest -q -x` stops at the first failure; `pytest -v` shows each test name.
blocks.solution:
sed -i '' 's/num_addresses - 2/num_addresses - 1/' src/netkit/subnet.py
pytest -q
sed -i '' 's/num_addresses - 1/num_addresses - 2/' src/netkit/subnet.py
pytest -q

why.text: A failing test names the function, the expected value and the actual value. Fixing the code, never the test, is the discipline that makes a suite worth having. Note the BSD `sed -i ''` form on macOS.

blocks.verify: pytest -q | tail -1 | grep -q passed && echo OK

blocks.title: Add --max-loss to ping

task.text: Add `--max-loss PCT` to the `ping` subcommand: exit status 1 when any host's `loss_pct` exceeds the value. Add a test in `tests/test_cli.py` that monkeypatches `netkit.ping.ping` to return a fixed `PingStats` with 50 percent loss and checks that `cli.main(["ping", "x", "--max-loss", "10", "-q"])` returns 1.

hints: In `cli.py`, `pingmod.ping` is looked up when called, so `monkeypatch.setattr("netkit.ping.ping", fake)` takes effect.
Construct `PingStats("x", 4, 2, 50.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0)` for the fake.
blocks.solution:
# cli.py, in the ping subparser:
s.add_argument("--max-loss", type=float, metavar="PCT", help="exit 1 if loss exceeds PCT")
# in cmd_ping, extend the failure test:
if stats.received == 0 or (args.max_avg and stats.avg_ms > args.max_avg) \
        or (args.max_loss is not None and stats.loss_pct > args.max_loss):
    worst = FAILED
# tests/test_cli.py
def test_ping_max_loss(monkeypatch):
    from netkit.models import PingStats
    monkeypatch.setattr("netkit.ping.ping", lambda host, count=4: PingStats("x", 4, 2, 50.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0))
    assert cli.main(["ping", "x", "--max-loss", "10", "-q"]) == 1

why.text: Testing the CLI without a network works by replacing the one function that touches the network. The same trick tests a DNS failure, a timeout or a flapping host, which you could never reproduce on demand with real pings.

blocks.title: Use netkit in a pipeline

task.text: Using only `netkit` and standard tools, print the three client addresses that transferred the most bytes in `~/lab/access.log`, one per line, with the byte count. Use CSV output and `awk`, `sort`, `head`.

hints: Rows with section `bytes_by_client` carry the data; columns are section, key, value.
blocks.solution: netkit logs ~/lab/access.log --top 100 -f csv | awk -F, '$1=="bytes_by_client" {print $2, $3}' | sort -k2 -nr | head -3

why.text: Machine-readable output is what lets a small tool join a pipeline. `--top 100` widens the limit so `sort` sees every client, and the CSV `section` column makes `awk` filtering a one-liner.

questions.q: Why does `cli.py` return an integer from `main()` instead of calling `sys.exit` inside each command?

options.text: Commands become easy to test by comparing the return value, and one place decides the process exit
Python requires main to return an integer

questions.why: Functions that return a status can be called from tests like any other function. `sys.exit(main())` at the entry point converts the value for the shell.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in `scan.py` rather than `cli.py`?

options.text: Opening TCP connections and returning `ScanResult` objects

questions.why: The doing layer returns data. Presentation, argument handling and logging belong to the command-line layer.

questions.q: `pip install -e .[dev]` fails in zsh with `no matches found`. What is the fix?
questions.why: `[dev]` is a glob pattern to zsh. Single quotes pass it through unchanged.

questions.q: What does exit status 1 mean in netkit's contract?

options.text: The command ran and the answer is bad (no open ports, loss above threshold, bad input line)

questions.why: Status 2 is for misuse or refusal; 1 reports a negative result, as `grep` does when nothing matches.

questions.q: Why does the CLI test replace `sys.stdin` with `io.StringIO` instead of piping real input?

options.text: The code reads `sys.stdin` as a file-like object, so a fake file exercises the same path with no shell involved

questions.why: Because pipes and files expose the same file-like interface, a `StringIO` stands in for a pipe.

chapters.title: Capstone: a LAN Dashboard, Front to Back
chapters.sub: Build, test, debug and share a full-stack app: Express API, JSON file store, TCP port checks, XML and RSS feeds, and a plain-JavaScript dashboard
goals: Structure a Node project so the API, the storage, the network checks and the feeds can each be tested alone
Build a REST API with validation errors a form can display, backed by a JSON file written atomically
Check device ports with net.Socket and a timeout, only on your own LAN, and publish changes as events and RSS
Write a dashboard front end from semantic HTML, a CSS grid with dark and light themes, and three JavaScript modules
Test the API with node --test against a real server on a random port, and find a planted bug with DevTools
Run the app safely on your Mac and, deliberately, on your LAN

blocks.text: You will build `lan-dashboard`, a small web application that watches the devices on your home network. A Node server keeps the device list in `data/devices.json`, checks every 30 seconds whether each device answers on its TCP port, records changes as events, and offers them as JSON, an XML export and an RSS feed. The browser side is one HTML page, one stylesheet and three ES modules, with no framework and no build step: a grid of status cards, filters with a debounced search, a form that shows the server's validation messages next to the right field, live polling with a visible "last updated" time, and a banner when the server is unreachable.

Every part comes from an earlier chapter. The port check is the TCP connect test from [Python for networking](#py-net) and [the netkit capstone](#capstone), with the same safety rule. The API follows [HTTP and TLS](#http) and [Node.js](#node). The XML follows [XML and friends](#xml). The page uses [HTML](#html), [CSS](#css), [the DOM](#dom) and [DevTools](#devtools). Plan three hours, commit after each step, and run the tests whenever they exist.
What you are building

blocks.code:
Safari / Chrome / phone                          Node process (server.js)
 ┌────────────────────────────┐   HTTP    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ index.html  style.css      │◀─────────▶│ express.static(public/)                          │
 │ app.js  ── state, events,  │  GET /    │                                                  │
 │            polling 10 s    │           │ /api router (src/app.js)                         │
 │ render.js ─ DOM from data  │  JSON     │   validate.js ──▶ 422 { error, fields }          │
 │ api.js ──── fetch wrapper ─┼──────────▶│   store.js ───▶ data/devices.json (atomic write) │
 └────────────────────────────┘  /api/*   │   monitor.js ──▶ check.js ── net.connect ──┐     │
        ▲  RSS reader, curl, xmllint      │      │ 'change' events                     │     │
        └──────── /feed.rss  /api/devices.xml ◀── feeds.js (escaped XML)               │     │
                                          └────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────┘
                                                           TCP SYN to 192.168.1.x:port ▼  your LAN only

blocks.text: The rule that keeps it testable is the same as in the Python capstone: **modules return data; only the edges do I/O.** `validate.js` and `feeds.js` are pure functions. `store.js` owns the file. `check.js` owns sockets. `monitor.js` schedules checks and emits events. `app.js` turns HTTP into calls to those modules and back. `server.js` reads the configuration and starts listening. The tests start the app with a throwaway data file and a free port, so they never touch your real data or a running server.
The API contract

head: Method and path
Success
Errors
rows: 400 broken JSON, 409 name taken, 413 too large, 415 not JSON, 422 invalid fields

blocks.text: A device is `{ id, name, ip, port, type, notes }`. Validation errors come back as `422 {"error":"validation failed","fields":{"ip":"..."}}`, one message per field, which is the shape a form needs. The practice server from the earlier chapters answers the same paths with a slightly simpler device shape (`online` instead of `status`), which lets you try a reduced front end right now.
The layout

~/lab/dashboard/
├── package.json        "type": "module", scripts start / dev / test, express ^5
├── server.js           config from env and .env, listen, start the monitor, clean shutdown

├── src/
│   ├── app.js          Express: routes, static files, feeds, error handler
│   ├── http-app.js     the same API on node:http (Step 11, optional)
│   ├── validate.js     the rules for a device (pure)
│   ├── feeds.js        escaped XML and RSS builders (pure)
│   ├── store.js        in-memory Map + atomic JSON file writes

blocks.text: The real version adds edit, per-device checks, field-level errors, a theme switch and offline handling, and it talks to your own server instead of the practice one.
Design decisions
Express, with a no-dependency variant

The API needs routing with parameters, JSON bodies with a size limit, static files with correct types and traversal protection, and one error funnel. Express provides all four, well tested, so the code you write is about devices. The cost is a dependency tree of about 65 packages to keep updated with `npm audit`. [Node.js](#node/express) built the same features by hand on `node:http`, and Step 11 does it again for this API, reusing every module except `app.js`, and passes the identical test suite. Read it after the Express version: the difference is exactly what the framework does.
A JSON file, written atomically

A home LAN has tens of devices, one server process and a few writes per day, so a database would be ceremony. The store keeps devices in a `Map` and rewrites the whole file after each change. Two details make it safe. Writes are **atomic**: the new content goes to a temporary file that is then `rename`d over the old one, and on the same volume `rename(2)` replaces the directory entry in one step, so a crash leaves either the old file or the new one, never half of each. Writes are **serialised** through a promise chain, so two requests in the same millisecond cannot interleave their bytes. The limit is just as clear: one process only. Two servers on the same file would overwrite each other's changes.
The server validates; the page only helps

The form has `required` and `maxlength`, but it carries `novalidate`, and every message you see comes from the server's 422 response. Anything a browser sends can be forged with `curl`, so the server's rules are the only ones that count, and having one source of messages means the page and the API never disagree. Client-side checks are a convenience you can add later, never a replacement.
Polling with a version number

The page asks `/api/status` every 10 seconds. That answer is small: counts, per-device states, a `version` that grows with every change to the device list, and the id of the latest event. When the version is unchanged, the page repaints badges in place; when it changed (someone added a device from another tab or with `curl`), it reloads the list. This is the idea behind HTTP's `ETag` revalidation, done by hand. Polling stops while the tab is hidden. Server-Sent Events or WebSockets would push changes instead; with ten devices and a 30-second check interval, polling is simpler and good enough.
Safety: your LAN only

`check.js` opens a TCP connection, which is a (very small) port scan. The rules from [Ports and sockets](#ports) apply: probe only machines you own or may test. The validator accepts only private, loopback and link-local addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 127/8, 169.254/16), and `checkDevice` checks again before every connection, in case someone edits `devices.json` by hand. The checker connects and immediately closes: no data is sent, nothing is retried in a loop, and the sweep runs at most every 30 seconds.

blocks.text: Seed the store with your LAN. The first entry is the dashboard itself, so at least one device is always up; change the others to your router, Pi, NAS and printer, with a port each one really listens on (80 for a router's admin page, 22 for SSH, 445 for SMB, 631 for IPP printing):
**Checkpoint 1.** `npm ls` shows `express@5.x`, and `git status` does not list `node_modules/`. Commit: `git add -A && git commit -m "project skeleton"`.
Step 2: The rules for a device

`validate.js` is pure: data in, data out, no I/O. `validateDevice` returns either a clean device (trimmed name, default port 80, type `other`, unknown fields dropped) or one message per bad field. Two details deserve a look. Octets with leading zeros are refused, because some parsers read `010` as octal 8, so `192.168.010.5` means different hosts to different programs. And a port may arrive as a number or a digit string (from a form), but `true` or `2.5` are refused even though `Number(true)` is 1.
The LAN rule is easy to get subtly wrong, so try it here before reading on. Which of these are LAN addresses?

`172.16.0.0/12` ends at 172.31.255.255, so `172.32.0.5` is public. `100.64.0.0/10` is carrier-grade NAT space from [Addressing](#addressing): private to your ISP, not to you, so the dashboard refuses it.
Step 3: XML and RSS without injection

Building XML by gluing strings together is safe only if every value is escaped, every time. `feeds.js` makes forgetting impossible: `el(name, attrs, ...children)` escapes every attribute and every child that is not itself an `el()` result. A device note such as `R&D <lab>` becomes `R&D <lab>` whatever path it takes. XML 1.0 also forbids most control characters outright, even escaped, so `escapeXml` drops them; otherwise one note containing `\u0001` would make the whole export unparseable. This is the server-side counterpart of building XML with DOM methods in [XML and friends](#xml).
`pubDate` uses `toUTCString()`, which produces the RFC 822 date format RSS 2.0 expects (`Sun, 25 Oct 2026 12:22:37 GMT`).

blocks.text: Step 4: The store

The store is a factory function returning an object of closures, so `devices`, `nextId` and the write queue are private without a class. `version` is exposed through a getter so callers can read it but not set it. `nextId` is stored in the file instead of computed from the highest id, so a deleted device's id is never reused: an RSS reader or a bookmark that still points at `/api/devices/4` gets a 404, never a different device.

blocks.name: fs.rename()
blocks.sum: Rename or move a file; on the same volume it atomically replaces an existing target.

how.text: Wraps `rename(2)`. When both paths are on the same file system (APFS volume), the kernel swaps the directory entry in one step: every reader opens either the complete old file or the complete new one. That makes "write to a temp file, then rename" the standard way to update a file safely. Across volumes it fails with `EXDEV`, so keep the temporary file next to the target, as `store.js` does with `devices.json.<pid>.tmp`.

examples.desc: Replace a file atomically
Watch the inode change on each save (a new file replaced the old one)
examples.code: ls -i data/devices.json; curl -s -X DELETE localhost:3000/api/devices/5; ls -i data/devices.json

gotchas: `writeFile` straight onto the real file truncates it first; a crash or a full disk at that moment leaves an empty or partial `devices.json`.

blocks.text: Step 5: Port checks and the monitor

`check.js` is the Node version of `connect_ex` from [Python for networking](#py-net): open a TCP connection, wait for the handshake, close at once. The three outcomes map to three states you will see in the dashboard: the handshake completes (`up`), the host answers with a reset because nothing listens (`down`, `ECONNREFUSED`, typically within milliseconds), or nothing answers before the timeout (`down`, `ETIMEDOUT`, after 1.5 s), which usually means the host is off, firewalled or not at that address.

blocks.name: net.connect()
blocks.sum: Open a TCP connection; with setTimeout and the connect, timeout and error events it becomes a port check.
blocks.syntax: const socket = net.connect({ host, port })    socket.setTimeout(ms)    socket.once('connect' | 'timeout' | 'error', fn)    socket.destroy()

how.text: Returns a `net.Socket` immediately and starts the three-way handshake in the background. `'connect'` fires when the handshake completes. `'error'` fires with `err.code` such as `ECONNREFUSED` (an RST came back), `EHOSTUNREACH` or `ENETUNREACH`. `setTimeout(ms)` makes the socket emit `'timeout'` after that long without activity, including while connecting, but it does not close anything: you must call `destroy()`. Wrapping the three events in one promise that settles on the first gives a check that always finishes.

examples.desc: Is SSH listening on the Pi?
Compare with BSD netcat from the Ports chapter

gotchas: Without `destroy()` after a timeout, the socket keeps trying in the background and holds a file descriptor until the operating system gives up, which takes over a minute on macOS.

blocks.text: The monitor is an `EventEmitter`, as in [Node.js](#node/streams). It keeps the latest result per device, runs a sweep of all devices in parallel, and starts the next sweep only after the previous one finished (a `setTimeout` loop, never `setInterval`, so slow sweeps cannot pile up). It emits `'change'` when a device's state changes, except for a device's first `up`, so a fresh start produces alerts only for what is actually down.
Step 6: The Express app and the server

`createApp` builds everything and returns it unstarted: the Express app, an `http.Server` wrapping it, the store, the monitor and the event list. `server.js` decides when to listen and when to start sweeping; the tests do neither sweep nor bind to 3000.

tokens.exp: set the status code: Created
set the Location header to the new resource's URL
serialise the device plus its current check result, set Content-Type and Content-Length, end the response

blocks.text: Read `parseBody` once more: it is the single place where a request body becomes a device, and it answers 415, 422 and 409 in that order. The order matters. A form-encoded body would otherwise reach validation as `undefined` and produce a misleading "body must be a JSON object". The `/feed.rss` route builds absolute links from the `Host` header; every value still goes through `escapeXml`, so a forged header cannot inject markup.

blocks.name: express.Router()
blocks.sum: A mini application with its own middleware and routes, mounted under a path prefix.
blocks.syntax: const api = express.Router(); api.get('/devices', fn); app.use('/api', api)

how.text: A router is a middleware stack you can mount: inside it, paths are relative to the mount point, so `api.get('/devices')` answers `/api/devices`. Routers keep a large app in readable pieces (one per resource) and let middleware apply to one prefix only, such as authentication for `/api` but not for static files. Register specific paths before parameterised ones when they could overlap.

Tests inside one file run in order, which the "changing devices" suite relies on (it creates `pi`, then the events test expects an `added` event). That is a deliberate trade: shorter tests that share one server, at the price of an order dependency you must respect when adding tests.
Step 8: The page: semantic HTML and a themed CSS grid

The HTML is the structure from [HTML](#html): a `header` with the summary and the "last updated" `<time>`, a `main` with the device `section` and an `aside` holding the form and the events, a `<template>` for one card, and labels tied to inputs with `for`/`id`. Every error paragraph is linked to its input with `aria-describedby`, so a screen reader reads the server's message when the field gets focus. The script is `type="module"`, so it is deferred automatically and can `import` the other two files; that is also why the page must come from `http://localhost:3000` and not `file://`.
